That he should be diligent and vigorous in his duty: <hi type="italic">I will lift up my hands to thy commandments,</hi> which denotes not only a vehement desire towards them (<reference osisRef="Ps.143.6">Ps. cxliii. 6</reference>)—"I will lay hold of them as one afraid of missing them, or letting them go;" but a close application of mind to the observance of them—"I will lay my hands to the command, not only to praise it, but practise it; nay, I will lift up my hands to it, that is, I will put forth all the strength I have to do it." The hands that hang down, through sloth and discouragement, shall be lifted up, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.12">Heb. xii. 12</reference>. (5.) That he should be thoughtful and considerate in his duty (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.48">v. 48</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I will meditate in thy statutes,</hi> not only entertain myself with thinking of them as matters of speculation, but contrive how I may observe them in the best manner." By <hi type="italic">this</hi> it will appear that we truly love God's commandments, if we apply both our minds and our hands to them.
entries.c260e5b2d9c6f540768185a3f15586e791bff3c9: <div eID="gen12708" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">7. ZAIN.</title> <div sID="gen12709" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">49</hi> Remember the word unto thy servant, upon which thou hast caused me to hope. <div eID="gen12709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12710" type="x-p"/> Two things David here pleads with God in prayer for that mercy and grace which he hoped for, according to the word, by which his requests were guided:—1. That God had given him the promise on which he hoped: "Lord, I desire no more than that thou wouldst <hi type="italic">remember thy word unto thy servant,</hi> and <hi type="italic">do as thou hast said;</hi>" see <reference osisRef="1Chr.17.23">1 Chron. xvii. 23</reference>. "Thou art wise, and therefore wilt perfect what thou hast purposed, and not change thy counsel. Thou art faithful, and therefore wilt perform what thou hast promised, and not break thy word." Those that make God's promises their portion may with humble boldness make them their plea. "Lord, is not that the word which thou hast spoken; and wilt thou not make it good?" <reference osisRef="Gen.32.9">Gen. xxxii. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.33.12">Exod. xxxiii. 12</reference>. 2. That God, who had given him the promise in the word, had by his grace wrought in him a hope in that promise and enabled him to depend upon it, and had raised his expectations of great things from it. Has God kindled in us desires towards spiritual blessings more than towards any temporal good things, and will he not be so kind as to satisfy those desires? Has he filled us with hopes of those blessings, and will he not be so just as to accomplish these hopes? He that did by his Spirit work faith in us will, according to our faith, work for us, and will not disappoint us.
entries.f719dc5d9e6243f4ded3a304fbc700e5fa9a7512: <div eID="gen12710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12711" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">50</hi> This <hi type="italic">is</hi> my comfort in my affliction: for thy word hath quickened me. <div eID="gen12711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12712" type="x-p"/> Here is David's experience of benefit by the word. 1. As a means of his sanctification: "<hi type="italic">Thy word has quickened me.</hi> It made me alive when I was dead in sin; it has many a time made me lively when I was dead in duty; it has quickened me to that which is good when I was backward and averse to it, and it has quickened me in that which is good when I was cold and indifferent." 2. Therefore as a means of his consolation when he was in affliction and needed something to support him: "Because thy word has quickened me at other times, it has comforted me then." The word of God has much in it that speaks <hi type="italic">comfort in affliction;</hi> but those only may apply it to themselves who have experienced in some measure the quickening power of the word. If through grace it make us holy, there is enough in it to make us easy, in all conditions, under all events.
entries.8322e23082636a1e2e2a837c9c21c2180649a8c2: <div eID="gen12712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12713" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">51</hi> The proud have had me greatly in derision: <hi type="italic">yet</hi> have I not declined from thy law. <div eID="gen12713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12714" type="x-p"/> David here tells us, and it will be of use to us to know it, 1. That he had been jeered for his religion. Though he was a man of honour, a man of great prudence, and had done eminent services to his country, yet, because he was a devout conscientious man, <hi type="italic">the proud had him greatly in derision;</hi> they ridiculed him, bantered him, and did all they could to expose him to contempt; they laughed at him for his praying, and called it <hi type="italic">cant,</hi> for his seriousness, and called it <hi type="italic">mopishness,</hi> for his strictness, and called it <hi type="italic">needless preciseness.</hi> They were the proud that sat in the scorner's seat and valued themselves on so doing. 2. That yet he had not been jeered out of his religion: "They have done all they could to make me quit it for shame, but none of these things move me: <hi type="italic">I have not declined from thy law</hi> for all this; but, <hi type="italic">if this be to be vile</hi>" (as he said when Michal had him greatly in derision), "<hi type="italic">I will be yet more vile.</hi>" He not only had not quite forsaken the law, but had not so much as declined from it. We must never shrink from any duty, nor let slip an opportunity of doing good, for fear of the reproach of men, or their revilings. The traveller goes on his way though the dogs bark at him. Those can bear but little for Christ that cannot bear a hard word for him.
entries.3b81214d41d8d80f0c16f32dcd373b561f3a3ad2: <div eID="gen12714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12715" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">52</hi> I remembered thy judgments of old, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> ; and have comforted myself. <div eID="gen12715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12716" type="x-p"/> When David was derided for his godliness he not only held fast his integrity, but, 1. He comforted himself. He not only bore reproach, but bore it cheerfully. It did not disturb his peace, nor break in upon the repose of his spirit in God. It was a comfort to him to think that it was for God's sake that he bore reproach, and that his worst enemies could find <hi type="italic">no occasion against him, save only in the matter of his God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.6.5">Dan. vi. 5</reference>. Those that are derided for their adherence to God's law may comfort themselves with this, that <hi type="italic">the reproach of Christ</hi> will prove, in the end, <hi type="italic">greater riches</hi> to them <hi type="italic">than the treasures of Egypt.</hi> 2. That which he comforted himself with was the remembrance of God's <hi type="italic">judgments of old,</hi> the providences of God concerning his people formerly, both in mercy to them and in justice against their persecutors. God's judgments of old, in our own early days and in the days of our fathers, are to be remembered by us for our comfort and encouragement in the way of God, for he is still the same.
entries.e1d507de2e6e903bf31bf37a0ede8595a143bedb: <div eID="gen12716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12717" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">53</hi> Horror hath taken hold upon me because of the wicked that forsake thy law. <div eID="gen12717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12718" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The character of wicked people; he means those that are openly and grossly wicked: <hi type="italic">They forsake thy law.</hi> Every sin is a transgression of the law, but a course and way of wilful and avowed sin is downright forsaking it and throwing it off. 2. The impression which the wickedness of the wicked made upon David; it frightened him, it put him into an amazement. He trembled to think of the dishonour thereby done to God, the gratification thereby given to Satan, and the mischiefs thereby done to the souls of men. He dreaded the consequences of it both to the sinners themselves (and cried out, <hi type="italic">O gather not my soul with sinners! let my enemy be as the wicked</hi>) and to the interests of God's kingdom among men, which he was afraid would be thereby sunk and ruined. He does not say, "<hi type="italic">Horror has taken hold on me</hi> because of their cruel designs against me," but "because of the contempt they put on God and his law." Sin is a monstrous horrible thing in the eyes of all that are sanctified, <reference osisRef="Jer.5.30">Jer. v. 30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.23.14">xxiii. 14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.6.10">Hos. vi. 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.2.12">Jer. ii. 12</reference>.
entries.ce366c9614607e6b013c8191bdb066e226d6b797: <div eID="gen12718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12719" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">54</hi> Thy statutes have been my songs in the house of my pilgrimage. <div eID="gen12719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12720" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. David's state and condition; he was <hi type="italic">in the house of</hi> his <hi type="italic">pilgrimage,</hi> which may be understood either as his peculiar trouble (he was often tossed and hurried, and forced to fly) or as his lot in common with all. This world is the house of our pilgrimage, the house in which we are pilgrims; it is our tabernacle; it is our inn. We must confess ourselves <hi type="italic">strangers and pilgrims upon earth,</hi> who are not at home here, nor must be here long. Even David's palace is but the house of his pilgrimage. 2. His comfort in this state: "<hi type="italic">Thy statutes have been my songs,</hi> with which I here entertain myself," as travellers are wont to divert the thoughts of their weariness, and take off something of the tediousness of their journey, by singing a pleasant song now and then. David was the sweet singer of Israel, and here we are told whence he fetched his songs; they were all borrowed from the word of God. God's statutes were as familiar to him as the songs which a man is accustomed to sing; and he conversed with them in his pilgrimage-solitudes. They were as pleasant to him as songs, and <hi type="italic">put gladness into his heart</hi> more than those have that <hi type="italic">chant to the sound of the viol,</hi> <reference osisRef="Amos.6.5">Amos vi. 5</reference>. <hi type="italic">Is any afflicted</hi> then? Let him sing over God's statutes, and try if he cannot so <hi type="italic">sing away sorrow,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.138.5">Ps. cxxxviii. 5</reference>.
entries.684e3fbb674d8e40a141bbf48740f2e86e16ae80: <div eID="gen12720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12721" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">55</hi> I have remembered thy name, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , in the night, and have kept thy law. 56 This I had, because I kept thy precepts. <div eID="gen12721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12722" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The converse David had with the word of God; he kept it in mind, and upon every occasion he called it to mind. God's name is the discovery he has made of himself to us in and by his word. <hi type="italic">This is his memorial unto all generations,</hi> and therefore we should always keep it in memory—remember it <hi type="italic">in the night,</hi> upon a waking bed, when we are communing with our own hearts. When others were sleeping David was remembering God's name, and, by repeating that lesson, increasing his acquaintance with it; in the night of affliction this he called to mind. 2. The conscience be made of conforming to it. The due remembrance of God's name, which is prefixed to his law, will have a great influence upon our observance of the law: <hi type="italic">I remembered thy name in the night,</hi> and therefore was careful to <hi type="italic">keep thy law</hi> all day. How comfortable will it be in the reflection if our own hearts can witness for us that we have thus remembered God's name, and kept his law! 3. The advantage he got by it (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.56">v. 56</reference>): <hi type="italic">This I had because I kept thy precepts.</hi> Some understand this indefinitely: <hi type="italic">This I had</hi> (that is I had that which satisfied me; I had every thing that is comfortable) <hi type="italic">because I kept thy precepts.</hi> Note, All that have made a business of religion will own that it has turned to a good account, and that they have been unspeakable gainers by it. Others refer it to what goes immediately before: "I had the comfort of keeping thy law because I kept it." Note, God's work is its own wages. A heart to obey the will of God is a most valuable reward of obedience; and the more we do the more we may do, and shall do, in the service of God; the branch that bears fruit is made <hi type="italic">more fruitful,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.15.2">John xv. 2</reference>.
entries.0d997e8dccc0efbc1b4aea574036e046ca4858d7: <div eID="gen12722" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">8. CHETH.</title> <div sID="gen12723" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">57</hi> <hi type="italic">Thou art</hi> my portion, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> : I have said that I would keep thy words. <div eID="gen12723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12724" type="x-p"/> We may hence gather the character of a godly man. 1. He makes the favour of God his felicity: <hi type="italic">Thou art my portion, O Lord!</hi> Others place their happiness in the wealth and honours of this world. Their portion is in this life; they look no further; they desire no more; these are <hi type="italic">their good things,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.16.25">Luke xvi. 25</reference>. But all that are sanctified take the Lord for the portion of their inheritance and their cup, and nothing less will satisfy them. David can appeal to God in this matter: "Lord, thou knowest that I have chosen thee for my portion, and depend upon thee to make me happy." 2. He makes the law of God his rule: "<hi type="italic">I have said that I would keep thy words;</hi> and what I have said by thy grace I will do, and will abide by it to the end." Note, Those that take God for their portion must take him for their prince, and swear allegiance to him; and, having promised to <hi type="italic">keep his word,</hi> we must often put ourselves in mind of our promise, <reference osisRef="Ps.39.1">Ps. xxxix. 1</reference>.
entries.b0a572552b2d7199766c67f5c036181f67c5c566: <div eID="gen12724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12725" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">58</hi> I intreated thy favour with <hi type="italic">my</hi> whole heart: be merciful unto me according to thy word. <div eID="gen12725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12726" type="x-p"/> David, having in the foregoing verse reflected upon his covenants with God, here reflects upon his prayers to God, and renews his petition. Observe, 1. What he prayed for. Having taken God for his portion, he <hi type="italic">entreated his favour,</hi> as one that knew he had forfeited it, was unworthy of it, and yet undone without it, but for ever happy if he could obtain it. We cannot demand God's favour as a debt, but must be humble suppliants for it, that God will not only be reconciled to us, but accept us and smile upon us. He prays, "<hi type="italic">Be merciful to me,</hi> in the forgiveness of what I have done amiss, and in giving me grace to do better for the future." 2. How he prayed—<hi type="italic">with his whole heart,</hi> as one that knew how to value the blessing he prayed for. The gracious soul is entirely set upon the favour of God, and is therefore importunate for it. <hi type="italic">I will not let thee go except thou bless me.</hi> 3. What he pleaded—the promise of God: "<hi type="italic">Be merciful to me, according to thy word.</hi> I desire the mercy promised, and depend upon the promise for it." Those that are governed by the precepts of the word and are resolved to keep them (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.57">v. 57</reference>) may plead the promises of the word and take the comfort of them.
entries.bfb68b1fa1842363107b1d4c15da4e9d853d2156: <div eID="gen12726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12727" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">59</hi> I thought on my ways, and turned my feet unto thy testimonies. <hi type="super">60</hi> I made haste, and delayed not to keep thy commandments. <div eID="gen12727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12728" type="x-p"/> David had said he <hi type="italic">would keep God's word</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.57">v. 57</reference>), and it was well said; now here he tells us how and in what method he pursued that resolution. 1. He <hi type="italic">thought on his ways.</hi> He thought beforehand what he should do, pondering the path of his feet (<reference osisRef="Prov.4.26">Prov. iv. 26</reference>), that he might walk surely, and not at all adventures. He thought after what he had done, reflected upon his life past, and recollected the paths he had walked in and the steps he had taken. The word signifies a fixed abiding thought. Some make it an allusion to those who work embroidery, who are very exact and careful to cover the least flaw, or to those who cast up their accounts, who reckon with themselves, What do I owe? What am I worth? "<hi type="italic">I thought</hi> not on my wealth (as the covetous man, <reference osisRef="Ps.49.11">Ps. xlix. 11</reference>) but <hi type="italic">on my ways,</hi> not on what I have, but what I do:" for what we do will follow us into another world when what we have must be left behind. Many are critical enough in their remarks upon other people's ways who never think of their own: but <hi type="italic">let every man prove his own work.</hi> 2. He <hi type="italic">turned his feet to God's testimonies.</hi> He determined to make the word of God his rule, and to walk by that rule. He turned from the by-paths to which he had turned aside, and returned to God's testimonies. He turned not only his eye to them, but his feet, his affections to the love of God's word and his conversation to the practice of it. The bent and inclinations of his soul were towards God's testimonies and his conversation was governed by them Penitent reflections must produce pious resolutions. 3. He did this immediately and without demur (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.60">v. 60</reference>): <hi type="italic">I made haste and delayed not.</hi> When we are under convictions of sin we must strike while the iron is hot, and not think to defer the prosecution of them, as Felix did, to <hi type="italic">a more convenient season.</hi> When we are called to duty we must lose no time, but set about it <hi type="italic">to-day, while it is called to-day.</hi> Now this account which David here gives of himself may refer either to his constant practice every day (he reflected on his ways at night, directed his feet to God's testimonies in the morning, and what his hand found to do that was good he did it without delay), or it may refer to his first acquaintance with God and religion, when he began to throw off the vanity of childhood and youth, and to remember his Creator; that blessed change was, by the grace of God, thus wrought. Note, (1.) Conversion begins in serious consideration, <reference osisRef="Ezek.18.28">Ezek. xviii. 28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.15.17">Luke xv. 17</reference>. (2.) Consideration must end in a sound conversion. To what purpose have we thought on our ways if we do not turn our feet with all speed to God's testimonies?
entries.cce0f7204f80c007e4e431b76d339b1c679f80fb: <div eID="gen12728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12729" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">61</hi> The bands of the wicked have robbed me: <hi type="italic">but</hi> I have not forgotten thy law. <div eID="gen12729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12730" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The malice of David's enemies against him. They were wicked men, who hated him for his godliness. There were bands or troops of them confederate against him. They did him all the mischief they could; they robbed him; having endeavoured to take away his good name (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.51">v. 51</reference>), they set upon his goods, and spoiled him of them, either by plunder in time of war or by fines and confiscations under colour of law. Saul (it is likely) seized his effects, Absalom his palace, and the Amalekites rifled Ziklag. Worldly wealth is what we may be robbed of. David, though a man of war, could not keep his own. <hi type="italic">Thieves break through and steal.</hi> 2. The testimony of David's conscience for him that he had held fast his religion when he was stripped of every thing else, as Job did when the bands of the Chaldeans and Sabeans had robbed him: <hi type="italic">But I have not forgotten thy law.</hi> No care nor grief should drive God's word out of our minds, or hinder our comfortable relish of it and converse with it. Nor must we ever think the worse of the ways of God for any trouble we meet with in those ways, nor fear being losers by our religion at last, however we may be losers for it now.
entries.dd56d0fe48ff6f6c574c5663f99c813b44038234: <div eID="gen12730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12731" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">62</hi> At midnight I will rise to give thanks unto thee because of thy righteous judgments. <div eID="gen12731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12732" type="x-p"/> Though David is, in this psalm, much in prayer, yet he did not neglect the duty of thanksgiving; for those that pray much will have much to give thanks for. See, 1. How much God's hand was eyed in his thanksgivings. He does not say, "<hi type="italic">I will give thanks</hi> because of thy favours to me, which I have the comfort of," but, "<hi type="italic">Because of thy righteous judgments,</hi> all the disposals of thy providence in wisdom and equity, which thou hast the glory of." We must give thanks for the asserting of God's honour and the accomplishing of his word in all he does in the government of the world. 2. How much David's heart was set upon his thanksgivings. He would <hi type="italic">rise at midnight to give thanks</hi> to God. Great and good thoughts kept him awake, and refreshed him, instead of sleep; and so zealous was he for the honour of God that when others were in their beds he was upon his knees at his devotions. He did not affect to be seen of men in it, but gave thanks in secret, where our heavenly Father sees. He had praised God <hi type="italic">in the courts of the Lord's house,</hi> and yet he will do it in his bed-chamber. Public worship will not excuse us from secret worship. When David found his heart affected with God's judgments, he immediately offered up those affections to God, in actual adorations, not deferring, lest they should cool. Yet observe his reverence; he did not lie still and give thanks, but rose out of his bed, perhaps in the cold and in the dark, to do it the more solemnly. And see what a good husband he was of time; when he could not lie and sleep, he would rise and pray.
entries.65b4091f311e1194212c1d7f331625972c1a4e79: <div eID="gen12732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12733" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">63</hi> I <hi type="italic">am</hi> a companion of all <hi type="italic">them</hi> that fear thee, and of them that keep thy precepts. <div eID="gen12733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12734" type="x-p"/> David had often expressed the great love he had to God; here he expresses the great love he had to the people of God; and observe, 1. Why he loved them; not so much because they were his best friends, most firm to his interest and most forward to serve him, but because they were such as <hi type="italic">feared God</hi> and <hi type="italic">kept his precepts,</hi> and so did him honour and helped to support his kingdom among men. Our love to the saints is <hi type="italic">then</hi> sincere when we love them for the sake of what we see of God in them and the service they do to him. 2. How he showed his love to them: He was <hi type="italic">a companion of them.</hi> He had not only a spiritual communion with them in the same faith and hope, but he joined with them in holy ordinances in the courts of the Lord, where rich and poor, prince and peasant, meet together. He sympathized with them in their joys and sorrows (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.33">Heb. x. 33</reference>); he conversed familiarly with them, communicated his experiences to them, and consulted theirs. He not only took such to be his companions as did fear God, but he vouchsafed himself to be a companion with all, with any, that did so, wherever he met with them. Though he was a king, he would associate with the poorest of his subjects that feared God, <reference osisRef="Ps.15.4">Ps. xv. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.2.1">Jam. ii. 1</reference>.
entries.6fabd40d389aa9c9125c99ac24880db92c2b8411: <div eID="gen12734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12735" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">64</hi> The earth, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , is full of thy mercy: teach me thy statutes. <div eID="gen12735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12736" type="x-p"/> Here, 1. David pleads that God is good to all the creatures according to their necessities and capacities; as the heaven is full of God's glory, so <hi type="italic">the earth is full of his mercy,</hi> full of the instances of his pity and bounty. Not only the land of Canaan, where God is known and worshipped, but the whole earth, in many parts of which he has no homage paid him, is full of his mercy. Not only the children of men upon the earth, but even the inferior creatures, taste of God's goodness. <hi type="italic">His tender mercies are over all his works.</hi> 2. He therefore prays that God would be good to him according to his necessity and capacity: "<hi type="italic">Teach me thy statutes.</hi> Thou feedest the young ravens that cry, with food proper for them; and wilt thou not feed me with spiritual food, the bread of life, which my soul needs and craves, and cannot subsist without? <hi type="italic">The earth is full of thy mercy;</hi> and is not heaven too? Wilt thou not then give me spiritual blessings in heavenly places?" A gracious heart will fetch an argument from any thing to enforce a petition for divine teaching. Surely he that will not let his birds be unfed will not let his children be untaught.
entries.f530d2feaf2d4a73b453e3e281116877d25acc85: <div eID="gen12736" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">9. TETH.</title> <div sID="gen12737" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">65</hi> Thou hast dealt well with thy servant, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , according unto thy word. <hi type="super">66</hi> Teach me good judgment and knowledge: for I have believed thy commandments. <div eID="gen12737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12738" type="x-p"/> Here, 1. David makes a thankful acknowledgment of God's gracious dealings with him all along: <hi type="italic">Thou hast dealt well with thy servant.</hi> However God has dealt with us, we must own he has dealt <hi type="italic">well</hi> with us, better than we deserve, and all in love and with design to work for our good. In many instances God has done well for us beyond our expectations. He has done well for all his servants; never any of them complained that he had used them hardly. <hi type="italic">Thou hast dealt well with</hi> me, not only according to thy mercy, but <hi type="italic">according to thy word.</hi> God's favours look best when they are compared with the promise and are seen flowing from that fountain. 2. Upon these experiences he grounds a petition for divine instruction: "<hi type="italic">Teach me good judgment and knowledge,</hi> that, by thy grace, I may render again, in some measure, according to the benefit done unto me." Teach me <hi type="italic">a good taste</hi> (so the word signifies), a good relish, to discern things that differ, to distinguish between truth and falsehood, good and evil; for <hi type="italic">the ear tries words, as the mouth tastes meat.</hi> We should pray to God for a sound mind, that we may have <hi type="italic">spiritual senses exercised,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.5.14">Heb. v. 14</reference>. Many have knowledge who have little judgment; those who have both are well fortified against the snares of Satan and well furnished for the service of God and their generation. 3. This petition is backed with a plea: "<hi type="italic">For I have believed thy commandments,</hi> received them, and consented to them that they are good, and submitted to their government; therefore, Lord, <hi type="italic">teach me.</hi>" Where God has given a good heart a good head too may in faith be prayed for.
entries.f0725549567565d752e5897f59cb81552dac59d6: <div eID="gen12738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12739" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">67</hi> Before I was afflicted I went astray: but now have I kept thy word. <div eID="gen12739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12740" type="x-p"/> David here tells us what he had experienced, 1. Of the temptations of a prosperous condition: "<hi type="italic">Before I was afflicted,</hi> while I lived in peace and plenty, and knew no sorrow, <hi type="italic">I went astray</hi> from God and my duty." Sin is going astray; and we are most apt to wander from God when we are easy and think ourselves at home in the world. Prosperity is the unhappy occasion of much iniquity; it makes people conceited of themselves, indulgent of the flesh, forgetful of God, in love with the world, and deaf to the reproofs of the word. See <reference osisRef="Ps.30.6">Ps. xxx. 6</reference>. It is good for us, when we are afflicted, to remember how and wherein we went astray <hi type="italic">before we were afflicted,</hi> that we may answer the end of the affliction. 2. Of the benefit of an afflicted state: "<hi type="italic">Now have I kept thy word,</hi> and so have been recovered from my wanderings." God often makes use of afflictions as a means to reduce those to himself who have wandered from him. Sanctified afflictions humble us for sin and show us the vanity of the world; they soften the heart, and open the ear to discipline. The prodigal's distress brought him to himself first and then to his father.
entries.7f4635a9d336d4e365d87268f9a30623bb8b233a: <div eID="gen12740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12741" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">68</hi> Thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> good, and doest good; teach me thy statutes. <div eID="gen12741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12742" type="x-p"/> Here, 1. David praises God's goodness and gives him the glory of it: <hi type="italic">Thou art good and doest good.</hi> All who have any knowledge of God and dealings with him wilt own that he does good, and therefore will conclude that he is good. The streams of God's goodness are so numerous, and run so full, so strong, to all the creatures, that we must conclude the fountain that is in himself to be inexhaustible. We cannot conceive how much good our God does every day, much less can we conceive how good he is. Let us acknowledge it with admiration and with holy love and thankfulness. 2. He prays for God's grace, and begs to be under the guidance and influence of it: <hi type="italic">Teach me thy statutes.</hi> "Lord, thou doest good to all, art the bountiful benefactor of all the creatures; this is the good I beg thou wilt do to me,—Instruct me in my duty, incline me to it, and enable me to do it. <hi type="italic">Thou art good, and doest good;</hi> Lord, <hi type="italic">teach me thy statutes,</hi> that I may be good and do good, may have a good heart and live a good life." It is an encouragement to poor sinners to hope that God will <hi type="italic">teach them his way</hi> because he is <hi type="italic">good and upright,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.25.8">Ps. xxv. 8</reference>.
entries.eee2409d49bdea34d82bac99a10d6cb88a33267b: <div eID="gen12742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12743" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">69</hi> The proud have forged a lie against me: <hi type="italic">but</hi> I will keep thy precepts with <hi type="italic">my</hi> whole heart. 70 Their heart is as fat as grease; <hi type="italic">but</hi> I delight in thy law. <div eID="gen12743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12744" type="x-p"/> David here tells us how he was affected as to the proud and wicked people that were about him. 1. He did not fear their malice, nor was he by it deterred from his duty: <hi type="italic">They have forged a lie against me.</hi> Thus they aimed to take away his good name. Nay, all we have in the world, even life itself, may be brought into danger by those who make no conscience of forging a lie. Those that were proud envied David's reputation, because it eclipsed them, and therefore did all they could to blemish him. They took a pride in trampling upon him. They therefore persuaded themselves it was no sin to tell a deliberate lie if it might but expose him to contempt. Their wicked wit forged lies, invented stories which there was not the least colour for, to serve their wicked designs. And what did David do when he was thus belied? He will bear it patiently; he will keep that precept which forbids him to render railing for railing, and will with all his heart sit down silently. He will go on in his duty with constancy and resolution: "Let them say what they will, <hi type="italic">I will keep thy precepts,</hi> and not dread their reproach." 2. He did not envy their prosperity, nor was he by it allured from his duty. <hi type="italic">Their heart is as fat as grease.</hi> The proud are <hi type="italic">at ease</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.123.4">Ps. cxxiii. 4</reference>); they are full of the world, and the wealth and pleasures of it; and this makes them, (1.) Senseless, secure, and stupid; they are past feeling: thus the phrase is used, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.10">Isa. vi. 10</reference>. <hi type="italic">Make the heart of this people fat.</hi> They are not sensible of the touch of the word of God or his rod. (2.) Sensual and voluptuous: "<hi type="italic">Their eyes stand out with fatness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.7">Ps. lxxiii. 7</reference>); they roll themselves in the pleasures of sense, and take up with them as their chief good; and much good may it do them. I would not change conditions with them. <hi type="italic">I delight in thy law;</hi> I build my security upon the promises of God's word and have pleasure enough in communion with God, infinitely preferable to all their delights." The children of God, who are acquainted with spiritual pleasures, need not envy the children of this world their carnal pleasures.
entries.a1db90040b7f29e2c2585fb4af4cc53b6ef3dfec: <div eID="gen12744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12745" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">71</hi> <hi type="italic">It is</hi> good for me that I have been afflicted; that I might learn thy statutes. <div eID="gen12745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12746" type="x-p"/> See here, 1. That it has been the lot of the best saints to be afflicted. The proud and the wicked lived in pomp and pleasure, while David, though he kept close to God and his duty, was still in affliction. <hi type="italic">Waters of a full cup are wrung out to</hi> God's people, <reference osisRef="Ps.73.10">Ps. lxxiii. 10</reference>. 2. That it has been the advantage of God's people to be afflicted. David could speak experimentally: <hi type="italic">It was good for me;</hi> many a good lesson he had learnt by his afflictions, and many a good duty he had been brought to which otherwise would have been unlearnt and undone. <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> God visited him with affliction, that he might learn God's statutes; and the intention was answered: the afflictions had contributed to the improvement of his knowledge and grace. He that chastened him taught him. <hi type="italic">The rod and reproof give wisdom.</hi>
entries.99f6849f760f3615fb99df1452e6f5befad4d8ee: <div eID="gen12746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12747" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">72</hi> The law of thy mouth <hi type="italic">is</hi> better unto me than thousands of gold and silver. <div eID="gen12747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12748" type="x-p"/> This is a reason why David reckoned that when by his afflictions he learned God's statutes, and the profit did so much counterbalance the loss, he was really a gainer by them; for God's <hi type="italic">law,</hi> which he got acquaintance with by his affliction, was <hi type="italic">better</hi> to him than all the <hi type="italic">gold and silver</hi> which he lost by his affliction. 1. David had but a little of the word of God in comparison with what we have, yet see how highly he valued it; how inexcusable then are we, who have both the Old and New Testament complete, and yet account them as a strange thing! Observe, <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> he valued the law, because it is <hi type="italic">the law of God's mouth,</hi> the revelation of his will, and ratified by his authority. 2. He had a great deal of gold and silver in comparison with what we have, yet see how little he valued it. His riches increased, and yet he did not set his heart upon them, but upon the word of God. That was better to him, yielded him better pleasures, and better maintenance, and a better inheritance, than all the treasures he was master of. Those that have read, and believe, David's <hi type="italic">Psalms</hi> and Solomon's <hi type="italic">Ecclesiastes,</hi> cannot but prefer the word of God far before the wealth of this world.
entries.0d122c73960860cba038ba2dd01992d5ecfb4c20: <div eID="gen12748" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">10. JOD.</title> <div sID="gen12749" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">73</hi> Thy hands have made me and fashioned me: give me understanding, that I may learn thy commandments. <div eID="gen12749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12750" type="x-p"/> Here, 1. David adores God as the God of nature and the author of his being: <hi type="italic">Thy hands have made me and fashioned me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.10.8">Job x. 8</reference>. Every man is as truly the work of God's hands as the first man was, <reference osisRef="Ps.139.15-Ps.139.16">Ps. cxxxix. 15, 16</reference>. "<hi type="italic">Thy hands have</hi> not only <hi type="italic">made me,</hi> and given me a being, otherwise I should never have been, but <hi type="italic">fashioned me,</hi> and given me this being, this noble and excellent being, endued with these powers and faculties;" and we must own that we are <hi type="italic">fearfully and wonderfully made.</hi> 2. He addresses himself to God as the God of grace, and begs he will be the author of his new and better being. God made us to serve him and enjoy him; but by sin we have made ourselves unable for his service and indisposed for the enjoyment of him; and we must have a new and divine nature, otherwise we had the human nature in vain; therefore David prays, "Lord, since thou hast made me by thy power for thy glory, make me anew by thy grace, that I may answer the ends of my creation and live to some purpose: <hi type="italic">Give me understanding, that I may learn thy commandments.</hi>" The way in which God recovers and secures his interest in men is by giving them an understanding; for by that door he enters into the soul and gains possession of it.
entries.9196d627ddb44adda5369d6d2a19bd7528e0c348: <div eID="gen12750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12751" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">74</hi> They that fear thee will be glad when they see me; because I have hoped in thy word. <div eID="gen12751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12752" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The confidence of this good man in the hope of God's salvation: "<hi type="italic">I have hoped in thy word;</hi> and I have not found it in vain to do so; it has not failed me, nor have I been disappointed in my expectations from it. It is a hope that <hi type="italic">maketh not ashamed;</hi> but is present satisfaction, and fruition at last." 2. The concurrence of other good men with him in the joy of that salvation: "<hi type="italic">Those that fear thee will be glad when they see me</hi> relieved by my hope in thy word and delivered according to my hope." The comforts which some of God's children have in God, and the favours they have received from him, should be matter of joy to others of them. Paul often expressed the hope that for God's grace to him thanks would be rendered by many, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.11">2 Cor. i. 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.15">iv. 15</reference>. Or it may be taken more generally; good people are glad to see one another; they are especially pleased with those who are eminent for their hope in God's word.
entries.0609a7b4d861fe7eb3d0c00742c4a43248bbe737: <div eID="gen12752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12753" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">75</hi> I know, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , that thy judgments <hi type="italic">are</hi> right, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> thou in faithfulness hast afflicted me. <div eID="gen12753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12754" type="x-p"/> Still David is in affliction, and being so he owns, 1. That his sin was justly corrected: <hi type="italic">I know, O Lord! that thy judgments are right,</hi> are righteousness itself. However God is pleased to afflict us, he does us no wrong, nor can we charge him with any iniquity, but must acknowledge that it is less than we have deserved. We know that God is holy in his nature and wise and just in all the acts of his government, and therefore we cannot but know, in the general, that his <hi type="italic">judgments are right,</hi> though, in some particular instances, there may be difficulties which we cannot easily resolve. 2. That God's promise was graciously performed. The former may silence us under our afflictions, and forbid us to repine, but this may satisfy us, and enable us to rejoice; for afflictions are in the covenant, and therefore they are not only not meant for our hurt, but they are really intended for our good: "<hi type="italic">In faithfulness thou hast afflicted me,</hi> pursuant to the great design of my salvation." It is easier to own, in general, that God's <hi type="italic">judgments are right,</hi> than to own it when it comes to be our own case; but David subscribes to it with application, "Even my afflictions are just and kind."
entries.d3302372fbb06b907c3ca8e8bbbd30c15c40fad4: <div eID="gen12754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12755" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">76</hi> Let, I pray thee, thy merciful kindness be for my comfort, according to thy word unto thy servant. <hi type="super">77</hi> Let thy tender mercies come unto me, that I may live: for thy law <hi type="italic">is</hi> my delight. <div eID="gen12755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12756" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. An earnest petition to God for his favour. Those that own the justice of God in their afflictions (as David had done, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.75">v. 75</reference>) may, in faith, and with humble boldness, be earnest for the mercy of God, and the tokens and fruits of that mercy, in their affliction. He prays for God's <hi type="italic">merciful kindness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.76">v. 76</reference>), his <hi type="italic">tender mercies,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.119.77">v. 77</reference>. He can claim nothing as his due, but all his supports under his affliction must come from mere mercy and compassion to one in misery, one in want. "Let these <hi type="italic">come to me,</hi>" that is, "the evidence of them (clear it up to me that thou hast a kindness for me, and mercy in store), and the effects of them; let them work my relief and deliverance." 2. The benefit he promised himself from God's lovingkindness: "Let it <hi type="italic">come to me for my comfort</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.76">v. 76</reference>); that will comfort me when nothing else will; that will comfort me whatever grieves me." Gracious souls fetch all their comfort from a gracious God, as the fountain of all happiness and joy: "Let it <hi type="italic">come to me, that I may live,</hi> that is, that I may be revived, and my life may be made sweet to me, for I have no joy of it while I am under God's displeasure. <hi type="italic">In his favour is life;</hi> in his frowns are death." A good man cannot live with any satisfaction any longer than he has some tokens of God's favour to him. 3. His pleas for the benefits of God's favour. He pleads, (1.) God's promise: "Let me have thy kindness, <hi type="italic">according to thy word unto thy servant,</hi> the kindness which thou hast promised and because thou hast promised it." Our Master has passed his word to all his servants that he will be kind to them, and they may plead it with him. (2.) His own confidence and complacency in that promise: "<hi type="italic">Thy law is my delight;</hi> I hope in thy word and rejoice in that hope." Note, Those that delight in the law of God may depend upon the favour of God, for it shall certainly make them happy.
entries.1d04e68e5fa993e096e6a7cd58b0ed578b5b3a91: <div eID="gen12756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12757" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">78</hi> Let the proud be ashamed; for they dealt perversely with me without a cause: <hi type="italic">but</hi> I will meditate in thy precepts. <hi type="super">79</hi> Let those that fear thee turn unto me, and those that have known thy testimonies. <div eID="gen12757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12758" type="x-p"/> Here David shows, <div eID="gen12758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12759" type="x-p"/> I. How little he valued the will—will of sinners. There were those that dealt perversely with him, that were peevish and ill-conditioned towards him, that sought advantages against him, and misconstrued all he said and did. Even those that deal most fairly may meet with those that deal perversely. But David regarded it not, for, 1. He knew it was <hi type="italic">without cause,</hi> and that for his love they were his adversaries. The causeless reproach, like the curse causeless, may be easily slighted; it does not hurt us, and therefore should not move us. 2. He could pray, in faith, that they might <hi type="italic">be ashamed</hi> of it; God's dealing favourably with him might make them ashamed to think that they had dealt perversely with him. "<hi type="italic">Let</hi> them <hi type="italic">be ashamed,</hi> that is, let them be brought either to repentance or to ruin." 3. He could go on in the way of his duty, and find comfort in that. "However they deal with me, <hi type="italic">I will meditate in thy precepts,</hi> and entertain myself with them." <div eID="gen12759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12760" type="x-p"/> II. How much he valued the good-will of saints, and how desirous he was to stand right in their opinion, and keep up his interest in them and communion with them: <hi type="italic">Let those that fear thee turn to me.</hi> He does not mean so much that they might side with him, and take up arms in his cause, as that they might love him, and pray for him, and associate with him. Good men desire the friendship and society of those that are good. Some think it intimates that when David had been guilty of that foul sin in the murder of Uriah, though he was a king, those that feared God grew strange to him and turned from him, for they were ashamed of him; this troubled him, and therefore he prays, Lord, let them <hi type="italic">turn to me again.</hi> He desires especially the company of those that were not only honest, but intelligent, <hi type="italic">that have known thy testimonies,</hi> have good heads as well as good hearts, and whose conversation will be edifying. It is desirable to have an intimacy with such.
entries.fe155b14f812c1b9d8c5a660872566c090b9ae69: <div eID="gen12760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12761" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">80</hi> Let my heart be sound in thy statutes; that I be not ashamed. <div eID="gen12761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12762" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. David's prayer for sincerity, that his heart might be brought to God's <hi type="italic">statutes,</hi> and that it might be <hi type="italic">sound</hi> in them, not rotten and deceitful, that he might not rest in the form of godliness, but be acquainted with the subject to the power of it,—that he might be hearty and constant in religion, and that his soul might be in health. 2. His dread of the consequences of hypocrisy: <hi type="italic">That I be not ashamed.</hi> Shame is the portion of hypocrites, either here, if it be repented of, or hereafter, if it be not: "<hi type="italic">Let my heart be sound,</hi> that I fall not into scandalous sin, that I fall not quite off from the ways of God, and so shame myself. <hi type="italic">Let my heart be sound,</hi> that I may come <hi type="italic">boldly to the throne of grace,</hi> and may lift up my face without spot at the great day."
entries.9683d09abb775e87aa2b6ccd63282ef5961aa08c: <div eID="gen12762" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">11. CAPH.</title> <div sID="gen12763" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">81</hi> My soul fainteth for thy salvation: <hi type="italic">but</hi> I hope in thy word. <hi type="super">82</hi> Mine eyes fail for thy word, saying, When wilt thou comfort me? <div eID="gen12763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12764" type="x-p"/> Here we have the psalmist, <div eID="gen12764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12765" type="x-p"/> I. Longing for help from heaven: <hi type="italic">My soul faints; my eyes fail.</hi> He longs <hi type="italic">for the salvation of the Lord</hi> and <hi type="italic">for his word,</hi> that is, salvation according to the word. He is not thus eager for the creatures of fancy, but for the objects of faith, salvation from the present calamities under which he was groaning and the doubts and fears which he was oppressed with. It may be understood of the coming of the Messiah, and so he speaks in the name of the Old-Testament church; the souls of the faithful even <hi type="italic">fainted to see</hi> that salvation of which the prophets testified. (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.10">1 Pet. i. 10</reference>); their eyes failed for it. Abraham saw it at a distance, and so did others, but at such a distance that it put their eyes to the stretch and they could not stedfastly see it. David was now under prevailing dejections, and, having been long so, his eyes cried out, "<hi type="italic">When wilt thou comfort me?</hi> Comfort me with <hi type="italic">thy salvation,</hi> comfort me with <hi type="italic">thy word.</hi>" Observe, 1. The salvation and consolation of God's people are secured to them by the word, which will certainly be fulfilled in its season. 2. The promised salvation and comfort may be, and often are, long deferred, so that they are ready to faint and fall in the expectation of them. 3. Though we think the time long ere the promised salvation and comfort come, yet we must still keep our eye upon that salvation, and resolve to take up with nothing short of it. "Thy salvation, thy word, thy comfort, are what my heart is still upon." <div eID="gen12765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12766" type="x-p"/> II. Waiting for that help, assured that it will come, and tarrying till it come: <hi type="italic">But I hope in thy word;</hi> and but for hope the heart would break. When the <hi type="italic">eyes fail</hi> yet the faith must not; for <hi type="italic">the vision is for an appointed time, and at the end it shall speak and shall not lie.</hi>
entries.e1a80d76e920cc76fe9512827e07707b7453814e: <div eID="gen12766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12767" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">83</hi> For I am become like a bottle in the smoke; <hi type="italic">yet</hi> do I not forget thy statutes. <div eID="gen12767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12768" type="x-p"/> David begs God would make haste to comfort him, 1. Because his affliction was great, and therefore he was an object of God's pity: Lord, make haste to help me, <hi type="italic">for I have become like a bottle in the smoke,</hi> a leathern bottle, which, if it hung any while in the smoke, was not only blackened with soot, but dried, and parched, and shrivelled up. David was thus wasted by age, and sickness, and sorrow. See how affliction will mortify the strongest and stoutest of men! David had been of a ruddy countenance, as fresh as a rose; but now he is withered, his colour is gone, his cheeks are furrowed. Thus does man's beauty consume under God's rebukes, as a moth fretting a garment. A bottle, when it is thus wrinkled with smoke, is thrown by, and there is no more use of it. Who will put wine into such old bottles? Thus was David, in his low estate, looked upon <hi type="italic">as a despised broken vessel,</hi> and as <hi type="italic">a vessel in which there was no pleasure.</hi> Good men, when they are drooping and melancholy, sometimes think themselves more slighted than really they are. 2. Because, though his affliction was great, yet it had not driven him from his duty, and therefore he was within the reach of God's promise: <hi type="italic">Yet do I not forget thy statutes.</hi> Whatever our outward condition is we must not cool in our affection to the word of God, nor let that slip out of our minds; no care, no grief, must crowd that out. As some <hi type="italic">drink and forget the law</hi> (<reference osisRef="Prov.31.5">Prov. xxxi. 5</reference>), so others weep and forget the law; but we must in every condition, both prosperous and adverse, have the things of God in remembrance; and, if we be mindful of God's statutes, we may pray and hope that he will be mindful of our sorrows, though for a time he seems to forget us.
entries.2f5435b2473151c92986098a2e9e2dbb65af607b: <div eID="gen12768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12769" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">84</hi> How many <hi type="italic">are</hi> the days of thy servant? when wilt thou execute judgment on them that persecute me? <div eID="gen12769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12770" type="x-p"/> Here, I. David prays against the instruments of his troubles, that God would make haste to execute judgment on those that persecuted him. He prays not for power to avenge himself (he bore no malice to any), but that God would take to himself the vengeance that belonged to him, and <hi type="italic">would repay</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.12.19">Rom. xii. 19</reference>), as the God that <hi type="italic">sits in the throne judging right.</hi> There is a day coming, and a great and terrible day it will be, when God will execute judgment on all the proud persecutors of his people, <hi type="italic">tribulation to those that troubled them;</hi> Enoch foretold it (<reference osisRef="Jude.1.14">Jude 14</reference>), whose prophecy perhaps David here had an eye to; and that day we are to look for and pray for the hastening of. <hi type="italic">Come, Lord Jesus, come quickly.</hi> 2. He pleads the long continuance of his trouble: "<hi type="italic">How many are the days of thy servant? The days of my life are but few</hi>" (so some); "therefore let them not all be miserable, and therefore make haste to appear for me against my enemies, <hi type="italic">before I go hence and shall be seen no more.</hi>" Or rather, "<hi type="italic">The days of my affliction are many;</hi> thou seest, Lord, how many they be; when wilt thou return in mercy to me? Sometimes, for the elect's sake, <hi type="italic">the days of trouble are shortened.</hi> O let the days of my trouble be shortened; I am <hi type="italic">thy servant;</hi> and therefore, as the eyes of a servant are to the hand of his master, so are mine to thee, until thou have mercy on me."
entries.65e37ee4e604b50bb66043cd7d50c5a5a6c79fdd: <div eID="gen12770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12771" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">85</hi> The proud have digged pits for me, which <hi type="italic">are</hi> not after thy law. <hi type="super">86</hi> All thy commandments <hi type="italic">are</hi> faithful: they persecute me wrongfully; help thou me. 87 They had almost consumed me upon earth; but I forsook not thy precepts. <div eID="gen12771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12772" type="x-p"/> David's state was <hi type="italic">herein</hi> a type and figure of the state both of Christ and Christians that he was grievously persecuted; as there are many of his psalms, so there are many of the verses of this psalm, which complain of this, as those here. Here observe, <div eID="gen12772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12773" type="x-p"/> I. The account he gives of his persecutors and their malice against him. 1. They were <hi type="italic">proud,</hi> and in their pride <hi type="italic">they persecuted him,</hi> glorying in this, that they could trample upon one who was so much cried up, and hoping to raise themselves on his ruins. 2. They were unjust: <hi type="italic">They persecuted him wrongfully;</hi> so far was he from giving them any provocation that he had studied to oblige them; but <hi type="italic">for his love they were his adversaries.</hi> 3. They were spiteful: <hi type="italic">They dug pits for him,</hi> which intimates that they were deliberate in their designs against him and that what they did was of malice prepense; it intimates likewise that they were subtle and crafty, and had the serpent's head as well as the serpent's venom, that they were industrious and would refuse no pains to do him a mischief, and treacherous, laying snares in secret for him, as hunters do take wild beasts, <reference osisRef="Ps.35.7">Ps. xxxv. 7</reference>. Such has been the enmity of the serpent's seed to the seed of the woman. 4. They herein showed their enmity to God himself. The pits they <hi type="italic">dug for him</hi> were <hi type="italic">not after God's law;</hi> he means they were very much against his law, which forbids to <hi type="italic">devise evil to our neighbour,</hi> and has particularly said, <hi type="italic">Touch not my anointed.</hi> The law appointed that, if a man dug a pit which occasioned any mischief, he should answer for the mischief (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.33-Exod.21.34">Exod. xxi. 33, 34</reference>), much more when it was dug with a mischievous design. 5. They carried on their designs against him so far that <hi type="italic">they had almost consumed him upon earth;</hi> they went near to ruin him and all his interests. It is possible that those who shall shortly be consummate in heaven may be, for the present, <hi type="italic">almost consumed on earth;</hi> and <hi type="italic">it is of the Lord's mercies</hi> (and, considering the malice of their enemies, it is a miracle of mercy) <hi type="italic">that they are not quite consumed.</hi> But the bush in which God is, though it burns, shall not be burnt up. <div eID="gen12773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12774" type="x-p"/> II. His application to God in his persecuted state. 1. He acknowledges the truth and goodness of his religion, though he suffered: "However it be, <hi type="italic">all thy commandments are faithful,</hi> and therefore, whatever I lose for my observance of them, I know I shall not lose by it." True religion, if it be worth any thing, is worth every thing, and therefore worth suffering for. "Men are false; I find them so; men of low degree, men of high degree, are so, there is no trusting them. But <hi type="italic">all thy commandments are faithful;</hi> on them I may rely." 2. He begs that God would stand by him, and succour him: "<hi type="italic">They persecute me; help thou me;</hi> help me under my troubles, that I may bear them patiently, and as becomes me, and may still hold fast my integrity, and in due time help me out of my troubles." <hi type="italic">God help me</hi> is an excellent comprehensive prayer; it is a pity that it should ever be used lightly and as a by-word. <div eID="gen12774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12775" type="x-p"/> III. His adherence to his duty notwithstanding all the malice of his persecutors (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.87">v. 87</reference>): <hi type="italic">But I forsook not thy precepts.</hi> That which they aimed at was to frighten him from the ways of God, but they could not prevail; he would sooner forsake all that was dear to him in this world than forsake the word of God, would sooner lose his life than lose the comfort of doing his duty.
entries.ab70b295ee8d19bd177f5a0f97b6cc44817b88fc: <div eID="gen12775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12776" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">88</hi> Quicken me after thy lovingkindness; so shall I keep the testimony of thy mouth. <div eID="gen12776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12777" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. David in care to be found in the way of his duty. His constant desire and design are to <hi type="italic">keep the testimony of God's mouth,</hi> to keep to it as his rule and to keep hold of it as his confidence and portion for ever. This we must keep, whatever we lose. 2. David at prayer for divine grace to assist him therein: "<hi type="italic">Quicken me after thy lovingkindness</hi> (make me alive and make me lively), <hi type="italic">so shall I keep thy testimonies,</hi>" implying that otherwise he should not keep them. We cannot proceed, nor persevere, in the good way, unless God quicken us and put life into us; we are therefore here taught to depend upon the grace of God for strength to do every good work, and to depend upon it as grace, as purely the fruit of God's favour. He had prayed before, <hi type="italic">Quicken me in thy righteousness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.40">v. 40</reference>); but here, <hi type="italic">Quicken me after thy lovingkindness.</hi> The surest token of God's good-will toward us is his good work in us.
entries.c8abd1e6b3ca4b3a320c43d0308e98f7e699a91d: <div eID="gen12777" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">12. LAMED.</title> <div sID="gen12778" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">89</hi> For ever, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , thy word is settled in heaven. <hi type="super">90</hi> Thy faithfulness <hi type="italic">is</hi> unto all generations: thou hast established the earth, and it abideth. <hi type="super">91</hi> They continue this day according to thine ordinances: for all <hi type="italic">are</hi> thy servants. <div eID="gen12778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12779" type="x-p"/> Here, 1. The psalmist acknowledges the unchangeableness of the word of God and of all his counsels: "<hi type="italic">For ever, O Lord! thy word is settled. Thou art for ever thyself</hi> (so some read it); thou art the same, and with thee there is no variableness, and this is a proof of it. <hi type="italic">Thy word,</hi> by which the heavens were made, <hi type="italic">is settled</hi> there in the abiding products of it;" or the settling of God's word in heaven is opposed to the changes and revolutions that are here upon earth. <hi type="italic">All flesh is grass;</hi> but <hi type="italic">the word of the Lord endures for ever.</hi> It <hi type="italic">is settled in heaven,</hi> that is, in the secret counsel of God, which is hidden in himself and is far above out of our sight, and is immovable, <hi type="italic">as mountains of brass.</hi> And his revealed will is as firm as his secret will; as he will fulfil the thoughts of his heart, so no word of his shall <hi type="italic">fall to the ground;</hi> for it follows here, <hi type="italic">Thy faithfulness is unto all generations,</hi> that is, the promise is sure to every age of the church and it cannot be antiquated by lapse of time. The promises that look ever so far forward shall be performed in their season. 2. He produces, for proof of it, the constancy of the course of nature: <hi type="italic">Thou hast established the earth for ever and it abides;</hi> it is what it was at first made, and where it was at first placed, poised with its own weight, and notwithstanding the convulsions in its own bowels, the agitations of the sea that is interwoven with it, and the violent concussions of the atmosphere that surrounds it, it remains unmoved. "<hi type="italic">They</hi>" (the heavens and the earth and all the hosts of both) "<hi type="italic">continue to this day according to thy ordinances;</hi> they remain in the posts wherein thou hast set them; they fill up the place assigned them, and answer the purposes for which they were intended." The stability of the ordinances of the day and night, of heaven and earth, is produced to prove the perpetuity of God's covenant, <reference osisRef="Jer.31.35-Jer.31.36">Jer. xxxi. 35, 36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.33.20-Jer.33.21">xxxiii. 20, 21</reference>. It is by virtue of God's promise to Noah (<reference osisRef="Gen.8.22">Gen. viii. 22</reference>) that <hi type="italic">day and night, summer and winter,</hi> observe a steady course. "They have continued to this day, and shall still continue to the end of time, acting according to the ordinances which were at first given them; for all are thy servants; they do thy will, and set forth thy glory, and in both <hi type="italic">are thy servants.</hi>" All the creatures are, in their places, and according to their capacities, serviceable to their Creator, and answer the ends of their creation; and shall man be the only rebel, the only revolter from his allegiance, and the only unprofitable burden of the earth?
entries.140c5075a8eb91acef0f4aa6a1b976109020bdbe: <div eID="gen12779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12780" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">92</hi> Unless thy law <hi type="italic">had been</hi> my delights, I should then have perished in mine affliction. <div eID="gen12780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12781" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The great distress that David was in. He was in affliction, and ready to <hi type="italic">perish in his affliction,</hi> not likely to die, so much as likely to despair; he was ready to give up all for gone, and to look upon himself as cut off from God's sight; he therefore admires the goodness of God to him, that he had not perished, that he kept the possession of his own soul, and was not driven out of his wits by his troubles, but especially that he was enabled to keep close to his God and was not driven off from his religion by them. Though we are not kept from affliction, yet, if we are kept from perishing in our affliction, we have no reason to say, <hi type="italic">We have cleansed our hands in vain;</hi> or, <hi type="italic">What profit is it that we have served God?</hi> 2. His support in this distress. God's law was his delight, (1.) It had been so formerly, and the remembrance of that was a comfort to him, as it afforded him a good evidence of his integrity. (2.) It was so now in his affliction; it afforded him abundant matter of comfort, and from these fountains of life he drew living waters, when the cisterns of the creature were broken or dried up. His converse with God's law, and his meditations on it, were his delightful entertainment in solitude and sorrow. A Bible is a pleasant companion at any time if we please.
entries.157402536e3d7e1d61bc19b78ce63e0a0cee22f2: <div eID="gen12781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12782" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">93</hi> I will never forget thy precepts: for with them thou hast quickened me. <div eID="gen12782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12783" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. A very good resolution: "<hi type="italic">I will never forget thy precepts,</hi> but will always retain a remembrance of and regard to thy word as my rule." It is a resolution for perpetuity, never to be altered. Note, The best evidence of our love to the word of God is never to forget it. We must resolve that we will never, at any time, cast off our religion, and never, upon any occasion, lay aside our religion, but that we will be constant to it and persevere in it. 2. A very good reason for it: "<hi type="italic">For by them thou hast quickened me;</hi> not only they are quickening, but," (1.) "They have been so to me; I have found them so." Those speak best of the things of God who speak by experience, who can say that by the word the spiritual life has been begun in them, maintained and strengthened in them, excited and comforted in them. (2.) "Thou hast made them so;" the word of itself, without the grace of God, would not quicken us. Ministers can but prophesy upon the dry bones, they cannot put life into them; but, ordinarily, the grace of God works by the word and makes use of it as a means of quickening, and this is a good reason why we should never forget it, but should highly value what God has put such honour upon, and dearly love what we have found and hope still to find such benefit by. See here what is the best help for bad memories, namely, good affections. If we are quickened by the word, we shall never forget it; nay, that word that does really quicken us to and in our duty is not forgotten; though the expressions be lost, if the impressions remain, it is well.
entries.9313f7fc2799515622a992be4cbbd1f1bf1456c2: <div eID="gen12783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12784" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">94</hi> I <hi type="italic">am</hi> thine, save me; for I have sought thy precepts. <div eID="gen12784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12785" type="x-p"/> Here, 1. David claims relation to God: "<hi type="italic">I am thine,</hi> devoted to thee and owned by thee, thine in covenant." He does not say, <hi type="italic">Thou art mine</hi> (as Dr. Manton observes), though that follows of course, because that were a higher challenge; but, <hi type="italic">I am thine,</hi> expressing himself in a more humble and dutiful way of resignation; nor does he say, <hi type="italic">I am thus,</hi> but, <hi type="italic">I am thine,</hi> not pleading his own good property or qualification, but God's propriety in him: "<hi type="italic">I am thine,</hi> not my own, not the world's." 2. He proves his claim: "<hi type="italic">I have sought thy precepts;</hi> I have carefully enquired concerning my duty and diligently endeavoured to do it." This will be the best evidence that we belong to God; all that are his, though they have not found perfection, are seeking it. 3. He improves his claim: "<hi type="italic">I am thine; save me;</hi> save me from sin, save me from ruin." Those that have in sincerity given up themselves to God to be his may be sure that he will protect them and preserve them to his heavenly kingdom, <reference osisRef="Mal.3.18">Mal. iii. 18</reference>.
entries.103dba728d157a907dd86af94ba21fa1627f219f: <div eID="gen12785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12786" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">95</hi> The wicked have waited for me to destroy me: <hi type="italic">but</hi> I will consider thy testimonies. <div eID="gen12786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12787" type="x-p"/> Here, 1. David complains of the malice of his enemies: <hi type="italic">The wicked</hi> (and none but such would be enemies to so good a man) <hi type="italic">have waited for me to destroy me.</hi> They were very cruel, and aimed at no less than his destruction; they were very crafty, and sought all opportunities to do him a mischief; and they were <hi type="italic">confident</hi> (they <hi type="italic">expected,</hi> so some read it), that they should destroy him; they thought themselves sure of their prey. 2. He comforts himself in the word of God as his protection: "While they are contriving my destruction, <hi type="italic">I consider thy testimonies,</hi> which secure to me my salvation." God's testimonies are <hi type="italic">then</hi> likely to be our support, when we consider them, and dwell in our thoughts upon them.
entries.792f00c47515e6d42c07442ebbecc146567cfe36: <div eID="gen12787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12788" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">96</hi> I have seen an end of all perfection: <hi type="italic">but</hi> thy commandment <hi type="italic">is</hi> exceeding broad. <div eID="gen12788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12789" type="x-p"/> Here we have David's testimony from his own experience, 1. Of the vanity of the world and its insufficiency to make us happy: <hi type="italic">I have seen an end of all perfection.</hi> Poor perfection which one sees an end of! Yet such are all those things in this world which pass for perfections. David, in his time, had seen Goliath, the strongest, overcome, Asahel, the swiftest, overtaken, Ahithophel, the wisest, befooled, Absalom, the fairest, deformed; and, in short, he had <hi type="italic">seen an end of perfection,</hi> of <hi type="italic">all perfection.</hi> He saw it by faith; he saw it by observation; he saw an end of the perfection of the creature both in respect of sufficiency (it was scanty and defective; there is that to be done for us which the creature cannot do) and in respect of continuance; it will not last our time, for it will not last to eternity as we must. The glory of man is but as the flower of the grass. 2. Of the fulness of the word of God, and its sufficiency for our satisfaction: <hi type="italic">But thy commandment is broad, exceedingly broad.</hi> The word of God reaches to all cases, to all times. The divine law lays a restraint upon the whole man, is designed to sanctify us wholly. There is a great deal required and forbidden in every commandment. The divine promise (for that also is commanded) extends itself to all our burdens, wants, and grievances, and has that in it which will make a portion and happiness for us when we <hi type="italic">have seen an end of all perfection.</hi>
entries.82da12deccee9b182b0c414b49c5b73bc68cdf21: <div eID="gen12789" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">13. MEM.</title> <div sID="gen12790" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">97</hi> MEM. O how love I thy law! it <hi type="italic">is</hi> my meditation all the day. <div eID="gen12790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12791" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. David's inexpressible love to the word of God: <hi type="italic">O how love I thy law!</hi> He protests his affection to the word of God with a holy vehemency; he found that love to it in his heart which, considering the corruption of his nature and the temptations of the world, he could not but wonder at, and at that grace which had wrought it in him. He not only loved the promises, but loved the law, and delighted in it after the inner man. 2. An unexceptionable evidence of this. What we love we love to think of; by <hi type="italic">this</hi> it appeared that David loved the word of God that it was his <hi type="italic">meditation.</hi> He not only read the book of the law, but digested what he read in his thoughts, and was delivered into it as into a mould: it was his meditation not only in the night, when he was silent and solitary, and had nothing else to do, but in the day, when he was full of business and company; nay, and <hi type="italic">all the day;</hi> some good thoughts were interwoven with his common thoughts, so full was he of the word of God.
entries.cdcdc8d06b37ea713d7dec66c0467cca9c5879fe: <div eID="gen12791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12792" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">98</hi> Thou through thy commandments hast made me wiser than mine enemies: for they <hi type="italic">are</hi> ever with me. <hi type="super">99</hi> I have more understanding than all my teachers: for thy testimonies <hi type="italic">are</hi> my meditation. <hi type="super">100</hi> I understand more than the ancients, because I keep thy precepts. <div eID="gen12792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12793" type="x-p"/> We have here an account of David's learning, not that of the Egyptians, but of the <hi type="italic">Israelites indeed.</hi> <div eID="gen12793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12794" type="x-p"/> I. The good method by which he got it. In his youth he minded business in the country as a shepherd; from his youth he minded business in the court and camp. Which way then could he get any great stock of learning? He tells us here how he came by it; he had it from God as the author: <hi type="italic">Thou hast made me wise.</hi> All true wisdom is from God. He had it by the word of God as the means, by <hi type="italic">his commandments</hi> and <hi type="italic">his testimonies.</hi> These are able to <hi type="italic">make us wise to salvation</hi> and <hi type="italic">to furnish the man of God for every good work.</hi> 1. These David took for his constant companions: "<hi type="italic">They are ever with me,</hi> ever in my mind, ever in my eye." A good man, wherever he goes, carries his Bible along with him, if not in his hands, yet in his head and in his heart. 2. These he took for the delightful subject of his thoughts; they were his <hi type="italic">meditation,</hi> not only as matters of speculation for his entertainment, as scholars meditate on their notions, but as matters of concern, for his right management, as men of business think of their business, that they may do it in the best manner. 3. These he took for the commanding rules of all his actions: <hi type="italic">I keep thy precepts,</hi> that is, I make conscience of doing my duty in every thing. The best way to improve in knowledge is to abide and abound in all the instances of serious godliness; for, <hi type="italic">if any man do his will, he shall know of the doctrine</hi> of Christ, shall know more and more of it, <reference osisRef="John.7.17">John vii. 17</reference>. The love of the truth prepares for the light of it; the <hi type="italic">pure in heart shall see God</hi> here. <div eID="gen12794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12795" type="x-p"/> II. The great eminency he attained to in it. By studying and practising God's commandments, and making them his rule, he learnt to <hi type="italic">behave himself wisely in all his ways,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.14">1 Sam. xviii. 14</reference>. 2. He outwitted his enemies; God, by these means, made him wiser to baffle and defeat their designs against him than they were to lay them. Heavenly wisdom will carry the point, at last, against carnal policy. By keeping the commandments we secure God on our side and make him our friend, and therein are certainly wiser than those that make him their enemy. By keeping the commandments we preserve in ourselves that peace and quiet of mind which our enemies would rob us of, and so are wise for ourselves, wiser than they are for themselves, for this world as well as for the other. 2. He outstripped his <hi type="italic">teachers,</hi> and had more understanding than all of them. He means either those who would have been his teachers, who blamed his conduct and undertook to prescribe to him (by keeping God's commandments he managed his matters so that it appeared, in the event, he had taken the right measures and they had taken the wrong), or those who should have been his teachers, the priests and Levites, who sat in Moses's chair, and whose lips ought to have kept knowledge, but who neglected the study of the law, and minded their honours and revenues, and the formalities only of their religion; and so David, who conversed much with the scriptures, by that means became more intelligent than they. Or he may mean those who had been his teachers when he was young; he built so well upon the foundation which they had laid that, with the help of his Bible, he became able to teach them, to teach them all. He was not now a babe that needed milk, but had <hi type="italic">spiritual senses exercised,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.5.14">Heb. v. 14</reference>. It is no reflection upon our teachers, but rather an honour to them, to improve so as really to excel them, and not to need them. By meditation we preach to ourselves, and so we come to <hi type="italic">understand more than our teachers,</hi> for we come to understand our own hearts, which they cannot. 3.
