He outdid <hi type="italic">the ancients,</hi> either those of his day (he was young, like Elihu, and they were very old, but his keeping God's precepts taught more wisdom than the multitude of their years, <reference osisRef="Job.32.7-Job.32.8">Job xxxii. 7, 8</reference>) or those of former days; he himself quotes the proverb of the ancients (<reference osisRef="1Sam.24.13">1 Sam. xxiv. 13</reference>), but the word of God gave him to understand things better than he could do by tradition and all the learning that was handed down from preceding ages. In short, the written word is a surer guide to heaven than all the doctors and fathers, the teachers and ancients, of the church; and the sacred writings kept, and kept to, will teach us more wisdom than all their writings.
entries.84ffb44bde604b53cde12a8190f40416722703fa: <div eID="gen12795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12796" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">101</hi> I have refrained my feet from every evil way, that I might keep thy word. <div eID="gen12796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12797" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. David's care to avoid the ways of sin: "<hi type="italic">I have refrained my feet from the evil ways</hi> they were ready to step aside into. I checked myself and drew back as soon as I was aware that I was entering into temptation." Though it was a broad way, a green way, a pleasant way, and a way that many walked in, yet, being a sinful way, it was an evil way, and he refrained his feet from it, foreseeing the end of that way. And his care was universal; he shunned every evil way. <hi type="italic">By the words of thy lips I have kept myself from the paths of the destroyer,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.17.4">Ps. xvii. 4</reference>. 2. His care to be found in the way of duty; <hi type="italic">That I might keep thy word,</hi> and never transgress it. His abstaining from sin was, (1.) An evidence that he did conscientiously aim to keep God's word and had made that his rule. (2.) It was a means of his keeping God's word in the exercises of religion; for we cannot with any comfort or boldness attend on God in holy duties, so as in them to keep his word, while we are under guilt or in any by-way.
entries.e8fcb6aebc8e38c465e6d3a47a61ea08ea059506: <div eID="gen12797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12798" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">102</hi> I have not departed from thy judgments: for thou hast taught me. <div eID="gen12798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12799" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. David's constancy in his religion. He had <hi type="italic">not departed from God's judgments;</hi> he had not chosen any other rule than the word of God, nor had he wilfully deviated from that rule. A constant adherence to the ways of God in trying times will be a good evidence of our integrity. 2. The cause of his constancy: "<hi type="italic">For thou hast taught me;</hi> that is, they were divine instructions that I learned; I was satisfied that the doctrine was of God, and therefore I stuck to it." Or rather, "It was divine grace in my heart that enabled me to receive those instructions." All the saints are taught of God, for he it is that gives the understanding; and those, and those only, that are taught of God, will continue to the end in the things that they have learned.
entries.49dbff2e91d8fb377eb16e9392050b7cb2f14a89: <div eID="gen12799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12800" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">103</hi> How sweet are thy words unto my taste! <hi type="italic">yea, sweeter</hi> than honey to my mouth! <hi type="super">104</hi> Through thy precepts I get understanding: therefore I hate every false way. <div eID="gen12800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12801" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The wonderful pleasure and delight which David took in the word of God; it was <hi type="italic">sweet to his taste, sweeter than honey.</hi> There is such a thing as a spiritual taste, an inward savour and relish of divine things, such an evidence of them to ourselves, by experience, as we cannot give to others. We have <hi type="italic">heard him ourselves,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.4.2">John iv. 42</reference>. To this scripture-taste the word of God is sweet, very sweet, sweeter than any of the gratifications of sense, even those that are most delicious. David speaks as if he wanted words to express the satisfaction he took in the discoveries of the divine will and grace; no pleasure was comparable to it. 2. The unspeakable profit and advantage he gained by the word of God. (1.) It helped him to a good head: "<hi type="italic">Through thy precepts I get understanding</hi> to discern between truth and falsehood, good and evil, so as not to mistake either in the conduct of my own life or in advising others." (2.) It helped him to a good heart: "<hi type="italic">Therefore,</hi> because I have got understanding of the truth, <hi type="italic">I hate every false way,</hi> and am stedfastly resolved not to turn aside into it." Observe here, [1.] The way of sin is a false way; it deceives, and will ruin, all that walk in it; it is the wrong way, and yet it seems to a man right, <reference osisRef="Prov.14.12">Prov. xiv. 12</reference>. [2.] It is the character of every good man that he hates the way of sin, and hates it because it is a false way; he not only refrains his feet from it (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.101">v. 101</reference>), but he <hi type="italic">hates it,</hi> has an antipathy to it and a dread of it. [3.] Those who hate sin as sin will hate all sin, hate every false way, because every false way leads to destruction. And, [4.] The more understanding we get by the word of God the more rooted will our hatred of sin be (for <hi type="italic">to depart from evil, that is understanding,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.28.28">Job xxviii. 28</reference>), and the more ready we are in the scriptures the better furnished we are with answers to temptation.
entries.8b67831318a6e1b78ea1341ca63ff00041876408: <div eID="gen12801" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">14. NUN.</title> <div sID="gen12802" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">105</hi> NUN. Thy word <hi type="italic">is</hi> a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path. <div eID="gen12802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12803" type="x-p"/> Observe here, 1. The nature of the word of God, and the great intention of giving it to the world; it is a <hi type="italic">lamp and a light.</hi> It discovers to us, concerning God and ourselves, that which otherwise we could not have known; it shows us what is amiss, and will be dangerous; it directs us in our work and way, and a dark place indeed the world would be without it. It is a lamp which we may set up by us, and take into our hands for our own particular use, <reference osisRef="Prov.6.23">Prov. vi. 23</reference>. The commandment is a lamp kept burning with the oil of the Spirit; it is like the lamps in the sanctuary, and the pillar of fire to Israel. 2. The use we should make of it. It must be not only a <hi type="italic">light to our eyes,</hi> to gratify them, and fill our heads with speculations, but a <hi type="italic">light to our feet</hi> and <hi type="italic">to our path,</hi> to direct us in the right ordering of our conversation, both in the choice of our way in general and in the particular steps we take in that way, that we may not take a false way nor a false step in the right way. We are then truly sensible of God's goodness to us in giving us such a lamp and light when we make it a guide to our feet, our path.
entries.af198f7f0039f433ad277904281603d693f3123d: <div eID="gen12803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12804" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">106</hi> I have sworn, and I will perform <hi type="italic">it,</hi> that I will keep thy righteous judgments. <div eID="gen12804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12805" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The notion David had of religion; it is <hi type="italic">keeping God's righteous judgments.</hi> God's commands are his judgments, the dictates of infinite wisdom. They are righteous judgments, consonant to the eternal rules of equity, and it is our duty to keep them carefully. 2. The obligation he here laid upon himself to be religious, binding himself, by his own promise, to that which he was already bound to by the divine precept, and all little enough. "<hi type="italic">I have sworn (I have lifted up my head to the Lord, and I cannot go back</hi>) and therefore must go forward: <hi type="italic">I will perform it.</hi>" Note, (1.) It is good for us to bind ourselves with a solemn oath to be religious. We must swear to the Lord as subjects swear allegiance to their sovereign, promising fealty, appealing to God concerning our sincerity in this promise, and owning ourselves liable to the curse of we do not perform it. (2.) We must often call to mind the vows of God that are upon us, and remember that we have sworn. (3.) We must make conscience of performing unto the Lord our oaths (an honest man will be as good as his word); nor have we sworn to our own hurt, but it will be unspeakably to our hurt if we do not perform.
entries.dae08b49f699d094d602dcc985b89fbdd865ff8c: <div eID="gen12805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12806" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">107</hi> I am afflicted very much: quicken me, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , according unto thy word. <div eID="gen12806" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12807" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The representation David makes of the sorrowful condition he was in: <hi type="italic">I am afflicted very much,</hi> afflicted in spirit; he seems to mean that especially. He laboured under many discouragements; without were fightings, within were fears. This is often the lot of the best saints; therefore think it not strange if sometimes it be ours. 2. The recourse he has to God in this condition; he prays for his grace: "<hi type="italic">Quicken me, O Lord!</hi> make me lively, make me cheerful; quicken me by afflictions to greater diligence in my work. <hi type="italic">Quicken me,</hi> that is, deliver me out of my afflictions, which will be as life from the dead." He pleads the promise of God, guides his desires by it, and grounds his hopes upon it: <hi type="italic">Quicken me according to thy word.</hi> David resolved to perform his promises to God (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.106">v. 106</reference>) and therefore could, with humble boldness, beg of God to make good his word to him.
entries.becb50a6471227504a62990c06ca4e04804cbb98: <div eID="gen12807" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12808" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">108</hi> Accept, I beseech thee, the freewill offerings of my mouth, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , and teach me thy judgments. <div eID="gen12808" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12809" type="x-p"/> Two things we are here taught to pray for, in reference to our religious performances:—1. Acceptance of them. This we must aim at in all we do in religion, that, whether present or absent, we may be accepted of the Lord. What David here earnestly prays for the acceptance of are the <hi type="italic">free-will-offerings,</hi> not of his purse, but of his <hi type="italic">mouth,</hi> his prayers and praises. <hi type="italic">The calves of our lips</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.14.2">Hos. xiv. 2</reference>), <hi type="italic">the fruit of our lips</hi> (<reference osisRef="Heb.13.15">Heb. xiii. 15</reference>), these are the spiritual offerings which all Christians, as spiritual priests, must offer to God; and they must be <hi type="italic">free-will-offerings,</hi> for we must offer them abundantly and cheerfully, and it is this willing mind that is accepted. The more there is of freeness and willingness in the service of God the more pleasing it is to him. 2. Assistance in them: <hi type="italic">Teach me thy judgments.</hi> We cannot offer any thing to God which we have reason to think he will accept of, but what he is pleased to instruct us in the doing of; and we must be as earnest for the grace of God in us as for the favour of God towards us.
entries.f987633c1acfcf12378d223c8a9fcef36cddd4b2: <div eID="gen12809" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12810" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">109</hi> My soul <hi type="italic">is</hi> continually in my hand: yet do I not forget thy law. <hi type="super">110</hi> The wicked have laid a snare for me: yet I erred not from thy precepts. <div eID="gen12810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12811" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. David in danger of losing his life. There is but a step between him and death, for the <hi type="italic">wicked have laid a snare</hi> for him; Saul did so many a time, because he hated him for his piety. Wherever he was he found some design or other laid against him to take away his life, for it was that they aimed at. What they could not effect by open force they hoped to compass by treachery, which made him say, <hi type="italic">My soul is continually in my hand.</hi> It was so with him, not only as a <hi type="italic">man</hi> (so it is true of us all; wherever we are we lie exposed to the strokes of death; what we carry in our hands is easily snatched away from us by violence, or if sandy, as our life is, it easily of itself slips through our fingers), but as a <hi type="italic">man of war,</hi> a soldier, who often jeoparded his life in the high places of the field, and especially as <hi type="italic">a man after God's own heart,</hi> and, as such, hated and persecuted, and <hi type="italic">always delivered to death</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.11">2 Cor. iv. 11</reference>), <hi type="italic">killed all the day long.</hi> 2. David in no danger of losing his religion, notwithstanding this, thus in jeopardy every hour and yet constant to God and his duty. None of these things move him; for, (1.) He <hi type="italic">does not forget the law,</hi> and therefore he is likely to persevere. In the multitude of his cares for his own safety he finds room in his head and heart for the word of God, and has that in his mind as fresh as ever; and where that dwells richly it will be a <hi type="italic">well of living water.</hi> (2.) He has not yet erred from God's precepts, and therefore it is to be hoped he will not. He had stood many a shock and kept his ground, and surely that grace which had helped him hitherto would not fail him, but would still prevent his wanderings.
entries.00623ef8d3921c3a3fe683c5bc18a3da107acfe7: <div eID="gen12811" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12812" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">111</hi> Thy testimonies have I taken as a heritage for ever: for they <hi type="italic">are</hi> the rejoicing of my heart. <hi type="super">112</hi> I have inclined mine heart to perform thy statutes alway, <hi type="italic">even unto</hi> the end. <div eID="gen12812" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12813" type="x-p"/> The psalmist here in a most affectionate manner, like an Israelite indeed, resolves to stick to the word of God and to live and die by it. <div eID="gen12813" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12814" type="x-p"/> I. He resolves to portion himself in it, and there to seek his happiness, nay, there to enjoy it; "<hi type="italic">Thy testimonies</hi> (the truths, the promises, of thy word) <hi type="italic">have I taken as a heritage for ever, for they are the rejoicing of my heart.</hi>" The present delight he took in them was an evidence that the good things contained in them were in his account the best things, and the treasure which he set his heart upon. 1. He expected an eternal happiness in God's testimonies. The covenant God had made with him was an everlasting covenant, and therefore he took it as <hi type="italic">a heritage for ever.</hi> If he could not yet say, "They are my heritage," yet he could say, "I have made choice of them for my heritage; and will never take up with a portion in this life," <reference osisRef="Ps.17.14-Ps.17.15">Ps. xvii. 14, 15</reference>. God's testimonies are a heritage to all that have received the Spirit of adoption; for, <hi type="italic">if children, then heirs.</hi> They are a <hi type="italic">heritage for ever,</hi> and that no earthly heritage is (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.4">1 Pet. i. 4</reference>); all the saints accept them as such, take up with them, live upon them, and can therefore be content with but little of this world. 2. He enjoyed a present satisfaction in them: <hi type="italic">They are the rejoicing of my heart,</hi> because they will be <hi type="italic">my heritage for ever.</hi> It requires the heart of a good man to see his portion in the promise of God and not in the possessions of this world. <div eID="gen12814" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12815" type="x-p"/> II. He resolves to govern himself by it and thence to take his measures: <hi type="italic">I have inclined my heart to do thy statutes.</hi> Those that would have the blessings of God's testimonies must come under the bonds of his statutes. We must look for comfort only in the way of duty, and that duty must be done, 1. With full consent and complacency: "<hi type="italic">I have,</hi> by the grace of God, <hi type="italic">inclined my heart to it,</hi> and conquered the aversion I had to it." A good man brings his heart to his work and then it is done well. A gracious disposition to do the will of God is the acceptable principle of all obedience. 2. With constancy and perseverance. He would perform God's statutes always, in all instances, in the duty of every day, in a constant course of holy walking, and this <hi type="italic">to the end,</hi> without weariness. This is following the Lord fully.
entries.3b6f51c4cc92acff2b87c2b9ed08d51a2e22684f: <div eID="gen12815" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">15. SAMECH.</title> <div sID="gen12816" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">113</hi> I hate <hi type="italic">vain</hi> thoughts: but thy law do I love. <div eID="gen12816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12817" type="x-p"/> Here we have, 1. David's dread of the risings of sin, and the first beginnings of it: <hi type="italic">I hate</hi> vain <hi type="italic">thoughts.</hi> He does not mean that he hated them in others, for there he could not discern them, but he hated them in his own heart. Every good man makes conscience of his thoughts, for they are words to God. Vain thoughts, how light soever most make of them, are sinful and hurtful, and therefore we should account them hateful and dreadful, for they do not only divert the mind from that which is good, but open the door to all evil, <reference osisRef="Jer.4.14">Jer. iv. 14</reference>. Though David could not say that he was free from vain thoughts, yet he could say that he hated them; he did not countenance them, nor give them any entertainment, but did what he could to keep them out, at least to keep them under. <hi type="italic">The evil I do I allow not.</hi> 2. David's delight in the rule of duty: <hi type="italic">But thy law do I love,</hi> which forbids those vain thoughts, and threatens them. The more we love the law of God the more we shall get the mastery of our vain thoughts, the more hateful they will be to us, as being contrary to the whole law, and the more watchful we shall be against them, lest they draw us from that which we love.
entries.3e5dc915b1ff7ebc2805a9dd20da31ab7654fc7f: <div eID="gen12817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12818" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">114</hi> Thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> my hiding place and my shield: I hope in thy word. <div eID="gen12818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12819" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. God's care of David to protect and defend him, which he comforted himself with when his enemies were very malicious against him: <hi type="italic">Thou art my hiding-place and my shield.</hi> David, when Saul pursued him, often betook himself to close places for shelter; in war he guarded himself with his shield. Now God was both these to him, a hiding-place to preserve him from danger and a shield to preserve him in danger, his life from death and his soul from sin. Good people are safe under God's protection. He is their <hi type="italic">strength and their shield,</hi> their <hi type="italic">help and their shield,</hi> their <hi type="italic">sun and their shield,</hi> their <hi type="italic">shield and their great reward,</hi> and here their <hi type="italic">hiding-place and their shield.</hi> They may by faith retire to him, and repose in him as their hiding-place, where they are kept in secret. They may by faith oppose his power to all the might and malice of their enemies, as their shield to quench every fiery dart. 2. David's confidence in God. He is safe, and therefore he is easy, under the divine protection: "<hi type="italic">I hope in thy word,</hi> which has acquainted me with thee and assured me of thy kindness to me." Those who depend on God's promise shall have the benefit of his power and be taken under his special protection.
entries.0d68f4fc7df527bf4cb7389d0eea6126755f03b7: <div eID="gen12819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12820" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">115</hi> Depart from me, ye evildoers: for I will keep the commandments of my God. <div eID="gen12820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12821" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. David's firm and fixed resolution to live a holy life: <hi type="italic">I will keep the commandments of my God.</hi> Bravely resolved! like a saint, like a soldier; for true courage consists in a steady resolution against all sin and for all duty. Those that would keep God's commandments must be often renewing their resolutions to do so: "<hi type="italic">I will keep them.</hi> Whatever others do, this I will do; though I be singular, though all about me be evil-doers, and desert me; whatever I have done hitherto, I will for the future walk closely with God. They are the commandments of God, of my God, and therefore I will keep them. He is God and may command me, my God and will command me nothing but what is for my good." 2. His farewell to bad company, pursuant to this resolution: <hi type="italic">Depart from me, you evil-doers.</hi> Though David, as a good magistrate, was a terror to evil-doers, yet there were many such, even about court, intruding near his person; these he here abdicates, and resolves to have no conversation with them. Note, Those that resolve to keep the commandments of God must have no society with evil-doers; for bad company is a great hindrance to a holy life. We must not choose wicked people for our companions, nor be intimate with them; we must not do as they do nor do as they would have us do, <reference osisRef="Ps.1.1">Ps. i. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.11">Eph. v. 11</reference>.
entries.2ee1281bbcf5fe39aa216a0eb4dd5e85bef2c355: <div eID="gen12821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12822" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">116</hi> Uphold me according unto thy word, that I may live: and let me not be ashamed of my hope. <hi type="super">117</hi> Hold thou me up, and I shall be safe: and I will have respect unto thy statutes continually. <div eID="gen12822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12823" type="x-p"/> Here, 1. David prays for sustaining grace; for this grace sufficient he besought the Lord twice: <hi type="italic">Uphold me;</hi> and again, <hi type="italic">Hold thou me up.</hi> He sees himself not only unable to go on in his duty by any strength of his own, but in danger of falling into sin unless he was prevented by divine grace; and therefore he is thus earnest for that grace to uphold him in his integrity (<reference osisRef="Ps.41.12">Ps. xli. 12</reference>), to keep him from falling and to keep him from tiring, that he might neither turn aside to evil-doing nor be weary of well-doing. We stand no longer than God holds us and go no further than he carries us. 2. He pleads earnestly for this grace. (1.) He pleads the promise of God, his dependence upon the promise, and his expectation from it: "<hi type="italic">Uphold me, according to thy word,</hi> which word I hope in; and, if it be not performed, I shall be made <hi type="italic">ashamed of my hope,</hi> and be called a fool for my credulity." But those that hope in God's word may be sure that the word will not fail them, and therefore their hope will not make them ashamed. (2.) He pleads the great need he had of God's grace and the great advantage it would be of to him: <hi type="italic">Uphold me, that I may live,</hi> intimating that he could not live without the grace of God; he should fall into sin, into death, into hell, if God did not hold him up; but, supported by his hand, he shall live; his spiritual life shall be maintained and be an earnest of eternal life. <hi type="italic">Hold me up, and I shall be safe,</hi> out of danger and out of the fear of danger. Our holy security is grounded on divine supports. (3.) He pleads his resolution, in the strength of this grace, to proceed in his duty: "<hi type="italic">Hold me up,</hi> and then <hi type="italic">I will have respect unto thy statutes continually</hi> and never turn my eyes or feet aside from them." <hi type="italic">I will employ myself</hi> (so some), I <hi type="italic">will delight myself</hi> (so others) <hi type="italic">in thy statutes.</hi> If God's right hand uphold us, we must, in his strength, go on in our duty both with diligence and pleasure.
entries.cd13f91a2c66d5a2dbfa29e6888992920ced2c3f: <div eID="gen12823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12824" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">118</hi> Thou hast trodden down all them that err from thy statutes: for their deceit <hi type="italic">is</hi> falsehood. <hi type="super">119</hi> Thou puttest away all the wicked of the earth <hi type="italic">like</hi> dross: therefore I love thy testimonies. <hi type="super">120</hi> My flesh trembleth for fear of thee; and I am afraid of thy judgments. <div eID="gen12824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12825" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. God's judgment on wicked people, on those that <hi type="italic">wander from his statutes,</hi> that take their measures from other rules and will not have God to reign over them. All departure from God's statutes is certainly an error, and will prove a fatal one. These are <hi type="italic">the wicked of the earth;</hi> they mind earthly things, lay up their treasures in the earth, live in pleasure on the earth, and are strangers and enemies to heaven and heavenly things. Now see how God deals with them, that you may neither fear them nor envy them. 1. He <hi type="italic">treads them all down.</hi> He brings them to ruin, to utter ruin, to shameful ruin; he makes them his footstool. Though they are ever so high, he can bring them low (<reference osisRef="Amos.2.9">Amos ii. 9</reference>); he has done it many a time, and he will do it, for he resists the proud and will triumph over those that oppose his kingdom. Proud persecutors trample upon his people, but, sooner or later, he will trample upon them. 2. He <hi type="italic">puts them all away like dross.</hi> Wicked people are as dross, which, though it be mingled with the good metal in the ore, and seems to be of the same substance with it, must be separated from it. And in God's account they are worthless things, the scum and refuse of the earth, and no more to be compared with the righteous than dross with fine gold. There is a day coming which will put them away from among the righteous (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.49">Matt. xiii. 49</reference>), so that they shall have no place <hi type="italic">in their congregation</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.1.5">Ps. i. 5</reference>), which will put them away into everlasting fire, the fittest place for the dross. Sometimes, in this world, the wicked are, by the censures of the church, or the sword of the magistrate, or the judgments of God, <hi type="italic">put away as dross,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.25.4-Prov.25.5">Prov. xxv. 4, 5</reference>. <div eID="gen12825" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12826" type="x-p"/> II. The reasons of these judgments. God casts them off because they <hi type="italic">err from his statutes</hi> (those that will not submit to the commands of the word shall feel the curses of it) and because <hi type="italic">their deceit is falsehood,</hi> that is, because they deceive themselves by setting up false rules, in opposition to God's statutes, which they err from, and because they go about to deceive others with their hypocritical pretences of good and their crafty projects of mischief. <hi type="italic">Their cunning is falsehood,</hi> so Dr. Hammond. The utmost of their policy is treachery and perfidiousness; this the God of truth hates and will punish. <div eID="gen12826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12827" type="x-p"/> III. The improvement David made of these judgments. He took notice of them and received instruction from them. The ruin of the wicked helped to increase, 1. His love to the word of God. "I see what comes of sin; <hi type="italic">therefore I love thy testimonies,</hi> which warn me to take heed of those dangerous courses and <hi type="italic">keep me from the paths of the destroyer.</hi>" We see the word of Go fulfilled in his judgments on sin and sinners, and therefore we should love it. 2. His fear of the wrath of God: <hi type="italic">My flesh trembles for fear of thee.</hi> Instead of insulting over those who fell under God's displeasure, he humbled himself. What we read and hear of the judgments of God upon wicked people would make us, (1.) To reverence his terrible majesty, and to stand in awe of him: <hi type="italic">Who is able to stand before this holy Lord God?</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.6.20">1 Sam. vi. 20</reference>. (2.) To fear lest we offend him and become obnoxious to his wrath. Good men have need to be restrained from sin by <hi type="italic">the terrors of the Lord,</hi> especially when judgment <hi type="italic">begins at the house of God</hi> and hypocrites are discovered and <hi type="italic">put away as dross.</hi>
entries.fc39fc89d06e75053dda40f15ee161c2c37f768b: <div eID="gen12827" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">16. AIN.</title> <div sID="gen12828" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">121</hi> I have done judgment and justice: leave me not to mine oppressors. <hi type="super">122</hi> Be surety for thy servant for good: let not the proud oppress me. <div eID="gen12828" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12829" type="x-p"/> David here appeals to God, 1. As his witness that he had not done wrong; he could truly say, "<hi type="italic">I have done judgment and justice,</hi> that is, I have made conscience of rendering to all their due, and have not by force or fraud hindered any of their right." Take him as a king, he <hi type="italic">executed judgment and justice to all his people,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.15">2 Sam. viii. 15</reference>. Take him in a private capacity, he could appeal to Saul himself that <hi type="italic">there was no evil or transgression in his hand,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.24.11">1 Sam. xxiv. 11</reference>. Note, Honesty is the best policy and will be our rejoicing in the day of evil. 2. As his Judge, that he might not be wronged. Having done justice for others that were oppressed, he begs that God would do him justice and avenge him of his adversaries: "<hi type="italic">Be surety for thy servant, for good;</hi> undertake for me against those that would run me down and ruin me." He is sensible that he cannot make his part good himself, and therefore begs that God would appear for him. Christ is our surety with God; and, if he be so, Providence shall be our surety against all the world. Who or what shall harm us if God's power and goodness be engaged for our protection and rescue? He does not prescribe to God what he should do for him; only let it be <hi type="italic">for good,</hi> in such way and manner as Infinite Wisdom sees best; "only <hi type="italic">let me not be left to my oppressors.</hi>" Though David had <hi type="italic">done judgment and justice,</hi> yet he had many enemies; but, having God for his friend, he hoped they should not have their will against him; and in that hope he prayed again, <hi type="italic">Let not the proud oppress me.</hi> David, one of the best of men, was oppressed by the proud, whom God beholds afar off; the condition therefore of the persecuted is better than that of the persecutors, and will appear so at last.
entries.927cba022f12057fc58b788fc638010376ca8962: <div eID="gen12829" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12830" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">123</hi> Mine eyes fail for thy salvation, and for the word of thy righteousness. <div eID="gen12830" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12831" type="x-p"/> David, being oppressed, is here waiting and wishing for the salvation of the Lord, which would make him easy. 1. He cannot but think that it comes slowly: <hi type="italic">My eyes fail for thy salvation.</hi> His eyes were towards it and had been long so. He looked for help from heaven (and we deceive ourselves if we look for it any other way), but it did not come so soon as he expected, so that his eyes began to fail, and he was sometimes ready to despair, and to think that, because the salvation did not come when he looked for it, it would never come. It is often the infirmity even of good men to be weary of waiting God's time when <hi type="italic">their</hi> time has elapsed. 2. Yet he cannot hope that it comes surely; for he expects <hi type="italic">the word of God's righteousness,</hi> and no other salvation than what is secured by that word, which cannot fall to the ground because it is a word of righteousness. Though our eyes fail, yet God's word does not, and therefore those that build upon it, though now discouraged, shall in due time see his salvation.
entries.757701aded5bad1355c260970926aa41d02977da: <div eID="gen12831" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12832" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">124</hi> Deal with thy servant according unto thy mercy, and teach me thy statutes. <hi type="super">125</hi> I <hi type="italic">am</hi> thy servant; give me understanding, that I may know thy testimonies. <div eID="gen12832" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12833" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. David's petition for divine instruction: "<hi type="italic">Teach me thy statutes;</hi> give me to know all my duty; when I am in doubt, and know not for certain what is my duty, direct me, and make it plain to me; now that I am afflicted, oppressed, and <hi type="italic">my eyes</hi> are ready to <hi type="italic">fail for thy salvation,</hi> let me know what my duty is in this condition." In difficult times we should desire more to be told what we must do than what we may expect, and should pray more to be led into the knowledge of scripture-precepts than of scripture-prophecies. If God, who gave us his statutes, do not teach us, we shall never learn them. How God teaches is implied in the next petition: <hi type="italic">Give me understanding</hi> (a renewed understanding, apt to receive divine light), <hi type="italic">that I may know thy testimonies.</hi> It is God's prerogative to give an understanding, that understanding without which we cannot know God's testimonies. Those who know most of God's testimonies desire to know more, and are still earnest with God to teach them, never thinking they know enough. 2. His pleas to enforce this petition. (1.) He pleads God's goodness to him: <hi type="italic">Deal with me according to thy mercy.</hi> The best saints count this their best plea for any blessing, "Let me have it according to thy mercy;" for we deserve no favour from God, nor can we claim any as a debt, but we are most likely to be easy when we cast ourselves upon God's mercy and refer ourselves to it. Particularly, when we come to him for instruction, we must beg it as a mercy, and reckon that in being taught we are well dealt with. (2.) He pleads his relation to God: "<hi type="italic">I am thy servant,</hi> and have work to do for thee; therefore <hi type="italic">teach me</hi> to do it and to do it well." The servant has reason to expect that, if he be at a loss about his work, his master should teach him, and, if it were in his power, give him an understanding. "Lord," says David, "I desire to serve thee; show me how." If any man resolve to do God's will as his servant, he shall be made to know his testimonies, <reference osisRef="John.7.17">John vii. 17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.25.14">Ps. xxv. 14</reference>.
entries.57c45636e59f412744deaf0efd12b38baf61661d: <div eID="gen12833" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12834" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">126</hi> <hi type="italic">It is</hi> time for <hi type="italic">thee,</hi> <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , to work: <hi type="italic">for</hi> they have made void thy law. <div eID="gen12834" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12835" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. A complaint of the daring impiety of the wicked. David, having in himself a holy indignation at it, humbly represents it to God: "Lord, there are those that <hi type="italic">have made void thy law,</hi> have set thee and thy government at defiance, and have done what in them lay to cancel and vacate the obligation of thy commands." Those that sin through infirmity transgress the law, but presumptuous sinners do in effect make void the law, saying, <hi type="italic">Who is the Lord? What is the Almighty, that we should fear him?</hi> It is possible a godly man may sin against the commandment, but a wicked man would sin away the commandment, would repeal God's laws and enact his own lusts. This is the sinfulness of sin and the malignity of the carnal mind. 2. A desire that God would appear, for the vindication of his own honour: "<hi type="italic">It is time for thee, Lord, to work,</hi> to do something for the effectual confutation of atheists and infidels, and the silencing of those that set their mouth against the heavens." God's time to work is when vice has become most daring and the measure of iniquity is full. <hi type="italic">Now will I arise, saith the Lord.</hi> Some read it, and the original will bear it, <hi type="italic">It is time to work for thee, O Lord!</hi> it is time for every one in his place to appear on the Lord's side—against the threatening growth of profaneness and immorality. We must do what we can for the support of the sinking interests of religion, and, after all, we must beg of God to take the work into his own hands.
entries.61e77981593aac28e488bb25603a95e9d679777d: <div eID="gen12835" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12836" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">127</hi> Therefore I love thy commandments above gold; yea, above fine gold. <hi type="super">128</hi> Therefore I esteem all <hi type="italic">thy</hi> precepts <hi type="italic">concerning</hi> all <hi type="italic">things to be</hi> right; <hi type="italic">and</hi> I hate every false way. <div eID="gen12836" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12837" type="x-p"/> David here, as often in this psalm, professes the great love he had to the word and law of God; and, to evidence the sincerity of it, observe, 1. The degree of his love. He loved his Bible better than he loved his money—<hi type="italic">above gold, yea, above fine gold.</hi> Gold, fine gold, is what most men set their hearts upon; nothing charms them and dazzles their eyes so much as gold does. It is fine gold, a fine thing in their eyes; they will venture their souls, their God, their all, to get and keep it. But David saw that the word of God answers all purposes better than money does, for it enriches the soul towards God; and therefore he loved it better than gold, for it had done that for him which gold could not do, and would stand him in stead when the wealth of the world would fail him. 2. The ground of his love. He loved all God's commandments because he esteemed them to be right, all reasonable and just, and suited to the end for which they were made. They are all as they should be, and no fault can be found with them; and we must love them because they bear God's image and are the revelations of his will. If we thus <hi type="italic">consent to the law that it is good,</hi> we shall delight in it after the inner man. 3. The fruit and evidence of this love: He <hi type="italic">hated every false way.</hi> The way of sin being directly contrary to God's precepts, which are right, is a false way, and therefore those that have a love and esteem for God's law hate it and will not be reconciled to it.
entries.0d42d0b49f9b541498c8eef7785371db23ecdb57: <div eID="gen12837" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">17. PE.</title> <div sID="gen12838" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">129</hi> Thy testimonies <hi type="italic">are</hi> wonderful: therefore doth my soul keep them. <div eID="gen12838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12839" type="x-p"/> See here how David was affected towards the word of God. 1. He admired it, as most excellent in itself: <hi type="italic">Thy testimonies are wonderful.</hi> The word of God gives us admirable discoveries of God, and Christ, and another world; admirable proofs of divine love and grace. The majesty of the style, the purity of the matter, the harmony of the parts, are all wonderful. Its effects upon the consciences of men, both for conviction and comfort, are wonderful; and it is a sign that we are not acquainted with God's testimonies, or do not understand them, if we do not admire them. 2. He adhered to it as of constant use to him: "<hi type="italic">Therefore doth my soul keep them,</hi> as a treasure of inestimable value, which I cannot be without." We do not keep them to any purpose unless our souls keep them. There they must be deposited, as the tables of testimony in the ark, there they must have the innermost and uppermost place. Those that see God's word to be admirable will prize it highly and preserve it carefully, as that which they promise themselves great things from.
entries.6447d03c894d8cc8b99e12bd4fbc6ef55607912c: <div eID="gen12839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12840" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">130</hi> The entrance of thy words giveth light; it giveth understanding unto the simple. <div eID="gen12840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12841" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The great use for which the word of God was intended, to give light, that is, to give understanding, to give us to understand that which will be of use to us in our travels through this world; and it is the outward and ordinary means by which the Spirit of God enlightens the understanding of all that are sanctified. God's testimonies are not only wonderful for the greatness of them, but useful, as a light in a dark place. 2. Its efficacy for this purpose. It admirably answers the end; for, (1.) Even <hi type="italic">the entrance of God's word gives light.</hi> If we begin at the beginning, and take it before us, we shall find that the very first verses of the Bible give us surprising and yet satisfying discoveries of the origin of the universe, about which, without that, the world is utterly in the dark. As soon as the word of God enters into us, and has a place in us, it enlightens us; we find we begin to see when we begin to study the word of God. The very first principles of the oracles of God, the plainest truths, the milk appointed for the babes, bring a great light into the soul, much more will the soul be illuminated by the sublime mysteries that are found there. "The exposition or explication of thy word gives light;" then it is most profitable when ministers do their part <hi type="italic">in giving the sense,</hi> <reference osisRef="Neh.8.8">Neh. viii. 8</reference>. Some understand it of the New Testament, which is the opening or unfolding of the Old, which would give light concerning life and immortality. (2.) It would <hi type="italic">give understanding</hi> even <hi type="italic">to the simple,</hi> to the weakest capacities; for it shows us a way to heaven so plain that the <hi type="italic">wayfaring men, though fools, shall not err therein.</hi>
entries.3434752ab6b8f2ebfc539257c6839b0c53e251f0: <div eID="gen12841" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12842" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">131</hi> I opened my mouth, and panted: for I longed for thy commandments. <div eID="gen12842" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12843" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The desire David had towards the word of God: <hi type="italic">I longed for thy commandments.</hi> When he was under a forced absence from God's ordinances he longed to be restored to them again; when he enjoyed ordinances he greedily sucked in the word of God, <hi type="italic">as new-born babes desire the milk.</hi> When Christ is formed in the soul there are gracious longings, unaccountable to one that is a stranger to the work. 2. The degree of that desire appearing in the expressions of it: <hi type="italic">I opened my mouth and panted,</hi> as one overcome with heat, or almost stifled, pants for a mouthful of fresh air. Thus strong, thus earnest, should our desires be towards God and the remembrance of his name, <reference osisRef="Ps.42.1-Ps.42.2">Ps. xlii. 1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.50">2. Luke xii. 50</reference>.
entries.0f4839dea4327eae0b2c92d81cf054376fdf4c3d: <div eID="gen12843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12844" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">132</hi> Look thou upon me, and be merciful unto me, as thou usest to do unto those that love thy name. <div eID="gen12844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12845" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. David's request for God's favour to himself: "<hi type="italic">Look</hi> graciously <hi type="italic">upon me;</hi> let me have thy smiles, and the light of thy countenance. Take cognizance of me and my affairs, <hi type="italic">and be merciful to me;</hi> let me taste the sweetness of thy mercy and receive the gifts of thy mercy." See how humble his petition is. He asks not for the operations of God's hand, only for the smiles of his face; a good look is enough; and for that he does not plead merit, but implores mercy. 2. His acknowledgment of his favour to all his people: <hi type="italic">As thou usest to do unto those that love thy name.</hi> This is either, (1.) A plea for mercy: "Lord, I am one of <hi type="italic">those that love thy name,</hi> love thee and thy word, and thou usest to be kind to those that do so; and wilt thou be worse to me than to others of thy people?" Or, (2.) A description of the favour and mercy he desired—"that which thou usest to bestow on those that love thy name, which <hi type="italic">thou bearest to thy chosen,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ps.106.4-Ps.106.5">Ps. cvi. 4, 5</reference>. He desires no more, no better, than neighbour's fare, and he will take up with no less; common looks and common mercies will not serve, but such as are reserved for those that love him, which are such as <hi type="italic">eye has not seen,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.9">1 Cor. ii. 9</reference>. Note, The dealings of God with those that love him are such that a man needs not desire to be any better dealt with, for he will make them truly and eternally happy. And as long as God deals with us no otherwise than as he uses to deal with those that love him we have no reason to complain, <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.13">1 Cor. x. 13</reference>.
entries.e7dc6897d413c59976839537491f5f98145e7dd4: <div eID="gen12845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12846" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">133</hi> Order my steps in thy word: and let not any iniquity have dominion over me. <div eID="gen12846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12847" type="x-p"/> Here David prays for two great spiritual blessings, and is, in this verse, as earnest for the good work of God in him as, in the verse before, for the good-will of God towards him. He prays, 1. For direction in the paths of duty: "<hi type="italic">Order my steps in thy word;</hi> having led me into the right way, let every step I take in that way be under the guidance of thy grace." We ought to walk by rule; all the motions of the soul must not only be kept within the bounds prescribed by the word, so as not to transgress them, but carried out in the paths prescribed by the word, so as not to trifle in them. And therefore we must beg of God that by his good Spirit he would order our steps accordingly. 2. For deliverance from the power of sin: "<hi type="italic">Let no iniquity have dominion over me,</hi> so as to gain my consent to it, and that I should be led captive by it." The dominion of sin is to be dreaded and deprecated by every one of us; and, if in sincerity we pray against it, we may receive that promise as an answer to the prayer (<reference osisRef="Rom.6.14">Rom. vi. 14</reference>), <hi type="italic">Sin shall not have dominion over you.</hi>
entries.56f7848f268313fa17ed6aa8195cd884428f3334: <div eID="gen12847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12848" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">134</hi> Deliver me from the oppression of man: so will I keep thy precepts. <div eID="gen12848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12849" type="x-p"/> Here, 1. David prays that he might live a quiet and peaceable life, and might not be harassed and discomposed by those that studied to be vexatious: "<hi type="italic">Deliver me from the oppression of man</hi>—man, whom God can control, and whose power is limited. Let them know themselves to be <hi type="italic">but men</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.9.20">Ps. ix. 20</reference>), and let me be delivered out of the hands of my enemies, that I may serve God without fear; <hi type="italic">so will I keep thy precepts.</hi>" Not but that he would keep God's precepts, though he should be continued under oppression; "but so shall I keep thy precepts more cheerfully and with more enlargement of heart, my bonds being loosed." <hi type="italic">Then</hi> we may expect temporal blessings when we desire them with this in our eye, that we may serve God the better.
entries.66f5f0c327b15757e4d9a7f642ed6a657087f553: <div eID="gen12849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12850" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">135</hi> Make thy face to shine upon thy servant; and teach me thy statutes. <div eID="gen12850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12851" type="x-p"/> David here, as often as elsewhere, writes himself God's servant, a title he gloried in, though he was a king; now here, as became a good servant, 1. He is very ambitious of his Master's favour, accounting that his happiness and chief good. He asks not for corn and wine, for silver and gold, but, "<hi type="italic">Make thy face to shine upon thy servant;</hi> let me be accepted of thee, and let me know that I am so. Comfort me with the light of thy countenance in every cloudy and dark day. If the world frown upon me, yet do thou smile." 2. He is very solicitous about his Master's work, accounting that his business and chief concern. This he would be instructed in, that he might do it, and do it well, so as to be accepted in the doing of it: <hi type="italic">Teach me thy statutes.</hi> Note, We must pray as earnestly for grace as for comfort. If God hides his face from us, it is because we have been careless in keeping his statutes; and therefore, that we may be qualified for the returns of his favour, we must pray for wisdom to do our duty.
entries.a422b65f19baa72a47172fc46663e33378267b59: <div eID="gen12851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12852" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">136</hi> Rivers of waters run down mine eyes, because they keep not thy law. <div eID="gen12852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12853" type="x-p"/> Here we have David in sorrow. 1. It is a great sorrow, to such a degree that he weeps <hi type="italic">rivers of tears.</hi> Commonly, where there is a gracious heart, there is a weeping eye, in conformity to Christ, who was a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief. David had prayed for comfort in God's favour (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.135">v. 135</reference>), now he pleads that he was qualified for that comfort, and had need of it, for he was one of those that mourned in Zion, and those that do so shall be comforted, <reference osisRef="Isa.61.3">Isa. lxi. 3</reference>. 2. It is godly sorrow. He wept not for his troubles, though they were many, but for the dishonour done to God: <hi type="italic">Because they keep not thy law,</hi> either <hi type="italic">because my eyes keep not thy law,</hi> so some (the eye is the inlet and outlet of a great deal of sin, and therefore it ought to be a weeping eye), or, rather, <hi type="italic">they,</hi> that is, those about me, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.139">v. 139</reference>. Note, The sins of sinners are the sorrows of saints. We must mourn for that which we cannot mend.
entries.41286380d4ffc3b3a83ddb32f251cb6149c67270: <div eID="gen12853" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">18. TZADDI.</title> <div sID="gen12854" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">137</hi> Righteous <hi type="italic">art</hi> thou, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , and upright <hi type="italic">are</hi> thy judgments. 138 Thy testimonies <hi type="italic">that</hi> thou hast commanded <hi type="italic">are</hi> righteous and very faithful. <div eID="gen12854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12855" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The righteousness of God, the infinite rectitude and perfection of his nature. As he is what he is, so he is what he should be, and in every thing acts as becomes him; there is nothing wanting, nothing amiss, in God; his will is the eternal rule of equity, and he is righteous, for he does all according to it. 2. The righteousness of his government. He rules the world by his providence, according to the principles of justice, and never did, nor ever can do, any wrong to any of his creatures: <hi type="italic">Upright are thy judgments,</hi> the promises and threatenings and the executions of both. Every word of God is pure, and he will be true to it; he perfectly knows the merits of every cause and will judge accordingly. 3. The righteousness of his commands, which he has given to be the rule of our obedience: "<hi type="italic">Thy testimonies that thou hast commanded,</hi> which are backed with thy sovereign authority, and to which thou dost require our obedience, <hi type="italic">are</hi> exceedingly <hi type="italic">righteous and faithful,</hi> righteousness and faithfulness itself." As he acts like himself, so his law requires that we act like ourselves and like him, that we be just to ourselves and to all we deal with, true to all the engagements we lay ourselves under both to God and man. That which we are commanded to practise is righteous; that which we are commanded to believe is faithful. It is necessary to our faith and obedience that we be convinced of this.
entries.14f218d70135a2000809658eb84242bc2267b2e7: <div eID="gen12855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12856" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">139</hi> My zeal hath consumed me, because mine enemies have forgotten thy words. <div eID="gen12856" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12857" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The great contempt which wicked men put upon religion: <hi type="italic">My enemies have forgotten thy words.</hi> They have often heard them, but so little did they heed them that they soon forgot them, they willingly forgot them, not only through carelessness let them slip out of their minds, but contrived how to cast them behind their backs. This is at the bottom of all the wickedness of the wicked, and particularly of their malignity and enmity to the people of God; they have forgotten the words of God, else those would give check to their sinful courses. 2. The great concern which godly men show for religion. David reckoned those his enemies who forgot the words of God because they were enemies to religion, which he had entered into a league with, offensive and defensive. And therefore his <hi type="italic">zeal</hi> even <hi type="italic">consumed him,</hi> when he observed their impieties. He conceived such an indignation at their wickedness as preyed upon his spirits, even <hi type="italic">ate them up</hi> (as Christ's zeal, <reference osisRef="John.2.17">John ii. 17</reference>), swallowed up all inferior considerations, and made him forget himself. <hi type="italic">My zeal has pressed or constrained me</hi> (so Dr. Hammond reads it), <reference osisRef="Acts.18.5">Acts xviii. 5</reference>. Zeal against sin should constrain us to do what we can against it in our places, at least to do so much the more in religion ourselves. The worse others are the better we should be.
entries.f807177a22dd06d0b5d74aa831779ae81799e265: <div eID="gen12857" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12858" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">140</hi> Thy word <hi type="italic">is</hi> very pure: therefore thy servant loveth it. <div eID="gen12858" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12859" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. David's great affection for the word of God: <hi type="italic">Thy servant loves it.</hi> Every good man, being a servant of God, loves the word of God, because it lets him know his Master's will and directs him in his Master's work. Wherever there is grace there is a warm attachment to the word of God. 2. The ground and reason of that affection; he saw it to be <hi type="italic">very pure,</hi> and therefore he loved it. Our love to the word of God is <hi type="italic">then</hi> an evidence of our love to God when we love it for the sake of its purity, because it bears the image of God's holiness and is designed to make us partakers of his holiness. It commands purity, and, as it is itself refined from all corrupt mixture, so if we receive it in the light and love of it it will refine us from the dross of worldliness and fleshly-mindedness.
entries.18a242d8e58089a89940f20bdf2bca57773a7f9a: <div eID="gen12859" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12860" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">141</hi> I <hi type="italic">am</hi> small and despised: <hi type="italic">yet</hi> do not I forget thy precepts. <div eID="gen12860" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12861" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. David pious and yet poor. He was a man after God's own heart, one whom the King of kings did delight to honour, and yet <hi type="italic">small and despised</hi> in his own account and in the account of many others. Men's excellency cannot always secure them from contempt; nay, it often exposes them to the scorn of others and always makes them low in their own eyes. <hi type="italic">God has chosen the foolish things of the world,</hi> and it has been the common lot of his people to be a despised people. 2. David poor and yet pious, <hi type="italic">small and despised</hi> for his strict and serious godliness, yet his conscience can witness for him that he did <hi type="italic">not forget God's precepts.</hi> He would not throw off his religion, though it exposed him to contempt, for he knew that was designed to try his constancy. When we are small and despised we have the more need to remember God's precepts, that we may have them to support us under the pressures of a low condition.
entries.f05c102f3cc5be50bd2650171c225cf7a1fba257: <div eID="gen12861" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12862" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">142</hi> Thy righteousness <hi type="italic">is</hi> an everlasting righteousness, and thy law <hi type="italic">is</hi> the truth. <div eID="gen12862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12863" type="x-p"/> Observe, 1. That God's word <hi type="italic">is righteousness,</hi> and it <hi type="italic">is an everlasting righteousness.</hi> It is the rule of God's judgment, and it is consonant to his counsels from eternity and will direct his sentence for eternity. The word of God will judge us, it will judge us in righteousness, and by it our everlasting state will be determined. This should possess us with a very great reverence for the word of God that it is righteousness itself, the standard of righteousness, and it is everlasting in its rewards and punishments. 2. That God's word is a law, and that law is truth. See the double obligation we are under to be governed by the word of God. We are reasonable creatures, and as such we must be ruled by truth, acknowledging the force and power of it. If the principles be true, the practices must be agreeable to them, else we do not act rationally. We are creatures, and therefore subjects, and must be ruled by our Creator; and whatever he commands we are bound to obey as a law. See how these obligations are here twisted, these cords of a man. Here is truth brought to the understanding, there to sit chief, and direct the motions of the whole man; but, lest the authority of that should become weak through the flesh, here is a law to bind the will and bring that into subjection. God's truth is a law (<reference osisRef="John.18.37">John xviii. 37</reference>) <hi type="italic">and</hi> God's <hi type="italic">law is the truth;</hi> surely we cannot break such words as these asunder.
entries.d63e22dcd0e47840ab8794a3160751bd2f019d21: <div eID="gen12863" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12864" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">143</hi> Trouble and anguish have taken hold on me: <hi type="italic">yet</hi> thy commandments <hi type="italic">are</hi> my delights. <hi type="super">144</hi> The righteousness of thy testimonies <hi type="italic">is</hi> everlasting: give me understanding, and I shall live. <div eID="gen12864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12865" type="x-p"/> These two verses are almost a repetition of the two foregoing verses, but with improvement. 1. David again professes his constant adherence to God and his duty, notwithstanding the many difficulties and discouragements he met with. He had said (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.141">v. 141</reference>), <hi type="italic">I am small and despised,</hi> and yet adhere to my duty. Here he finds himself not only mean, but miserable, as far as this world could make him so: <hi type="italic">Trouble and anguish have taken hold on me</hi>—trouble without, anguish within; they surprised him, they seized him, they held him. Sorrows are often the lot of saints in this vale of tears; they are <hi type="italic">in heaviness through manifold temptations.</hi> There he had said, <hi type="italic">Yet do I not forget thy precepts;</hi> here he carries his constancy much higher: <hi type="italic">Yet thy commandments are my delights.</hi> All this trouble and anguish did not put his mouth out of taste for the comforts of the word of God, but he could still relish them and find that peace and pleasure in them which all the calamities of this present time could not deprive him of. There are delights, variety of delights, in the word of God, which the saints have often the sweetest enjoyment of when they are in trouble and anguish, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.5">2 Cor. i. 5</reference>. 2. He again acknowledges the everlasting righteousness of God's word as before (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.142">v. 142</reference>): <hi type="italic">The righteousness of thy testimonies is everlasting</hi> and cannot be altered; and, when it is admitted in its power into a soul, it is there an abiding principle, <hi type="italic">a well of living water,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.4.14">John iv. 14</reference>. We ought to meditate much and often upon the equity and the eternity of the word of God. Here he adds, by way of inference, (1.) His prayer for grace: <hi type="italic">Give me understanding.</hi> Those that know much of the word of God should still covet to know more; for there is more to be known. He does not say, "Give me a further revelation," but, <hi type="italic">Give me a further understanding;</hi> what is revealed we should desire to understand, and what we know to know better; and we must go to God for a heart to know. (2.) His hope of glory: "Give me this renewed understanding, and then <hi type="italic">I shall live,</hi> shall live for ever, shall be eternally happy, and shall be comforted, for the present, in the prospect of it." <hi type="italic">This is life eternal, to know God,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.17.3">John xvii. 3</reference>.
entries.58b62fd1c9be7c3ba364b2a5d2d00edf997c1bd8: <div eID="gen12865" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">19. KOPH.</title> <div sID="gen12866" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">145</hi> I cried with <hi type="italic">my</hi> whole heart; hear me, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> : I will keep thy statutes. 146 I cried unto thee; save me, and I shall keep thy testimonies. <div eID="gen12866" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12867" type="x-p"/> Here we have, I. David's good prayers, by which he sought to God for mercy; these he mentions here, not as boasting of them, or trusting to any merit in them, but reflecting upon them with comfort, that he had taken the appointed way to comfort. Observe here, 1. That he was inward with God in prayer; he prayed <hi type="italic">with his heart,</hi> and prayer is acceptable no further than the heart goes along with it. Lip-labour, if that be all, is lost labour. 2. He was importunate with God in prayer; he <hi type="italic">cried,</hi> as one in earnest, with fervour of affection and a holy vehemence and vigour of desire. <hi type="italic">He cried with his whole heart;</hi> all the powers of his soul were not only engaged and employed, but exerted to the utmost, in his prayers. <hi type="italic">Then</hi> we are likely to speed when we thus strive and wrestle in prayer. 3. That he directed his prayer to God: <hi type="italic">I cried unto thee.</hi> Whither should the child go but to his father when any thing ails him? 4. That the great thing he prayed for was salvation: <hi type="italic">Save me.</hi> A short prayer (for we mistake if we think we shall be heard for our much speaking), but a comprehensive prayer: "Not only rescue me from ruin, but make me happy." We need desire no more than God's salvation (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.23">Ps. l. 23</reference>) and the <hi type="italic">things that accompany</hi> it, <reference osisRef="Heb.6.9">Heb. vi. 9</reference>. 5. That he was earnest for an answer; and not only looked up in his prayers, but looked up after them, to see what became of them (<reference osisRef="Ps.5.3">Ps. v. 3</reference>): "Lord, <hi type="italic">hear me,</hi> and let me know that thou hearest me." <div eID="gen12867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12868" type="x-p"/> II. David's good purposes, by which he bound himself to duty when he was in the pursuit of mercy. "<hi type="italic">I will keep thy statutes;</hi> I am resolved that by thy grace I will;" for, <hi type="italic">if we turn away our ear from hearing the law,</hi> we cannot expect an answer of peace to our prayers, <reference osisRef="Prov.28.9">Prov. xxviii. 9</reference>. This purpose is used as a humble plea (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.146">v. 146</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Save me</hi> from my sins, my corruptions, my temptations, all the hindrances that lie in my way, that I may <hi type="italic">keep thy testimonies.</hi>" We must cry for salvation, not that we may have the ease and comfort of it, but that we may have an opportunity of serving God the more cheerfully.
entries.8f521f8e936f24a4a0770a0bbc5d0e54354eb05e: <div eID="gen12868" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12869" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">147</hi> I prevented the dawning of the morning, and cried: I hoped in thy word. <hi type="super">148</hi> Mine eyes prevent the <hi type="italic">night</hi> watches, that I might meditate in thy word. <div eID="gen12869" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12870" type="x-p"/> David goes on here to relate how he had abounded in the duty of prayer, much to his comfort and advantage: he cried unto God, that is, offered up to him his pious and devout affections with all seriousness. Observe, <div eID="gen12870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12871" type="x-p"/> I. The handmaids of his devotion. The two great exercises that attended his prayers, and were helpful to them, were, 1. Hope in God's word, which encouraged him to continue instant in prayer, though the answer did not come immediately: "I cried, and hoped that at last I should speed, because <hi type="italic">the vision is for an appointed time, and at the end it will speak and not lie. I hoped in thy word,</hi> which I knew would not fail me." 2. Meditation in God's word. The more intimately we converse with the word of God, and the more we dwell upon it in our thoughts, the better able we shall be to speak to God in his own language and the better we shall know what to pray for as we ought. Reading the word will not serve, but we must meditate in it. <div eID="gen12871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12872" type="x-p"/> II. The hours of his devotion. <hi type="italic">He anticipated the dawning of the morning,</hi> nay, and <hi type="italic">the night-watches.</hi> See here, 1. That David was an early riser, which perhaps contributed to his eminency. He was none of those that say, <hi type="italic">Yet a little sleep.</hi> 2. That he began the day with God. The first thing he did in the morning, before he admitted any business, was to pray, when his mind was most fresh and in the best frame. If our first thoughts in the morning be of God they will help to keep us in his fear all the day long. 3. That his mind was so full of God, and the cares and delights of his religion, that a little sleep served his turn. Even in <hi type="italic">the night-watches,</hi> when he awaked from his first sleep, he would rather meditate and pray than turn himself and go to sleep again. He <hi type="italic">esteemed the words of God's mouth more than his necessary</hi> repose, which we can as ill spare as our <hi type="italic">food,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.23.12">Job xxiii. 12</reference>. 4. That he would redeem time for religious exercises. He was full of business all day, but that will excuse no man from secret devotion; it is better to take time from sleep, as David did, than not to find time for prayer. And this is our comfort, when we pray in the night, that we can never come unseasonably to the throne of grace; for we may have access to it at all hours. Baal may be asleep, but Israel's God never slumbers, nor are there any hours in which he may not be spoken with.
entries.ca02545d3a781cc114033e2a7aacf05fe91401c5: <div eID="gen12872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12873" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">149</hi> Hear my voice according unto thy lovingkindness: <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , quicken me according to thy judgment. <div eID="gen12873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12874" type="x-p"/> Here, 1. David applies to God for grace and comfort with much solemnity. He begs of God to hear his voice: "Lord, I have something to say to thee; shall I obtain a gracious audience?" Well, what has he to say? What is his petition and what is his request? It is not long, but it has much in a little: "<hi type="italic">Lord, quicken me;</hi> stir me up to that which is good, and make me vigorous, and lively, and cheerful in it. Let habits of grace be drawn out into act." 2. He encourages himself to hope that he shall obtain his request; for he depends, (1.) Upon God's lovingkindness: "He is good, therefore he will be good to me, who hope in his mercy. His lovingkindness manifested to me will help to quicken me, and put life into me." (2.) Upon God's <hi type="italic">judgment,</hi> that is, his wisdom ("He knows what I need, and what is good for me, and therefore will quicken me"), or his promise, the word which he has spoken, mercy secured by the new covenant: <hi type="italic">Quicken me according to</hi> the tenour of that covenant.
entries.fe447d67cb80f9b53cd5c6236d87bb70e30b30dc: <div eID="gen12874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12875" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">150</hi> They draw nigh that follow after mischief: they are far from thy law. <hi type="super">151</hi> Thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> near, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> ; and all thy commandments <hi type="italic">are</hi> truth. <div eID="gen12875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12876" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The apprehension David was in of danger from his enemies. 1. They were very malicious, and industrious in prosecuting their malicious designs: They <hi type="italic">follow after mischief,</hi> any mischief they could do to David or his friends; they would let slip no opportunity nor let fall any pursuit that might be to his hurt. 2. They were very impious, and had no fear of God before their eyes: <hi type="italic">They are far from thy law,</hi> setting themselves as far as they can out of the reach of its convictions and commands. The persecutors of God's people are such as make light of God himself; we may therefore be sure that God will take his people's part against them. 3. They followed him closely and he was just ready to fall into their hands: <hi type="italic">They draw nigh,</hi> nigher than they were; so that they got ground of him. They were at his heels, just upon his back. God sometimes suffers persecutors to prevail very far against his people, so that, as David said (<reference osisRef="1Sam.20.3">1 Sam. xx. 3</reference>), <hi type="italic">There is but a step between them and death.</hi> Perhaps this comes in here as a reason why David was so earnest in prayer, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.149">v. 149</reference>. God brings us into imminent perils, as he did Jacob, that, like him, we may wrestle for a blessing. <div eID="gen12876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12877" type="x-p"/> II. The assurance David had of protection with God: "<hi type="italic">They draw nigh</hi> to destroy me, but <hi type="italic">thou art near, O Lord!</hi> to save me, not only mightier than they and therefore able to help me against them, but nearer than they and therefore ready to help." It is the happiness of the saints that, when trouble is near, God is near, and no trouble can separate between them and him. He is never far to seek, but he is within our call, and means are within his call, <reference osisRef="Deut.4.7">Deut. iv. 7</reference>. <hi type="italic">All thy commandments are truth.</hi> The enemies thought to defeat the promises God had made to David, but he was sure it was out of their power; they were inviolably true, and would be infallibly performed.
entries.65cad375d67f863d90b193a0499633c580fca762: <div eID="gen12877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12878" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">152</hi> Concerning thy testimonies, I have known of old that thou hast founded them for ever. <div eID="gen12878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12879" type="x-p"/> This confirms what he had said in the close of the foregoing verses, <hi type="italic">All thy commandments are truth;</hi> he means the covenant, the word which God has commanded to a thousand generations. This is firm, as true as truth itself. For, 1. God has founded it so; he has framed it for a perpetuity. Such is the constitution of it, and so well ordered is it in all things, that it cannot but be sure. The promises are <hi type="italic">founded for ever,</hi> so that when heaven and earth shall have passed away every iota and tittle of the promise shall stand firm, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.20">2 Cor. i. 20</reference>. 2. David had found it so, both by a work of God's grace upon his heart (begetting in him a full persuasion of the truth of God's word and enabling him to rely upon it with a full satisfaction) and by the works of his providence on his behalf, fulfilling the promise beyond what he expected. Thus he <hi type="italic">knew of old,</hi> from the days of his youth, ever since he began to look towards God, that the word of God is what one may venture one's all upon. This assurance was confirmed by the observations and experiences of his own life all along, and of others that had gone before him in the ways of God. All that ever dealt with God, and trusted in him will own that they have found him faithful.
entries.d0cac87ccb12949bbf207da4fd3f8e2a5798abab: <div eID="gen12879" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">20. RESH.</title> <div sID="gen12880" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">153</hi> Consider mine affliction, and deliver me: for I do not forget thy law. <hi type="super">154</hi> Plead my cause, and deliver me: quicken me according to thy word. <div eID="gen12880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12881" type="x-p"/> Here, I. David prays for succour in distress. <hi type="italic">Is any afflicted? let him pray;</hi> let him pray as David does here. 1. He has an eye to God's pity, and prays, "<hi type="italic">Consider my affliction;</hi> take it into thy thoughts, and all the circumstances of it, and sit not by as one unconcerned." God is never unmindful of his people's afflictions, but he will have us to <hi type="italic">put him in remembrance</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.43.26">Isa. xliii. 26</reference>), to spread our case before him, and then leave it to his compassionate consideration to do in it as in his wisdom he shall think fit, in his own time and way. 2. He has an eye to God's power and prays, <hi type="italic">Deliver me;</hi> and again, "<hi type="italic">Deliver me;</hi> consider my troubles and bring me out of them." God has promised deliverance (<reference osisRef="Ps.50.15">Ps. l. 15</reference>) and we may pray for it, with submission to his will and with regard to his glory, that we may serve him the better. 3. He has an eye to God's righteousness, and prays, "<hi type="italic">Plead my cause;</hi> be thou my patron and advocate, and take me for thy client." David had a just cause, but his adversaries were many and mighty, and he was in danger of being run down by them; he therefore begs of God to clear his integrity and silence their false accusations. If God do not plead his people's cause, who will? He is righteous, and they commit themselves to him, and therefore he will do it, and do it effectually, <reference osisRef="Isa.51.22">Isa. li. 22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.50.34">Jer. l. 34</reference>. (4.) He has an eye to God's grace, and prays, "<hi type="italic">Quicken me.</hi> Lord, I am weak, and unable to bear my troubles; my spirit is apt to droop and sink. O that thou wouldst revive and comfort me, till the deliverance is wrought!" <div eID="gen12881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12882" type="x-p"/> II. He pleads his dependence upon the word of God and his obedient regard to its directions: <hi type="italic">Quicken</hi> and <hi type="italic">deliver me according to thy word</hi> of promise, <hi type="italic">for I do not forget thy precepts.</hi> The more closely we cleave to the word of God, both as our rule and as our stay, the more assurance we may have of deliverance in due time.
entries.0ac209ace806cd93696f681252ec7400d19b6664: <div eID="gen12882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12883" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">155</hi> Salvation <hi type="italic">is</hi> far from the wicked: for they seek not thy statutes. <div eID="gen12883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12884" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The description of wicked men. They do not only do God's statutes, but they do not so much as seek them; they do not acquaint themselves with them, nor so much as desire to know their duty, nor in the least endeavour to do it. Those are wicked indeed who do not think the law of God worth enquiring after, but are altogether regardless of it, being resolved to live at large and to walk in the way of their heart. 2. Their doom: <hi type="italic">Salvation is far from</hi> them. They cannot upon any good grounds promise themselves temporal deliverance. <hi type="italic">Let not that man think that he shall receive any thing of the Lord.</hi> How can those expect to seek God's favour with success, when they are in adversity, who never sought his statutes when they were in prosperity? But eternal salvation is certainly far from them. They flatter themselves with a conceit that it is near, and that they are going to heaven; but they are mistaken: it is far from them. They thrust it from them by thrusting the Saviour from them; it is so far from them that they cannot reach it, and the longer they persist in sin the further it is; nay, while salvation is far from them, damnation is near; it slumbers not. <hi type="italic">Behold, the Judge stands before the door.</hi>
