entries.a30c5951bfa348d6a95b721483e6cf3fa72b77a7: <div eID="gen12884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12885" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">156</hi> Great <hi type="italic">are</hi> thy tender mercies, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> : quicken me according to thy judgments. <div eID="gen12885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12886" type="x-p"/> Here, 1. David admires God's grace: <hi type="italic">Great are thy tender mercies, O Lord!</hi> The goodness of God's nature, as it is his glory, so it is the joy of all the saints. His mercies are tender, for he is full of compassion; they are many, they are great, a fountain that can never be exhausted. He is rich in mercy to all that call upon him. David had spoken of the misery of the wicked (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.155">v. 155</reference>); but God is good notwithstanding; there were tender mercies sufficient in God to have saved them, if they had not "<hi type="italic">despised the riches of those mercies.</hi>" Those that are delivered from the sinner's doom are bound for ever to own the greatness of God's mercies which delivered them. 2. He begs for God's grace, reviving quickening grace, <hi type="italic">according to his judgments,</hi> that is, according to the tenour of the new covenant (that established rule by which he goes in dispensing that grace) or according to his manner, his custom or usage, with those that love his name, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.132">v. 132</reference>.
entries.4bafdbc1828f46f1f68d28bfe9f76c0c2590388c: <div eID="gen12886" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12887" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">157</hi> Many <hi type="italic">are</hi> my persecutors and mine enemies; <hi type="italic">yet</hi> do I not decline from thy testimonies. <div eID="gen12887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12888" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. David surrounded with difficulties and dangers: <hi type="italic">Many are my persecutors and my enemies.</hi> When Saul the king was his persecutor and enemy no marvel that many more were so: multitudes will follow the pernicious ways of abused authority. David, being a public person, had many enemies, but withal he had many friends, who loved him and wished him well; let him set the one over-against the other. In this David was a type both of Christ and his church. The enemies, the persecutors, of both, are many, very many. 2. David established in the way of his duty, notwithstanding: "<hi type="italic">Yet do I not decline from thy testimonies,</hi> as knowing that while I adhere to them God is for me; and then no matter who is against me." A man who is steady in the way of his duty, though he may have many enemies, needs fear none.
entries.b0fc98731eed4f2554e30c50c5d3a07791387615: <div eID="gen12888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12889" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">158</hi> I beheld the transgressors, and was grieved; because they kept not thy word. <div eID="gen12889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12890" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. David's sorrow for the wickedness of the wicked. Though he conversed much at home, yet sometimes he looked abroad, and could not but see the wicked walking on every side. He <hi type="italic">beheld the transgressors,</hi> those whose sins were open before all men, and it <hi type="italic">grieved</hi> him to see them dishonour God, serve Satan, debauch the world, and ruin their own souls, to see the transgressors so numerous, so daring, so very impudent, and so industrious to draw unstable souls into their snares. All this cannot but be a grief to those who have any regard to the glory of God and the welfare of mankind. 2. The reason of that sorrow. He was grieved, not because they were vexatious to him, but because they were provoking to God: <hi type="italic">They kept not thy word.</hi> Those that hate sin truly hate it as sin, as a transgression of the law of God and a violation of his word.
entries.e85118ba1fe46e71131093f6abe3c1aa509eb3b1: <div eID="gen12890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12891" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">159</hi> Consider how I love thy precepts: quicken me, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , according to thy lovingkindness. <div eID="gen12891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12892" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. David's appeal to God concerning his love to his precepts: "Lord, thou knowest all things, thou knowest that I love them; consider it then, and deal with me as thou usest to deal with those that love thy word, which thou hast magnified above all thy name." He does not say, "Consider how I fulfil thy precepts;" he was conscious to himself that in many things he came short; but, "Consider how I love them." Our obedience is pleasing to God, and pleasant to ourselves, only when it comes from a principle of love. 2. His petition thereupon: "<hi type="italic">Quicken me,</hi> to do my duty with vigour; revive me, keep me alive, not according to any merit of mine, though I love thy word, <hi type="italic">but according to thy lovingkindness;</hi>" to that we owe our lives, nay, that is better than life itself. We need not desire to be quickened any further than God's lovingkindness will quicken us.
entries.9f6e9e5c2cc036412571aed2007d0ea23fa6f9d4: <div eID="gen12892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12893" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">160</hi> Thy word <hi type="italic">is</hi> true <hi type="italic">from</hi> the beginning: and every one of thy righteous judgments <hi type="italic">endureth</hi> for ever. <div eID="gen12893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12894" type="x-p"/> David here comforts himself with the faithfulness of God's word, for the encouragement of himself and others to rely upon it. 1. It has always been found faithful hitherto, and never failed any that ventured upon it; <hi type="italic">It is true from the beginning.</hi> Ever since God began to reveal himself to the children of men all he said was true and to be trusted. The church, from its beginning, was built upon this rock. It has not gained its validity by lapse of time, as many governments, whose best plea is prescription and long usage, <hi type="italic">Quod initio non valet, tractu temporis convalescit—That which, at first, wanted validity, in the progress of time acquired it.</hi> But the <hi type="italic">beginning of God's word was true</hi> (so some read it); his government was laid on a sure foundation. And all, in every age, that have received God's word in faith and love, have found every saying in it <hi type="italic">faithful and well worthy of all acceptation.</hi> 2. It will be found faithful to the end, because righteous: "<hi type="italic">Every one of thy judgments remains for ever</hi> unalterable and of perpetual obligation, adjusting men's everlasting doom."
entries.f60e1add4e3d7ec6d18f955c072de9d9bcd4f2ed: <div eID="gen12894" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">21. SCHIN.</title> <div sID="gen12895" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">161</hi> Princes have persecuted me without a cause: but my heart standeth in awe of thy word. <div eID="gen12895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12896" type="x-p"/> David here lets us know, 1. How he was discouraged in his duty by the fear of man: <hi type="italic">Princes persecuted him.</hi> They looked upon him as a traitor and an enemy to the government, and under that notion sought his life, and bade him <hi type="italic">go serve other gods,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.26.19">1 Sam. xxvi. 19</reference>. It has been the common lot of the best men to be persecuted; and the case is the worse if princes be the persecutors, for they have not only the sword in their hand, and therefore can do the more hurt, but they have the law on their side, and can do it with reputation and a colour of justice. It is sad that the power which magistrates have from God, and should use for him, should ever be employed against him. But <hi type="italic">marvel not at the matter,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.8">Eccl. v. 8</reference>. It was a comfort to David that when princes persecuted him he could truly say it was without cause, he never gave them any provocation. 2. How he was kept to his duty, notwithstanding, by the fear of God: "They would make me stand in awe of them and their word, and do as they bid me; but <hi type="italic">my heart stands in awe of thy word,</hi> and I am resolved to please God, and keep in with him, whoever is displeased and falls out with me." Every gracious soul stands in awe of the word of God, of the authority of its precepts and the terror of its threatenings; and to those that do so nothing appears, in the power and wrath of man, at all formidable. We ought to obey God rather than men, and to make sure of God's favour, though we throw ourselves under the frowns of all the world, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.4-Luke.12.5">Luke xii. 4, 5</reference>. The heart that stands in awe of God's word is armed against the temptations that arise from persecution.
entries.8ad0eef39015a9f841dc25b0c6367f9ba7c19813: <div eID="gen12896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12897" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">162</hi> I rejoice at thy word, as one that findeth great spoil. <div eID="gen12897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12898" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. The pleasure David took in the word of God. He rejoiced at it, rejoiced that God had made such a discovery of his mind, that Israel was blessed with that light when other nations sat in darkness, that he was himself let into the understanding of it and had had experience of the power of it. He took a pleasure in reading it, hearing it, and meditating on it, and every thing he met with in it was agreeable to him. He had just now said that his heart stood in awe of his word, and yet here he declares that he rejoiced in it. The more reverence we have for the word of God the more joy we shall find in it. 2. The degree of that pleasure—<hi type="italic">as one that finds great spoil.</hi> This supposes a victory over the enemy. It is through much opposition that a soul comes to this, to <hi type="italic">rejoice in God's word.</hi> But, besides the pleasure and honour of a conquest, there is great advantage gained by the plunder of the field, which adds much to the joy. By the word of God we become more than conquerors, that is, unspeakable gainers.
entries.c3f00699c971407993c82676472d2fbe230c92b3: <div eID="gen12898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12899" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">163</hi> I hate and abhor lying: <hi type="italic">but</hi> thy law do I love. <div eID="gen12899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12900" type="x-p"/> Love and hatred are the leading affections of the soul; if those be fixed aright, the rest move accordingly. Here we have them fixed aright in David. 1. He had a rooted antipathy to sin; he could not endure to think of it: <hi type="italic">I hate and abhor lying,</hi> which may be taken for all sin, inasmuch as by it we deal treacherously and perfidiously with God and put a cheat upon ourselves. Hypocrisy is lying; false doctrine is lying; breach of faith is lying. Lying, in commerce or conversation, is a sin which every good man hates and abhors, hates and doubly hates, because of the seven things which the Lord hates <hi type="italic">one</hi> is a <hi type="italic">lying tongue</hi> and <hi type="italic">another</hi> is a <hi type="italic">false witness that speaks lies,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.6.16">Prov. vi. 16</reference>. Every man hates to have a lie told him; but we should more hate telling a lie because by the former we only receive an affront from men, by the latter we give an affront to God. 2. He had a rooted affection to the word of God: <hi type="italic">Thy law do I love.</hi> And therefore he abhorred lying, for lying is contrary to the whole law of God; and the reason why he loved the law of God was because of the truth of it. The more we see of the amiable beauty of truth the more we shall see of the detestable deformity of a lie.
entries.a1b662cae64f9718b313f30d00f3a1899f10422e: <div eID="gen12900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12901" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">164</hi> Seven times a day do I praise thee because of thy righteous judgments. <div eID="gen12901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12902" type="x-p"/> David, in this psalm, is full of complaints, yet those did neither jostle out his praises nor put him out of tune for them; whatever condition a child of God is in he does not want matter for praise and therefore should not want a heart. See here, 1. How often David praised God—<hi type="italic">Seven times a day,</hi> that is, very frequently, not only every day, but often every day. Many think that once a week will serve, or once or twice a day, but David would praise God seven times a day at least. Praising God is a duty which we should very much abound in. We must praise God at every meal, praise him upon all occasions, in every thing give thanks. We should praise God seven times a day, for the subject can never be exhausted and our affections should never be tired. See <reference osisRef="Ps.119.62">v. 62</reference>. 2. What he praised God for—<hi type="italic">because of thy righteous judgments.</hi> We must praise God for his precepts, which are all just and good, for his promises and threatenings and the performance of both in his providence. We are to praise God even for our afflictions, if through grace we get good by them.
entries.daf5da71d5735810086746ec3febe49fd5721196: <div eID="gen12902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12903" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">165</hi> Great peace have they which love thy law: and nothing shall offend them. <div eID="gen12903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12904" type="x-p"/> Here is an account of the happiness of good men, who are governed by a principle of love to the word of God, who make it their rule and are ruled by it. 2. They are easy, and have a holy serenity; none enjoy themselves more than they do: <hi type="italic">Great peace have those that love thy law,</hi> abundant satisfaction in doing their duty and pleasure in reflecting upon it. <hi type="italic">The work of righteousness is peace</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.32.17">Isa. xxxii. 17</reference>), such peace as the world can neither give nor take away. They may be in great troubles without and yet enjoy great peace within, <hi type="italic">sat lucis intus—abundance of internal light.</hi> Those that love the world have great vexation, for it does not answer their expectation; those that love God's word have great peace, for it outdoes their expectation, and in it they have sure footing. 2. They are safe, and have a holy security: <hi type="italic">Nothing shall offend them;</hi> nothing shall be a scandal, snare, or stumbling-block, to them, to entangle them either in guilt or grief. No event of providence shall be either an invincible temptation or an intolerable affliction to them, but their love to the word of God shall enable them both to hold fast their integrity and to preserve their tranquility. They will make the best of that which is, and not quarrel with any thing that God does. Nothing shall offend or hurt them, for every thing shall work for good to them, and therefore shall please them, and they shall reconcile themselves to it. Those in whom this holy love reigns will not be apt to perplex themselves with needless scruples, nor to take offence at their brethren, <reference osisRef="1Cor.13.6-1Cor.13.7">1 Cor. xiii. 6, 7</reference>.
entries.26e5e2b1f71c81d24ceb92846d0c6dddb1645daf: <div eID="gen12904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12905" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">166</hi> <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , I have hoped for thy salvation, and done thy commandments. <div eID="gen12905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12906" type="x-p"/> Here is the whole duty of man; for we are taught, 1. To keep our eye upon God's favour as our end: "<hi type="italic">Lord, I have hoped for thy salvation,</hi> not only temporal but eternal salvation. I have hoped for that as my happiness and laid up my treasure in it; I have hoped for it as thine, as a happiness of thy preparing, thy promising, and which consists in being with thee. Hope of this has raised me above the world, and borne me up under all my burdens in it." 2. To keep our eye upon God's word as our rule: <hi type="italic">I have done thy commandments,</hi> that is, I have made conscience of conforming myself to thy will in every thing. Observe here how God has joined these two together, and let no man put them asunder. We cannot, upon good grounds, hope for God's salvation, unless we set ourselves to do his commandments, <reference osisRef="Rev.22.14">Rev. xxii. 14</reference>. But those that sincerely endeavour to do his commandments ought to keep up a good hope of the salvation; and that hope will both engage and enlarge the heart in doing the commandments. The more lively the hope is the more lively the obedience will be.
entries.24267f7b6bc1934bcde72a61b00ddda74ad86de7: <div eID="gen12906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12907" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">167</hi> My soul hath kept thy testimonies; and I love them exceedingly. <hi type="super">168</hi> I have kept thy precepts and thy testimonies: for all my ways <hi type="italic">are</hi> before thee. <div eID="gen12907" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12908" type="x-p"/> David's conscience here witnesses for him, <div eID="gen12908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12909" type="x-p"/> I. That his practices were good. 1. He loved God's testimonies, he loved them exceedingly. Our love to the word of God must be a superlative love (we must love it better than the wealth and pleasure of this world), and it must be a victorious love, such as will subdue and mortify our lusts and extirpate carnal affections. 2. He kept them, his soul kept them. Bodily exercise profits little in religion; we must make heart-work of it or we make nothing of it. The soul must be sanctified and renewed, and delivered into the mould of the word; the soul must be employed in glorifying God, for he will be worshipped in the spirit. We must keep both the precepts and the testimonies, the commands of God by our obedience to them and his promises by our reliance on them. <div eID="gen12909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12910" type="x-p"/> II. That he was governed herein by a good principle: "<hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> I have kept thy precepts, because by faith I have seen thy eye always upon me; <hi type="italic">all my ways are before thee;</hi> thou knowest every step I take and strictly observest all I say and do. Thou dost see and accept all that I say and do well; thou dost see and art displeased with all I say and do amiss." Note, The consideration of this, that God's eye is upon us at all times, should make us very careful in every thing to keep his commandments, <reference osisRef="Gen.17.1">Gen. xvii. 1</reference>.
entries.c3f190efc1a2e43c6fde06e0aff3c14972cca3e6: <div eID="gen12910" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">22. TAU.</title> <div sID="gen12911" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">169</hi> Let my cry come near before thee, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> : give me understanding according to thy word. <hi type="super">170</hi> Let my supplication come before thee: deliver me according to thy word. <div eID="gen12911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12912" type="x-p"/> Here we have, I. A general petition for audience repeated: <hi type="italic">Let my cry come near before thee;</hi> and again, <hi type="italic">Let my supplication come before thee.</hi> He calls his prayer his <hi type="italic">cry,</hi> which denotes the fervency and vehemence of it, and his <hi type="italic">supplication,</hi> which denotes the humility of it. We must come to God as beggars come to our doors for an alms. He is concerned that his prayer might come before God, might come near before him, that is, that he might have grace and strength by faith and fervency to lift up his prayers, that no guilt might interpose to shut out his prayers and to separate between him and God, and that God would graciously receive his prayers and take notice of them. His prayer that his supplication might come before God implied a deep sense of his unworthiness, and a holy fear that his prayer should come short or miscarry, as not fit to come before God; nor would any of out prayers have had access to God if Jesus Christ had not approached to him as an advocate for us. <div eID="gen12912" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12913" type="x-p"/> II. Two particular requests, which he is thus earnest to present:—1. That God, by his grace, would give him wisdom to conduct himself well under his troubles: <hi type="italic">Give me understanding;</hi> he means that wisdom of the prudent which is to understand his way; "Give me to know thee and myself, and my duty to thee." 2. That God, by his providence, would rescue him out of his troubles: <hi type="italic">Deliver me,</hi> that is, with the temptation make a way to escape, <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.13">1 Cor. x. 13</reference>. <div eID="gen12913" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12914" type="x-p"/> III. The same general plea to enforce these requests—<hi type="italic">according to thy word.</hi> This directs and limits his desires: "Lord, give me such an understanding as thou hast promised and such a deliverance as thou hast promised; I ask for no other." It also encourages his faith and expectation: "Lord, that which I pray for is what thou hast promised, and wilt not thou be as good as thy word?"
entries.d315479b60df1e0be4113849145dc4d18e663a23: <div eID="gen12914" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12915" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">171</hi> My lips shall utter praise, when thou hast taught me thy statutes. <div eID="gen12915" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12916" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. A great favour which David expects from God, that he will teach him his <hi type="italic">statutes.</hi> This he had often prayed for in this psalm, and urged his petition for it with various arguments; and now that he is drawing towards the close of the psalm he speaks of it as taken for granted. Those that are humbly earnest with God for his grace, and resolve with Jacob that they will not let him go unless he bless them with spiritual blessings, may be humbly confident that they shall at length obtain what they are so importunate for. The God of Israel will grant them those things which they request of him. 2. The grateful sense he promises to have of that favour: <hi type="italic">My lips shall utter praise when thou hast taught me.</hi> (1.) Then he shall have cause to praise God. Those that are taught of God have a great deal of reason to be thankful, for this is the foundation of all these spiritual blessings, which are the best blessings, and the earnest of eternal blessings. (2.) Then he shall know how to praise God, and have a heart to do it. All that are taught of God are taught this lesson; when God opens the understanding, opens the heart, and so opens the lips, it is that the mouth may show forth his praise. We have learned nothing to purpose if we have not learned to praise God. (3.) <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> he is thus importunate for divine instructions, that he might praise God. Those that pray for God's grace must aim at God's glory, <reference osisRef="Eph.1.12">Eph. i. 12</reference>.
entries.cea0075f868309e9df129bd6cab795372f299960: <div eID="gen12916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12917" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">172</hi> My tongue shall speak of thy word: for all thy commandments <hi type="italic">are</hi> righteousness. <div eID="gen12917" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12918" type="x-p"/> Observe here, 1. The good knowledge David had of the word of God; he knew it so well that he was ready to own, with the utmost satisfaction, that all God's commandments are not only righteous, but righteousness itself, the rule and standard of righteousness. 2. The good use he resolved to make of that knowledge: <hi type="italic">My tongue shall speak of thy word,</hi> not only utter praise for it to the glory of God, but discourse of it for the instruction and edification of others, as that which he himself was full of (for out of the abundance of the heart the mouth will speak) and as that which he desired others also might be filled with. The more we see of the righteousness of God's commandments the more industrious we should be to bring others acquainted with them, that they may be ruled by them. We should always make the word of God the governor of our discourse, so as never to transgress it by sinful speaking or sinful silence; and we should often make it the subject-matter of our discourse, that it may feed many and <hi type="italic">minister grace to the hearers.</hi>
entries.9137da9f8aad82d22b190347f6317fdd3e42505b: <div eID="gen12918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12919" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">173</hi> Let thine hand help me; for I have chosen thy precepts. <hi type="super">174</hi> I have longed for thy salvation, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> ; and thy law <hi type="italic">is</hi> my delight. <div eID="gen12919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12920" type="x-p"/> Here, 1. David prays that divine grace would work for him: <hi type="italic">Let thy hand help me.</hi> He finds his own hands are not sufficient for him, nor can any creature lend him a helping hand to any purpose; therefore he looks up to God in hopes that the hand that had made him would help him; for, if the Lord do not help us, whence can any creature help us? All our help must be expected from God's hand, from his power and his bounty. 2. He pleads what divine grace had already wrought in him as a pledge of further mercy, being a qualification for it. Three things he pleads:—(1.) That he had made religion his serious and deliberate choice: "<hi type="italic">I have chosen thy precepts.</hi> I took them for my rule, not because I knew no other, but because, upon trial, I knew no better." Those are good, and do good indeed, who are good and do good, not by chance, but from choice; and those who have thus chosen God's precepts may depend upon God's helping hand in all their services and under all their sufferings. (2.) That his heart was upon heaven: <hi type="italic">I have longed for thy salvation.</hi> David, when he had got to the throne, met with enough in the world to court his stay, and to make him say, "It is good to be here;" but still he was looking further, and longing for something better in another world. There is an eternal salvation which all the saints are longing for, and therefore pray that God's hand would help them forward in their way to it. (3.) That he took pleasure in doing his duty: "<hi type="italic">Thy law is my delight.</hi> Not only I delight in it, but it is my delight, the greatest delight I have in this world." Those that are cheerful in their obedience may in faith beg help of God to carry them on in their obedience; and those that expect God's salvation must take delight in his law and their hopes must increase their delight.
entries.8e78f40dc93fe4fd89fe68926834bf0ac7cb8a4f: <div eID="gen12920" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12921" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">175</hi> Let my soul live, and it shall praise thee; and let thy judgments help me. <div eID="gen12921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12922" type="x-p"/> David's heart is still upon praising God; and therefore, 1. He prays that God would give him time to praise him: "<hi type="italic">Let my soul live, and it shall praise thee,</hi> that is, let my life be prolonged, that I may live to thy glory." The reason why a good man desires to live is that he may praise God in the land of the living, and do something to his honour. Not, "Let me live and serve my country, live and provide for my family;" but, "Let me live that, in doing this, I may praise God here in this world of conflict and opposition." When we die we hope to go to a better world to praise him, and that is more agreeable for us, though here there is more need of us. And therefore one would not desire to live any longer than we may do God some service here. <hi type="italic">Let my soul live,</hi> that is, let me be sanctified and comforted, for sanctification and comfort are the life of the soul, <hi type="italic">and</hi> then <hi type="italic">it shall praise thee.</hi> Our souls must be employed in praising God, and we must pray for grace and peace that we may be fitted to praise God. 2. He prays that God would give him strength to praise him: "<hi type="italic">Let thy judgments help me;</hi> let all ordinances and all providences" (both are God's judgments) "further me in glorifying God; let them be the matter of my praise and let them help to fit me for that work."
entries.4ef0c59df6d65b8c4f1b122e0ab374f413ca8d10: <div eID="gen12922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12923" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">176</hi> I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek thy servant; for I do not forget thy commandments. <div eID="gen12923" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12924" type="x-p"/> Here is, 1. A penitent confession: <hi type="italic">I have gone astray,</hi> or wander up and down, <hi type="italic">like a lost sheep.</hi> As unconverted sinners are like lost sheep (<reference osisRef="Luke.15.4">Luke xv. 4</reference>), so weak unsteady saints are like lost sheep, <reference osisRef="Matt.18.12-Matt.18.13">Matt. xviii. 12, 13</reference>. We are apt to wander like sheep, and very unapt, when we have gone astray, to find the way again. By going astray we lose the comfort of the green pastures and expose ourselves to a thousand mischiefs. 2. A believing petition: <hi type="italic">Seek thy servant,</hi> as the good shepherd seeks a wandering sheep to bring it back again, <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.12">Ezek. xxxiv. 12</reference>. "Lord, seek me, as I used to seek my sheep when they went astray;" for David had been himself a tender shepherd. "Lord, own me for one of thine; for, though I am a stray sheep, I have thy mark; concern thyself for me, send after me by the word, and conscience, and providences; bring me back by thy grace." <hi type="italic">Seek me,</hi> that is, <hi type="italic">find me;</hi> for God never seeks in vain. <hi type="italic">Turn me, and I shall be turned.</hi> 3. An obedient plea: "Though I have gone astray, yet I have not wickedly departed, <hi type="italic">I do not forget thy commandments.</hi>" Thus he concludes the psalm with a penitent sense of his own sin and believing dependence on God's grace. With these a devout Christian will conclude his duties, will conclude his life; he will live and die repenting and praying. Observe here, (1.) It is the character of good people that they do not <hi type="italic">forget God's commandments,</hi> being well pleased with their convictions and well settled in their resolutions. (2.) Even those who, through grace, are mindful of their duty, cannot but own that they have in many instances wandered from it. (3.) Those that have wandered from their duty, if they continue mindful of it, may with a humble confidence commit themselves to the care of God's grace.  <chapter eID="Ps.119"/> <div eID="gen12924" type="x-p"/>

entries.04f6cd0655edd3c5e927378c6b02ca6561ed8be3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6871"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 119</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.119.1-Ps.119.176">Psa 119:1-176</reference>. This celebrated Psalm has several peculiarities. It is divided into twenty-two parts or stanzas, denoted by the twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet. Each stanza contains eight verses, and the first letter of each verse is that which gives name to the stanza. Its contents are mainly praises of God's Word, exhortations to its perusal, and reverence for it, prayers for its proper influence, and complaints of the wicked for despising it. There are but two verses (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.122">Psa 119:122</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.132">132</reference>) which do not contain some term or description of God's Word. These terms are of various derivations, but here used, for the most part, synonymously, though the use of a variety of terms seems designed, in order to express better the several aspects in which our relations to the revealed word of God are presented. The Psalm does not appear to have any relation to any special occasion or interest of the Jewish Church or nation, but was evidently "intended as a manual of pious thoughts, especially for instructing the young, and its peculiar artificial structure was probably adopted to aid the memory in retaining the language."</title> <div sID="gen10538" type="x-p"/> ALEPH. (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.1-Ps.119.8">Psa 119:1-8</reference>).<div eID="gen10538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10539" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6871"/><hi type="bold">1. undefiled--</hi>literally, "complete," perfect, or sincere (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.37.37">Psa 37:37</reference>).<div eID="gen10539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10540" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in--</hi>or, "of"<div eID="gen10540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10541" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the way--</hi>course of life.<div eID="gen10541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10542" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">walk--</hi>act<div eID="gen10542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10543" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the law--</hi>according to it (compare <reference osisRef="Luke.1.6">Lu 1:6</reference>).<div eID="gen10543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10544" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">law--</hi>from a word meaning "to teach," is a term of rather general purport, denoting the instruction of God's Word. <div eID="gen10544" type="x-p"/>
entries.7aa31ef08f957ba34aef1b52eb9a3dfee83782ae: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6872"/><div sID="gen10545" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6872"/><hi type="bold">2. testimonies--</hi>The word of God is so called, because in it He testifies for truth and against sin.<div eID="gen10545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10546" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seek him--</hi>that is, a knowledge of Him, with desire for conformity to His will. <div eID="gen10546" type="x-p"/>
entries.39f703124f93dc4ef7ee0490add80f3b12f8f6ca: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6873"/><div sID="gen10547" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6873"/><hi type="bold">3. his ways--</hi>the course He reveals as right. <div eID="gen10547" type="x-p"/>
entries.8a748107a9d125a442f158de14083e4f09c76ccc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6874"/><div sID="gen10548" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6874"/><hi type="bold">4-6. precepts--</hi>are those directions which relate to special conduct, from a word meaning "to inspect."<div eID="gen10548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10549" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">statutes--</hi>or ordinances, positive laws of permanent nature. Both words originally denote rather positive than moral laws, such as derive force from the divine appointment, whether their nature or the reasons for them are apprehended by us or not.<div eID="gen10549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10550" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">commandments--</hi>or institutions. The term is comprehensive, but rather denotes fundamental directions for conduct, both enjoining and forbidding.<div eID="gen10550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10551" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">have respect unto--</hi>or regard carefully as to their whole purport. <div eID="gen10551" type="x-p"/>
entries.fc67e4de6fad177a1f117422978f297e90ed3686: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6875"/><div sID="gen10552" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6875"/><hi type="bold">7. judgments--</hi>rules of conduct formed by God's judicial decisions; hence the wide sense of the word in the Psalms, so that it includes decisions of approval as well as condemnation. <div eID="gen10552" type="x-p"/>
entries.a39100d5811307a92e3075ef6e7aa004192962c4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6876"/><div sID="gen10553" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6876"/>8. Recognizes the need of divine grace.<div eID="gen10553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10554" type="x-p"/> BETH. (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.9-Ps.119.16">Psa 119:9-16</reference>). <div eID="gen10554" type="x-p"/>
entries.a50c4cf6557e963c7c63c171882b6c7dfab679d6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6877"/><div sID="gen10555" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6877"/>9. The whole verse may be read as a question; for,<div eID="gen10555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10556" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by taking heed--</hi>is better, "for" taking heed, that is, so as to do it. The answer is implied, and inferable from <reference osisRef="Ps.119.5">Psa 119:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.10.18">10, 18</reference>, &c., that is, by God's grace. <div eID="gen10556" type="x-p"/>
entries.512e6f54d00d304528b2ddb43663e5dfa7d6a52d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6878"/><div sID="gen10557" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6878"/>10-16. We must carefully treasure up the word of God, declare it to others, meditate on it, and heartily delight in it; and then by His grace we shall act according to it.<div eID="gen10557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10558" type="x-p"/> GIMEL. (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.17-Ps.119.24">Psa 119:17-24</reference>). <div eID="gen10558" type="x-p"/>
entries.5bc291e82da8e44138404a26bceb5831a0763978: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6879"/><div sID="gen10559" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6879"/>17-20. Life is desirable in order to serve God; that we may do so aright, we should seek to have our eyes opened to behold His truth, and earnestly desire fully to understand it. <div eID="gen10559" type="x-p"/>
entries.6b6097abd9c9b2d7af8b5940933407d5411a3c22: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6880"/><div sID="gen10560" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6880"/>21-24. God will rebuke those who despise His word and deliver His servants from their reproach, giving them boldness in and by His truth, even before the greatest men.<div eID="gen10560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10561" type="x-p"/> DALETH. (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.25-Ps.119.32">Psa 119:25-32</reference>). <div eID="gen10561" type="x-p"/>
entries.4e59aefaf1ff11b617a550af78b9ad242cbedf1c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6881"/><div sID="gen10562" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6881"/>25-27. Submitting ourselves in depression to God, He will revive us by His promises, and lead us to declare His mercy to others. <div eID="gen10562" type="x-p"/>
entries.38835266f58f238b6b4031f1b80d3a1e8403d65c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6882"/><div sID="gen10563" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6882"/>28-32. In order to adhere to His word, we must seek deliverance from temptations to sin as well as from despondency.<div eID="gen10563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10564" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">enlarge--</hi>or, "expand"<div eID="gen10564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10565" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my heart--</hi>with gracious affections.<div eID="gen10565" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10566" type="x-p"/> HE. (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.33-Ps.119.40">Psa 119:33-40</reference>). <div eID="gen10566" type="x-p"/>
entries.a335c7d243ec26d29cf73565447b340c83073f5c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6883"/><div sID="gen10567" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6883"/>33-38. To encourage us in prayer for divine aid in adhering to His truth, we are permitted to believe that by His help we shall succeed.<div eID="gen10567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10568" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the way of thy statutes--</hi>that is, the way or manner of life prescribed by them. The help we hope to obtain by prayer is to be the basis on which our resolutions should rest. <div eID="gen10568" type="x-p"/>
entries.08a532f4c2d4fdd0620420acc66575c52c6eb139: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6886"/><div sID="gen10573" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6886"/>39-40. Our hope of freedom from the reproach of inconsistency is in God's power, quickening us to live according to His Word, which He leads us to love.<div eID="gen10573" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10574" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for thy judgments are good--</hi>The time must therefore be at hand when Thy justice will turn the "reproach" from Thy Church upon the world (<reference osisRef="Isa.25.8">Is 25:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.66.5">66:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zeph.2.8-Zeph.2.10">Zep 2:8-10</reference>).<div eID="gen10574" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10575" type="x-p"/> VAU. (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.41-Ps.119.48">Psa 119:41-48</reference>). <div eID="gen10575" type="x-p"/>
entries.59b17a53e200f2e002acd809d37ac5eb4cbf5557: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6887"/><div sID="gen10576" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6887"/>41-44. The sentiment more fully carried out. God's mercies and salvation, as revealed in His Word, provide hope of forgiveness for the past and security in a righteous course for the future. <div eID="gen10576" type="x-p"/>
entries.7479c42f582f1a1b021ee0f7e7b10622d551bcc8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6889"/><div sID="gen10578" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6889"/>45-48. To freedom from reproach, when imbued with God's truth, there is added "great boldness in the faith" [1Ti 3:13], accompanied with increasing delight in the holy law itself, which becomes an element of happiness. <div eID="gen10578" type="x-p"/>
entries.4f088b59a8bd277a576a995e35bdea9bcf95683c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6891"/><div sID="gen10581" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6891"/>49-51. Resting on the promises consoles under affliction and the tauntings of the insolent.<div eID="gen10581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10582" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">upon which--</hi>rather, "Remember Thy word unto Thy servant, because," &c. So the Hebrew requires [Hengstenberg]. <div eID="gen10582" type="x-p"/>
entries.386b1be49592d61cfa6270574aacb1cb9f92bbd3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6893"/><div sID="gen10585" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6893"/>52-56. The pious take comfort, when harassed and distressed by wickedness of men who forsake God's law, in remembering that the great principles of God's truth will still abide; and also God's<div eID="gen10585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10586" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">judgments of old--</hi>that is, His past interpositions in behalf of His people are a pledge that He will again interpose to deliver them; and they become the theme of constant and delightful meditation. The more we keep the more we love the law of God. <div eID="gen10586" type="x-p"/>
entries.ef66962c0ddbb3c64912811d28087462c364bd99: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6897"/><div sID="gen10592" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6897"/>57-60. Sincere desires for God's favor, penitence, and activity in a new obedience, truly evince the sincerity of those who profess to find God a portion (<reference osisRef="Num.18.20">Nu 18:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.16.5">Psa 16:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.3.24">La 3:24</reference>). <div eID="gen10592" type="x-p"/>
entries.12de6eee94d2f9dae8abcd5aa523b6004aba3100: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6900"/><div sID="gen10595" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6900"/>61-62. This the more, if opposition of enemies, or love of ease is overcome in thus honoring God's law.<div eID="gen10595" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10596" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">have robbed me--</hi>better, surrounded me, either as forcible constraints like fetters, or as the cords of their nets. Hengstenberg translates, "snares." <div eID="gen10596" type="x-p"/>
entries.2720a88cf551eefebc1a6542750711ce786f4810: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6902"/><div sID="gen10598" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6902"/>63. The communion of the saints. Delight in their company is an evidence of belonging to them (<reference osisRef="Ps.16.3">Psa 16:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.3.3">Am 3:3</reference>; Mal 3:16). <div eID="gen10598" type="x-p"/>
entries.4377069cad0e6dc70190e9cf353488b589ee07ec: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6903"/><div sID="gen10599" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6903"/>64. While opposed by the wicked, and opposing them, the pious delight in those who fear God, but, after all, rely for favor and guidance not on merit, but mercy.<div eID="gen10599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10600" type="x-p"/> TETH. (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.65-Ps.119.72">Psa 119:65-72</reference>). <div eID="gen10600" type="x-p"/>
entries.e6a7821ff18f6c4294bcb82e9b2359834413a4bd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6904"/><div sID="gen10601" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6904"/>65-67. The reliance on promises (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.49">Psa 119:49</reference>) is strengthened by experience of past dealings according with promises, and a prayer for guidance, encouraged by sanctified affliction. <div eID="gen10601" type="x-p"/>
entries.7da4d5aa3e34678d725e032059ca83dfe344a5fe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6907"/><div sID="gen10604" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6907"/>68. Compare as to the Lord Jesus (<reference osisRef="Acts.10.38">Ac 10:38</reference>). <div eID="gen10604" type="x-p"/>
entries.0570e4f83f4f25e0763db3bf014a5cd750e39f95: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6908"/><div sID="gen10605" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6908"/>69-70. The crafty malice of the wicked, in slandering him, so far from turning him away, but binds him closer to God's Word, which they are too stupid in sin to appreciate. Hengstenberg refers the "lie" to such slanders against the Jews during the captivity, as that in <reference osisRef="Ezra.4.1-Ezra.4.6">Ezr 4:1-6</reference>, of sedition. <div eID="gen10605" type="x-p"/>
entries.dfef8edf366d660c358b379b12a31c0ac514e5c0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6910"/><div sID="gen10607" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6910"/>71-72. So also affliction of any kind acts as a wholesome discipline in leading the pious more highly to value the truth and promises of God.<div eID="gen10607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10608" type="x-p"/> JOD. (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.73-Ps.119.80">Psa 119:73-80</reference>). <div eID="gen10608" type="x-p"/>
entries.0cd737f1abaae272528dc7c0beec6e4034da289f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6911"/><div sID="gen10609" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6911"/>73. As God made, so He can best control, us. So as to Israel, he owed to God his whole internal and external existence (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.6">De 32:6</reference>). <div eID="gen10609" type="x-p"/>
entries.12761eb70c8ebbf53de95984de25209eba31b1cb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6912"/><div sID="gen10610" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6912"/>74. So when He has led us to rely on His truth, He will "make us to the praise of His grace" by others. "Those who fear Thee will be glad at my prosperity, as they consider my cause their cause" (<reference osisRef="Ps.34.2">Psa 34:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.142.7">142:7</reference>). <div eID="gen10610" type="x-p"/>
entries.36ec2c2ca41f39f2306154b449653068de281665: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6913"/><div sID="gen10611" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6913"/><hi type="bold">75-78. in faithfulness--</hi>that is, without in the least violating Thy faithfulness; because my sins deserved and needed fatherly chastisement. Enduring chastisement with a filial temper (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.6-Heb.12.11">He 12:6-11</reference>), God's promises of mercy (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.28">Ro 8:28</reference>) will be fulfilled, and He will give comfort in sorrow (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.22">La 3:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.3">2Co 1:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.4">4</reference>). <div eID="gen10611" type="x-p"/>
entries.5191e9d49e0b47fbf8c242fd93e2a8af3cdb061d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6916"/><div sID="gen10614" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6916"/>79-80. Those who may have thought his afflictions an evidence of God's rejection will then be led to return to Him; as the friends of Job did on his restoration, having been previously led through his afflictions to doubt the reality of his religion. <div eID="gen10614" type="x-p"/>
entries.d1cd6d10297e6805ea7bd9a8601e067d5e4d1c49: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6918"/><div sID="gen10618" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6918"/>81-83. In sorrow the pious heart yearns for the comforts of God's promises (<reference osisRef="Ps.73.26">Psa 73:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.84.2">84:2</reference>). <div eID="gen10618" type="x-p"/>
entries.848beaefbaacd27fbe740efac19b16333a998874: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6921"/><div sID="gen10621" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6921"/>84-87. The shortness of my life requires that the relief afforded to me from mine enemies should be speedy. <div eID="gen10621" type="x-p"/>
entries.2ef2d60fc6a579269537530503c111f2a19c1be0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6924"/><div sID="gen10627" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6924"/>89-91. In all changes God's Word remains firm (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.25">1Pe 1:25</reference>). Like the heavens, it continually attests God's unfailing power and unchanging care (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.2">Psa 89:2</reference>).<div eID="gen10627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10628" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is settled in--</hi>that is, stands as firmly as the heaven in which it dwells, and whence it emanated. <div eID="gen10628" type="x-p"/>
entries.aa8bfed64b0f1db1ff09d4a2283bb6877a82bfe6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6927"/><div sID="gen10631" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6927"/>92-94. Hence the pious are encouraged and inclined to seek a knowledge of it, and persevere amidst the efforts of those planning and waiting to destroy them.<div eID="gen10631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10632" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my delights--</hi>plural, not merely delight, but equal to all other delights. <div eID="gen10632" type="x-p"/>
entries.d5075185c50feb79d277677dfad6cfdf615c84ff: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6929"/><div sID="gen10635" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6929"/>97. This characteristic love for God's law (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.1.2">Psa 1:2</reference>) ensures increase. <div eID="gen10635" type="x-p"/>
entries.cac8a20f122237cc391054311c3acfa5c0660506: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6930"/><div sID="gen10636" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6930"/>98-100. of knowledge, both of the matter of all useful, moral truth, and an experience of its application.<div eID="gen10636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10637" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wiser than mine enemies--</hi>with all their carnal cunning (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.6">De 4:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.4.8">8</reference>).<div eID="gen10637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10638" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they are ever with me--</hi>The Hebrew is, rather singular, "it is ever with me"; the commandments forming ONE complete whole, Thy law. <div eID="gen10638" type="x-p"/>
entries.0062e026559ed5077b9f4927c384a40af186e65a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6933"/><div sID="gen10641" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6933"/>101-104. Avoidance of sinful courses is both the effect and means of increasing in divine knowledge (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.19.10">Psa 19:10</reference>).<div eID="gen10641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10642" type="x-p"/> NUN. (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.105-Ps.119.112">Psa 119:105-112</reference>). <div eID="gen10642" type="x-p"/>
entries.386b6608ae09b123a6d1be32c1b5962319d4439c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6934"/><div sID="gen10643" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6934"/>105. Not only does the Word of God inform us of His will, but, as a light on a path in darkness, it shows us how to follow the right and avoid the wrong way. The lamp of the Word is not the sun. He would blind our eyes in our present fallen state; but we may bless God for the light shining as in a dark place, to guide us until the Sun of Righteousness shall come, and we shall be made capable of seeing Him (<reference osisRef="2Pet.1.19">2Pe 1:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.22.4">Re 22:4</reference>). The lamp is fed with the oil of the Spirit. The allusion is to the lamps and torches carried at night before an Eastern caravan. <div eID="gen10643" type="x-p"/>
entries.3498b2bd84b2c412eea8bc9ef07ab4e7fa1fac48: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6935"/><div sID="gen10644" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6935"/>106-108. Such was the national covenant at Sinai and in the fields of Moab. <div eID="gen10644" type="x-p"/>
entries.27398365cd9fa2423c850bcd3dddb6e83826a284: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6937"/><div sID="gen10646" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6937"/>109-110. In the midst of deadly perils (the phrase is drawn from the fact that what we carry in our hands may easily slip from them, <reference osisRef="Judg.12.3">Jud 12:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.28.21">1Sa 28:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.13.14">Job 13:14</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="1Sam.19.5">1Sa 19:5</reference>), and exposed to crafty enemies, his safety and guidance is in the truth and promises of God. <div eID="gen10646" type="x-p"/>
entries.a82ad3a68ef0ebb9d8fb92328670b0a808dadf9e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6938"/><div sID="gen10647" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6938"/>111-112. These he joyfully takes as his perpetual heritage, to perform the duties and receive the comforts they teach, evermore.<div eID="gen10647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10648" type="x-p"/> SAMECH. (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.113-Ps.119.120">Psa 119:113-120</reference>). <div eID="gen10648" type="x-p"/>
entries.85155820b0fe9cfe10158c652876549b8ddb5280: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6939"/><div sID="gen10649" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6939"/><hi type="bold">113. vain thoughts--</hi>better, "unstable persons," literally, "divided men," those of a divided, doubting mind (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.8">Jas 1:8</reference>); "a double-minded man" [Hengstenberg], skeptics, or, skeptical notions as opposed to the certainty of God's word. <div eID="gen10649" type="x-p"/>
entries.9f9bf4875a597c5c2aa9814aaca6516e0f6ee908: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6940"/><div sID="gen10650" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6940"/><hi type="bold">114. hiding-place--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.27.5">Psa 27:5</reference>).<div eID="gen10650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10651" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shield--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.3.3">Psa 3:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.7.10">7:10</reference>).<div eID="gen10651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10652" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hope in thy word--</hi>confidently rest on its teachings and promises. <div eID="gen10652" type="x-p"/>
entries.ed4561a2c7fc25d65d50d99c4142fe4ce939f1fa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6941"/><div sID="gen10653" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6941"/>115-117. Hence he fears not wicked men, nor dreads disappointment, sustained by God in making His law the rule of life.<div eID="gen10653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10654" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Depart from me--</hi>Ye can do nothing with me; for, &c. (<reference osisRef="Ps.6.8">Psa 6:8</reference>). <div eID="gen10654" type="x-p"/>
entries.20859445bb7da2b9e7fb87f8b9782648f80d0a7c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6942"/><div sID="gen10655" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6942"/>118-120. But the disobedient and rebellious will be visited by God's wrath, which impresses the pious with wholesome fear and awe.<div eID="gen10655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10656" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">their deceit is falsehood--</hi>that is, all their cunning deceit, wherewith they seek to entrap the godly, is in vain. <div eID="gen10656" type="x-p"/>
entries.7d7449b45eaf602123fbe5f6041ff9713a5896f4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6944"/><div sID="gen10659" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6944"/>121-126. On the grounds of his integrity, desire for God's word, and covenant relation to Him, the servant of God may plead for His protecting care against the wicked, gracious guidance to the knowledge of truth, and His effective vindication of the righteous and their cause, which is also His own. <div eID="gen10659" type="x-p"/>
entries.c923e8fb90e9c05868f4b651dc58bd94c495e106: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6946"/><div sID="gen10661" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6946"/><hi type="bold">127-128. Therefore--</hi>that is, In view of these benefits, or, Because of the glory of Thy law, so much praised in the previous parts of the Psalm.<div eID="gen10661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10662" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I love ... [and] Therefore (repeated)--</hi>All its precepts, on all subjects, are estimable for their purity, and lead one imbued with their spirit to hate all evil (<reference osisRef="Ps.19.10">Psa 19:10</reference>). The Word of God admits of no eclecticism; its least title is perfect (<reference osisRef="Ps.12.6">Psa 12:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.5.17-Matt.5.19">Mt 5:17-19</reference>).<div eID="gen10662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10663" type="x-p"/> PE. (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.129-Ps.119.136">Psa 119:129-136</reference>). <div eID="gen10663" type="x-p"/>
entries.623eaba128e70f5ea49a744262d7828229cee98f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6947"/><div sID="gen10664" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6947"/><hi type="bold">129. wonderful--</hi>literally, "wonders," that is, of moral excellence. <div eID="gen10664" type="x-p"/>
entries.7f9fd3242114297ab69167d6355acda701ca13ea: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6948"/><div sID="gen10665" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6948"/><hi type="bold">130. The entrance--</hi>literally, "opening"; God's words, as an open door, let in light, or knowledge. Rather, as Hengstenberg explains it, "The opening up," or, "explanation of thy word." To the natural man the doors of God's Word are shut. <reference osisRef="Luke.24.27">Lu 24:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.24.31">31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.17.3">Ac 17:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.1.18">Ep 1:18</reference>, confirm this view, "opening (that is, explaining) and alleging," &c.<div eID="gen10665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10666" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto the simple--</hi>those needing or desiring it (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.19.7">Psa 19:7</reference>). <div eID="gen10666" type="x-p"/>
entries.86c63a0176af6f532101b16a01863663edceebe0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6949"/><div sID="gen10667" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6949"/>131-135. An ardent desire (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.56.1">Psa 56:1</reference>, 2) for spiritual enlightening, establishment in a right course, deliverance from the wicked, and evidence of God's favor is expressed<div eID="gen10667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10668" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I opened my mouth, and panted--</hi>as a traveller in a hot desert pants for the cooling breeze (<reference osisRef="Ps.63.1">Psa 63:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.84.2">84:2</reference>). <div eID="gen10668" type="x-p"/>
entries.0539d563705a04ce678fb1d30d88d64626019446: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6952"/><div sID="gen10673" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6952"/>136. Literally, "Mine eyes come down (dissolved) like water brooks" (<reference osisRef="Lam.3.48">La 3:48</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.9.1">Jr 9:1</reference>).<div eID="gen10673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10674" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because, &c.--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="Ezek.9.4">Eze 9:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.13.17">Jr 13:17</reference>).<div eID="gen10674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10675" type="x-p"/> TZADDI. entries.b3f03d7e93442111c4581ae327a87421bfa8f40e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6957"/><div sID="gen10680" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6957"/>142-144. The principles of God's government are permanent and reliable, and in the deepest distress His people find them a theme of delightful meditation and a source of reviving power (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.17">Psa 119:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.116">116</reference>).<div eID="gen10680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10681" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">law is the truth--</hi>It therefore cannot deceive as to its promises.<div eID="gen10681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10682" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">everlasting--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.111.3">Psa 111:3</reference>), though to outward appearance seeming dead.<div eID="gen10682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10683" type="x-p"/> KOPH. (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.145-Ps.119.152">Psa 119:145-152</reference>). <div eID="gen10683" type="x-p"/>

Though the wicked are near to injure, because far from God's law, He is near to help, and faithful to His word, which abides for ever.<div eID="gen10687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10688" type="x-p"/> RESH. entries.f8ebcebee16dd76023c27e6506f0d2e682f77b43: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6968"/><div sID="gen10697" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6968"/>160. God has been ever faithful, and the principles of His government will ever continue worthy of confidence.<div eID="gen10697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10698" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from the beginning--</hi>that is, "every word from Genesis (called so by the Jews from its first words, 'In the beginning') to the end of the Scriptures is true." Hengstenberg translates more literally, "The sum of thy words is truth." The sense is substantially the same. The whole body of revelation is truth. "Thy Word is nothing but truth" [Luther].<div eID="gen10698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10699" type="x-p"/> SCHIN. (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.161-Ps.119.168">Psa 119:161-168</reference>). <div eID="gen10699" type="x-p"/>
entries.5610244b9bdb8a0df6e63f97988c1135be9648a4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6969"/><div sID="gen10700" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6969"/>161-165. (Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.119.46">Psa 119:46</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.86">86</reference>).<div eID="gen10700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10701" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">awe--</hi>reverential, not slavish fear, which could not coexist with love (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.163">Psa 119:163</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.4.8">1Jo 4:8</reference>). Instead of fearing his persecutors, he fears God's Word alone (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.4">Lu 12:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.5">5</reference>). The Jews inscribe in the first page of the great Bible (<reference osisRef="Gen.28.17">Ge 28:17</reference>), "How dreadful is this place! This is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven!" <div eID="gen10701" type="x-p"/>
entries.5f27513ba4ff8cba8411895801e7d5e856951384: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6973"/><div sID="gen10705" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6973"/>166-168. entries.dafcb6bdd3501facbae9b8ad5c8ba48055339f71: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6975"/><div sID="gen10708" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6975"/>169-170. entries.72fe9d2192c373d65609d9ad9a41d83640fb07f9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6976"/><div sID="gen10709" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6976"/><hi type="bold">171-172. shall utter--</hi>or, "pour out praise" (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.19.2">Psa 19:2</reference>); shall cause Thy praises to stream forth as from a bubbling, overflowing fountain. <div eID="gen10709" type="x-p"/>
entries.51f18ed1bf24f03fe0e9f7d7a5c334894d2312ae: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6978"/><div sID="gen10711" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6978"/>173-174. (Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.119.77">Psa 119:77</reference>, 81, 92).<div eID="gen10711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10712" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I have chosen--</hi>in preference to all other objects of delight. <div eID="gen10712" type="x-p"/>
entries.458a3e58528dbb8969701368cb77949ba264d038: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6979"/><div sID="gen10713" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6979"/>175. Save me that I may praise Thee.<div eID="gen10713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10714" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy judgments--</hi>as in <reference osisRef="Ps.119.149">Psa 119:149</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.156">156</reference>. <div eID="gen10714" type="x-p"/>
entries.3982a449322b9443a41d8dded9b3576abec11d3d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6980"/><div sID="gen10715" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6980"/>176. Though a wanderer from God, the truly pious ever desires to be drawn back to Him; and, though for a time negligent of duty, he never forgets the commandments by which it is taught.<div eID="gen10715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10716" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lost--</hi>therefore utterly helpless as to recovering itself (<reference osisRef="Jer.50.6">Jr 50:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.15.4">Lu 15:4</reference>). Not only the sinner before conversion, but the believer after conversion, is unable to recover himself; but the latter, after temporary wandering, knows to whom to look for restoration. <reference osisRef="Ps.119.175">Psa 119:175</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.176">176</reference> seem to sum up the petitions, confessions, and professions of the Psalm. The writer desires God's favor, that he may praise Him for His truth, confesses that he has erred, but, in the midst of all his wanderings and adversities, professes an abiding attachment to the revealed Word of God, the theme of such repeated eulogies, and the recognized source of such great and unnumbered blessings. Thus the Psalm, though more than usually didactic, is made the medium of both parts of devotion--prayer and praise. <chapter eID="Ps.119"/>

entries.9113ee9c2fae016a948d818022415fb420e8f389: <div eID="gen22711" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen22712" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen22713" type="x-p"/> The various excellencies and important uses of the law or revelation of God. <div eID="gen22713" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen22712" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen22714" type="x-p"/> This is another of the alphabetical or acrostic Psalms. It is divided into twenty-two parts, answering to the number of letters in the Hebrew alphabet. Every part is divided into eight verses; and each verse begins with that letter of the alphabet which forms the title of the part, e.g.: The eight first verses have א aleph prefixed, the second eight ב beth, each of the eight verses beginning with that letter; and so of the rest. All connection, as might be naturally expected, is sacrificed to this artificial and methodical arrangement. <div eID="gen22714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22715" type="x-p"/> It is not easy to give any general Analysis of this Psalm; it is enough to say that it treats in general on the privileges and happiness of those who observe the law of the Lord. That law is exhibited by various names and epithets tending to show its various excellences. Earnest prayers are offered to God for wisdom to understand it, and for grace to observe it faithfully. These particulars may be collected from the whole composition, and appear less or more in every part. <div eID="gen22715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22716" type="x-p"/> The words which express that revelation which God had then given to men, or some particular characteristic of it, are generally reckoned to be the ten following: <div eID="gen22716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22717" type="x-p"/> 1. Testimonies; <div eID="gen22717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22718" type="x-p"/> 2. Commandments, <div eID="gen22718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22719" type="x-p"/> 3. Precepts; <div eID="gen22719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22720" type="x-p"/> 4. Word; <div eID="gen22720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22721" type="x-p"/> 5. Law; <div eID="gen22721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22722" type="x-p"/> 6. Ways; <div eID="gen22722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22723" type="x-p"/> 7. Truth; <div eID="gen22723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22724" type="x-p"/> 8. Judgments; <div eID="gen22724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22725" type="x-p"/> 9. Righteousness; <div eID="gen22725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22726" type="x-p"/> 10. Statutes. <div eID="gen22726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22727" type="x-p"/> To these some add the following: <div eID="gen22727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22728" type="x-p"/> 1. Faithfulness, <div eID="gen22728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22729" type="x-p"/> 2. Judgment; <div eID="gen22729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22730" type="x-p"/> 3. Name; but these are not used in the sense of the other ten words. <div eID="gen22730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22731" type="x-p"/> I believe it is almost universally asserted that in every verse of this Psalm one or other of those ten words is used, except in <reference osisRef="Psa.119.122">Psa 119:122</reference>; but on a closer inspection we shall find that none of them is used in the above sense in <reference osisRef="Psa.119.84">Psa 119:84</reference> (note), <reference osisRef="Psa.119.90">Psa 119:90</reference> (note), <reference osisRef="Psa.119.121">Psa 119:121</reference> (note), <reference osisRef="Psa.119.122">Psa 119:122</reference> (note), <reference osisRef="Psa.119.132">Psa 119:132</reference> (note). <div eID="gen22731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22732" type="x-p"/> To save myself unnecessary repetition, and the reader time and trouble, I shall here, once for all, explain the above words, which the reader will do well to keep in remembrance. <div eID="gen22732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22733" type="x-p"/> I. The Law, תורה Torah, from ירה yarah, to direct, guide, teach, make straight, or even, point forward; because it gutdes, directs, and instructs in the way of righteousness; makes our path straight, shows what is even and right, and points us onward to peace, truth, and happiness. It is even our school master to bring us to Christ, that we may be justified through faith; and by it is the knowledge of sin. <div eID="gen22733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22734" type="x-p"/> II. Statutes, חקים Chukkim, from חק chak, to mark, trace out, describe, and ordain; because they mark out our way describe the line of conduct we are to pursue and order or ordain what we are to observe. <div eID="gen22734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22735" type="x-p"/> III. Precepts, פקודים Pikkudim, from פקד pakad, to take notice or care of a thing, to attend, have respect to, to appoint, to visit; because they take notice of our way, have respect to the whole of our life and conversation, superintend, overlook, and visit us in all the concerns and duties of life. <div eID="gen22735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22736" type="x-p"/> IV. Commandments, מצות Mitsvoth, from צוה tassah to command, order, ordain; because they show us what we should do, and what we should leave undone, and exact our obedience. <div eID="gen22736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22737" type="x-p"/> V. Testimonies, עדות Edoth, from עד ad, denoting beyond, farther, all along, to bear witness, or testimony. The rites and ceremonies of the law; because they point out matters beyond themselves, being types and representations of the good things that were to come. <div eID="gen22737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22738" type="x-p"/> VI. Judgments, משפטים Mishpatim, from שפט shaphat, to judge, determine, regulate, order, and discern, because they judge concerning our words and works; show the roses by which they should be regulated; and cause us to discern what is right and wrong, and decide accordingly. <div eID="gen22738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22739" type="x-p"/> VII. Truth, אמונה Emunah, from אמן aman, to make steady, constant, to settle, trust, believe. The law that is established steady, confirmed, and ordered in all things, and sure; which should be believed on the authority of God, and trusted to as an infallible testimony from Him who cannot lie nor deceive. <div eID="gen22739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22740" type="x-p"/> VIII. Word, דבר dabar, from the same root, to discourse, utter one's sentiments, speak consecutively and intelligibly; in which it appears to differ from מלל malal, to utter articulate sounds. Any prophecy or immediate communication from heaven, as well as the whole body of Divine revelation, is emphatically called דבר יהוה debar Yehovah, the word of Jehovah. On the same ground we call the whole Old and New Testament The Word of the Lord, as we term the volume in which they are contained The Bible-The Book. In his revelation God speaks to man; shows him, in a clear, concise, intelligible, and rational way, his interest, his duty, his privileges; and, in a word, the reasonable service that he requires of him. <div eID="gen22740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22741" type="x-p"/> IX. Way, דרך Debech, from the same root, to proceed, go on, walk, tread. The way in which God goes in order to instruct and save man; the way in which man must tread in order to be safe, holy, and happy. God's manner of acting or proceeding in providence and grace; and the way that man should take in order to answer the end of his creation and redemption. <div eID="gen22741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22742" type="x-p"/> X. Righteousness, צדקה Tsedakah from צדק tsadak, to do justice, to give full weight. That which teaches a man to give to all their due; to give God his due, Man his due, and Himself his due; for every man has duties to God, his neighbor, and himself, to perform. This word is applied to God's judgments, testimonies, and commandments; they are all righteous, give to all their due, and require what is due from every one. <div eID="gen22742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22743" type="x-p"/> The three words, which some add here, are, <div eID="gen22743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22744" type="x-p"/> The first is Faithfulness, אמונה Emunah: but see this under No. VII., nor does it appear in <reference osisRef="Psa.119.90">Psa 119:90</reference>, where it occurs, to be used as a characteristic of God's law, but rather his exact fulfillment of his promises to man. <div eID="gen22744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22745" type="x-p"/> The second is Judgment, משפט mishpat. See this under No. VI.: it occurs in <reference osisRef="Psa.119.84">Psa 119:84</reference> and <reference osisRef="Psa.119.121">Psa 119:121</reference> : "When wilt thou execute judgment," etc.; but is not used in those places as one of the ten words. <div eID="gen22745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22746" type="x-p"/> The third is Name, שם shem, see <reference osisRef="Psa.119.132">Psa 119:132</reference> : but this is no characteristic of God's law; it refers here simply to himself. Those that love thy Name is the same as those that love Thee. Bishop Nicholson inserts promises among the ten words: but this occurs no where in the Psalm. <div eID="gen22746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22747" type="x-p"/> We might, and with much more propriety, add a fourth, אמרה Imrah, from אמר amar, to branch out, spread, or diffuse itself, as the branches of a tree, and which is often used for a word spoken, a speech. This often occurs in the Psalm: and we regularly translate it word, and put no difference or distinction between it and דבר dabar, No. VIII.: but it is not exactly the sane; דבר dabar may apply more properly to history, relation, description and such like; while, אמרתך imrathecha, thy word, may mean an immediate oracle, delivered solemnly from God to his prophet for the instruction of men. But the two words appear often indifferently used; and it would not be easy to ascertain the different shades of meaning between these two roots. <div eID="gen22747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22748" type="x-p"/> Having thus far introduced the Psalm to the reader's attention, I should probably speak at large of the elegance of its composition, and the importance and utility of its matter. Like all other portions of Divine revelation, it is elegant, important, and useful; and while I admire the fecundity of the psalmist's genius, the unabating flow of his poetic vein, his numerous synonyms, and his copia verborum, by which he is enabled to expand, diversify, and illustrate the same idea; presenting it to his reader in all possible points of view, so as to render it pleasing, instructive, and impressive; I cannot rob the rest of the book of its just praise by setting this, as many have done, above all the pieces it contains. It is by far the largest, the most artificial, and most diversified; yet, in proportion to its length, it contains the fewest ideas of any Psalm in the Book. <div eID="gen22748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22749" type="x-p"/> Several of the ancients, particularly the Greek fathers, have considered it as an abridgement of David's life; in which he expresses all the states through which he had passed; the trials, persecutions, succours, and encouragements he had received. The Latin fathers perceive in it all the morality of the Gospel, and rules for a man's conduct in every situation of life. Cassiodorus asserts that it contains the sentiments of the prophets, apostles, martyrs, and all the saints. In the introduction to the Book of Psalms I have conjectured that many of them were composed from notes taken at different times, and in widely different circumstances; hence the different states described in the same Psalm, which could not have been at one and the same time the experience of the same person.
