If David was its author, it is the most artificial and operose in its composition of all his psalms, and he has exhibited in the treatment of his subject — which is the celebration of the perfection of God’s law, and the happiness of those who obey it — an extraordinary fecundity of expression, as if one of his intentions had been to show in how many various shapes, and with what copiousness of words, he could enunciate and illustrate a few and the same topics. The aspirations for instruction, consolation, and protection, with which almost every portion of this psalm is mingled, have a soothing and delightful effect, whilst the language throughout is rendered impressive by its peculiar strength and concinnity. It may, however, be doubtful, whether it be just to elevate it, as has been done by some, above all the other psalms. Dr Adam Clarke justly remarks, “Like all other portions of divine revelation, it is elegant, important, and useful; and while I admire the fecundity of the Psalmist’s genius, the unabating flow of his poetic vein, his numerous synonymes, and his copia verborum, by which he is enabled to expound, diversify, and illustrate the same idea: presenting it to his reader in all possible points of view, so as to render it pleasing, instructive, and impressive; I cannot rob the rest of the book of its just praise by setting this, as many have done, above all the pieces it contains. It is by far the longest, the most artificial, and most diversified, yet, in proportion to its length, it contains the fewest ideas of any in the book.”
It may be proper to take notice of certain terms which frequently occur in the psalm. Of the term תורה, torah, I say nothing, which, having its derivation from a word which signifies to instruct, is yet uniformly taken for law. Some of the Rabbis affirm that חוקים, chukim, signifies statutes, or divinely appointed rites, the, reason of which is very obvious. They say that פקדים, phikudim, denotes those precepts which relate to natural justice. It is certain that משפטים, mishpatim, signifies commandments, because this is proved by the etymology of the word. As to עדות, edoth, the Hebrews understand it of the doctrine of the law, but with the certain indication, pointing out to us that it is comprehensive of the manner in which God enters into covenant with his people. The precepts of the law are denominated judgments and righteousness, to inform us that God enjoins nothing except what is right and just, and that mankind ought to seek for no other rule for the perfecting of holiness, but what consists in regulating their life by rendering obedience to the law. The meaning is almost synonymous when they are called the ways of the Lord, intimating that those who do not depart from the direction of the law, may safely conclude that they are in no danger of going astray. The ordinances of God, and the edicts offerings, have the term חוקים, chukim, applied to them indiscriminately, and,פקודים , phikudim, refers to different kinds of justice, as is manifest from many parts of Scripture which demonstrates that there is no foundation for the subtle distinction and difference formerly noticed. And in this psalm almost all these terms are synonym as the context will show.
Others deny that these and other similar terms, which frequently occur in this psalm, are mere synonymes; and they have endeavoured to show from etymological investigation, that, although all of them designate the law, yet they present it under a different aspect. Jebb has attempted, at some length, to point out the specific differences between these words. The following is an abstract of his remarks: — “The next peculiarity to be observed in this psalm is, the regular recurrence of nine characteristic words, at least one or other of which is found in each distich, with one solitary exception, the second distich of the 12th division. These words are law, testimonies, precepts, statutes, commandments, judgments, word, saying; and a word which only twice occurs as a characteristic, — way.
“These are, doubtless, all designations of the Divine Law; but it were doing a deep injury to the cause of revealed truth to affirm that they are mere synonyms; in other words, that the sentiments of this compendium of heavenly wisdom are little better than a string of tautologies. The fact is, as some critics, both Jewish and Christian, have observed, that each of these terms designates the same law of God, but each under a different aspect, signifying the different modes of its promulgation, and of its reception. Each of these words will now be examined in order, and an attempt will be made to discriminate them.
“1. Law. This word is formed from a verb which means to direct, to guide, to aim, to shoot forwards. Its etymological meaning, then, would be a rule of conduct, a κανών σαφὴς. It means God’s law in general, whether it be that universal rule called the law of nature, or that which was revealed to his Church by Moses, and perfected by Christ. In strictness, the law means a plain rule of conduct, rather placed clearly in man’s sight, than enforced by any command; that is to say, this word does not necessarily include its sanctions.
“2. Testimonies are derived from a word which signifies to bear witness, to testify. The ark of the tabernacle is so called, as are the two tables of stone, and the tabernacle: the earnests and witnesses of God’s inhabitation among his people. Testimonies are more particularly God’s revealed law: the witnesses and confirmation of his promises made to his people, and earnests of his future salvation.
“3. Precepts, from a word which means to place in trust, mean something intrusted to man, ‘that which is committed to thee:’ appointments of God, which consequently have to do with the conscience, for which man is responsible, as an intelligent being.
“4. Statutes. The verb from which this word is formed means to engrave or inscribe. The word means a definite prescribed written law. The term is applied to Joseph’s law about the portion of the priests in Egypt, to the law about the Passover, etc. But in this psalm it has a more internal meaning; — that moral law of God, which is engraved on the fleshy tables of the heart; the inmost and spiritual apprehension of his will: not so obvious as the law and testimonies, and a matter of more direct spiritual communication than his precepts: the latter being more elaborated by the efforts of the mind itself, divinely guided indeed, but perhaps more instrumentally, and less passively, employed.
“5. Commandments, derived from a verb signifying to command or ordain. Such was God’s command to Adam about the tree; to Noah about constructing the ark.
“6. Judgments, derived from a word signifying to govern, to judge or determine, mean judicial ordinances and decisions: legal sanctions.
“7. Word. There are two terms, quite distinct in the Hebrew, but both rendered word, in each of our authorized versions. The latter of these is rendered saying in the former volume of this work. They are closely connected; since out of twenty-two passages in which word occurs, in fourteen it is parallel to, or in connection with, saying. From this very circumstance it is evident they are not synonymous.
“The term here rendered word means the Λόγος, or Word of God, in its most divine sense; the announcement of God’s revealed will; his command; his oracle; at times, the special communication to the prophets. The ten commandments are called by this term in Exodus: and דביר is the oracle in the temple. In this psalm it may be considered as, — 1. God’s revealed commandments in general. 2. As a revealed promise of certain blessings to the righteous. 3. As a thing committed to him as the minister of God. 4. As a rule of conduct; a channel of illumination.
“8. As to the remaining word way, that occurs but twice as a characteristic word, and the places in which it occurs must rather be considered as exceptions to the general rule: so that I am not disposed to consider it as intended to be a cognate expression with the above. At all events, its meaning is so direct and simple as to require no explanation: a plain rule of conduct; in its higher sense, the assisting grace of God through Christ our Lord, who is the Way, the Truth, and the Life.” — Jebb’s Literal Translation of the book of Psalms, with Dissertations, volume 2, pages 279-293.
To procure greater respect for the law, the prophet adorns it with a variety of titles, taking care constantly to enjoin upon us the same doctrine. I now proceed to the consideration of the contents of the psalm.
1 Blessed are they who are upright In these words the prophet sets forth the same paradox which we met with at the commencement of the Book of Psalms. All men naturally aspire after happiness, but instead of searching for it in the right path, they designedly prefer wandering up and down through endless by-paths, to their ruin and destruction. The Holy Spirit deservedly condemns this apathy and blindness. And but for man’s cupidity, which, with brutish impetuosity, hurries him in the opposite direction, the meaning of the words would appear quite plain to him. And the further a man wanders from God, the happier does he imagine himself to be; and hence all treat, as a fable, what the Holy Spirit declares about true piety and the service of God. This is a doctrine which scarcely one among a hundred receives.
The term way, is here put for the manner, or course and way of life: and hence he calls those upright in their way, whose sincere and uniform desire it is to practice righteousness, and to devote their life to this purpose. In the next clause of the verse, he specifics more clearly, that a godly and righteous life consists in walking in the law of God If a person follow his own humor and caprice, he is certain to go astray; and even should he enjoy the applause of the whole world, he will only weary himself with very vanity. But it may be asked, whether the prophet excludes from the hope of happiness all who do not worship God perfectly? Were this his meaning, it would follow that none except angels alone would be happy, seeing that the perfect observance of the law is to be found in no part, of the earth. The answer is easy: When uprightness is demanded of the children of God, they do not lose the gracious remission of their sins, in which their salvation alone consists. While, then, the servants of God are happy, they still need to take refuge in his mercy, because their uprightness is not complete. In this manner are they who faithfully observe the law of God said to be truly happy; and thus is fulfilled that which is declared in Psalm 32:2, “Blessed are they to whom God imputeth not sins.” In the second verse, the same doctrine is confirmed more fully, by pronouncing blessed, not. such as are wise in their own conceit, or assume a sort of fantastical holiness, but those who dedicate themselves to the covenant of God, and yield obedience to the dictates of hits law. Farther, by these words, he tells us that God is by no means satisfied with mere external service, for he demands the sincere and honest affection of the heart. And assuredly, if God be the sole judge and disposer of our life:, the truth must occupy the principal place in our heart, because it is not sufficient to have our hands and feet only enlisted in his service.
COMMENTARY
ON
THE BOOK OF PSALMS
 
BY JOHN CALVIN
 
 
TRANSLATED FROM THE ORIGINAL LATIN, AND COLLATED WITH THE AUTHOR'S FRENCH VERSION,
BY THE REV. JAMES ANDERSON
 
 
VOLUME FIFTH
 
 
CHRISTIAN CLASSICS ETHEREAL LIBRARY GRAND RAPIDS, MI
http://www.ccel.org
VOLUME FIFTH
TRANSLATOR’S PREFACE.
In bringing to a close his labors on Calvin’s Commentary On The Psalms, the Editor begs leave to state, that in addition to the General Index, and the Indices Of Texts Of Scripture, and of Hebrew Words, originally contemplated, it has been deemed highly desirable to give at the end of the Commentary a Translation; or Calvin’s Version Of The, Psalms arranged in parallelisms, together with a Table Of Those Passages In The Psalms Which Are Quoted In The New Testament, and a Table Of The Particular Subjects Of Each Psalm, according to Calvin’s interpretation. These additions, it is hoped, will be considered as improvements. From the extent to which they have increased the size of this Volume, it has been found necessary to omit the Appendix of Additional Criticisms to which reference is made in some of the footnotes throughout the work.
To exhibit the Psalms arranged in the metrical order, was an idea which appears never to have suggested itself to the mind of Calvin. In his time, indeed, and long after it, the peculiar character of Hebrew Poetry was not understood. It was not till a recent period that any steady light was; thrown on the laws of its composition. A vast amount of learning had indeed been expended on the subject, and a variety of hypotheses had been suggested by successive writers to unravel a question so intricate and mysterious; but no satisfactory result was attained until it was investigated by the learned Bishop Lowth, to whose genius and erudition we are indebted for the discovery of this long lost secret. He has proved, with a clearness and force of evidence which has now commanded universal assent, that Hebrew Poetry bears no resemblance in its structure to the Poetry of Greece and Rome, that it has no rhyming termination of lines as in the Poetry of our own language, and that its peculiar, and perhaps its sole characteristic, lies in a felicitous arrangement of words into what he denominates Parallelism. In other words, its leading peculiarity is that. each sentence consists generally of two parts, closely corresponding to each other, not indeed in the number of syllables, but in the ideas which they express, or in their grammatical constructive form, the second being synonymous (or, as Bishop Jebb would denominate it, cognate) with the first, — or antipathetic to it in its terms and sentiments, — or similar to it in the form of grammatical construction, such as noun answering to noun, verb to verb, member to member, negative to negative, interrogative to interrogative.
This sentence expresses the three specific heads into which Lowth discovered Hebrew parallelism, — which involves in it much variety and many gradations, — may be generally And more loosely distributed, Parallels Synonymous, (or, according to JEBB, Parallels Cognate,) Parallels Autithetic, and Parallels Synthetic or Constructive. For an example of the first, see Psalm 1:1-5; of the second, see Psalm 20:7, 8; and of the third, see Psalm 148:7-13.
The division of these sacred poems into hemistichs or lines is, therefore, the form in which they ought naturally to be arranged; and such an arrangement is attended with great advantages. It exhibits to the eve the peculiar structure of Hebrew poetical composition, and is, besides, an important aid in Scriptural Interpretation, as it often contributes to the elucidation of obscure and difficult passages, and enables even the mere English reader to discover a thousand beauties, which, without such a help, would escape his notice.
In translating this parallel version, two of Calvin’s translations of the Hebrew text were at the service of the Editor, — the Latin and the French. The former is strictly literal, rarely changing the Hebrew idiom, or even inserting a supplementary term, and uniformly giving the arrangement of the words as they stand in the inspired original. The latter is also upon the whole literal, though in some instances it changes the Hebrew idiom into the French, as well as frequently inserts such supplementary terms as the sense seems to require; and disregarding the arrangement of the words in the original, it gives them in the order most suitable to the genius of the French tongue. The Editor has followed Calvin’s Latin; Version, and has rendered it literally, retaining the Hebrew modes of expression, and the arrangement of the words in the sequence of the Hebrew text, except in a very few instances where a deviation seemed necessary to render the reading intelligible. Occasionally he has found it necessary to insert some supplementary words. These, when taken from Calvin’s French Version, as is generally the case, are printed simply in italics, and when supplied by the Editor are printed in italics and enclosed within brackets. By adhering to the Hebrew order of the words, the arrangements may sometimes appear harsh and uncouth; but very often they give much beauty and force to the expression. And in retaining the Hebrew idioms, the Editor has felt little scruple, considering that as our English Bible is a literal verbal translation of the Original Hebrew, many of these are quite familiar to us, and from their peculiar grace have even become naturalized in our language.
“The Hebrew idioms,” says Addison, “run into the English with a peculiar grace and beauty. Our language has received innumerable elegance’s and improvements from that infusion of Hebraisms which are derived to it out of the poetical passages in Holy Writ. They give a force and energy to our expressions, warm and animate our language, and convey our thoughts in more ardent and intense phrases than any that are to be met with in our own tongue. There is something so pathetic in this kind of diction, that it often sets the mind in a flame, and makes our heart burn within Us.”
The utility of the two Tables adverted to is too obvious to require to be dwelt upon. From the former the reader will perceive how completely the inspiration of the Psalms is established by New Testament authority, and how highly they were appreciated by Christ And His Apostles, there being no portion of Old Testament Scripture from which they so frequently quoted. The other Table will readily serve as a guide to the selection of such Psalms as may be adapted to the doctrines of the Christian system, the duties of the Christian life, or the varied circumstances, whether prosperous or adverse, in which the Christian or the Church of God may be placed.
J.A. EDINBURGH, April 1849.
Psalm 119:121-128
121. ע I have done judgment and righteousness: give me not up to my oppressors. 122. ע Become surety for thy servant for good, that the proud may not oppress me. 123. ע My eyes have failed for thy salvation, and for thy righteous word.
Literally, “for the word of thy righteousness.” Calvin understands it of the divine promises. Phillips translates “for the word of thy justice,” “that is,” says he, “for the sentence of justice. on my oppressors, as the first part of the verse teaches; for the passing this sentence will be equivalent to the granting the salvation which the Psalmist so ardently desired.”
124. ע Deal with thy servant according to thy goodness, and teach me thy statutes. 125. ע I am thy servant, give me understanding, that I may learn thy testimonies. 126. ע It is time for thee, O Jehovah! to be doing for they have destroyed thy law. 127. ע And therefore I have loved thy statutes above gold,
“Above gold. מזהב, mizahab, more than resplendent gold; gold without any stain or rust.” — Dr. Adam Clarke
yea even above the most fine gold
“Ou, marguerites.” — Fr. marg. “Or, pearls.” “ומפז, umipaz, above solid gold; gold separated from the dross, perfectly refined.” — Dr. Adam Clarke.
128. ע Therefore I have esteemed all thy commandments to be altogether right, and have hated every way of lying.

<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="119" type="Psalm">
                  <ns0:head>PSAL. CXIX.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:argument>
                     <ns0:p>The Author of this Psalm was <ns0:hi>David;</ns0:hi> which I know none that deny; and of which there is no just reason to doubt. The scope and design of it is manifest, to commend the serious and diligent study and the stedfast belief and the constant practice of Gods Word, as incomparably the best counsellor and comforter in the world, and as the onely way to true blessedness. And this he confirmeth by his own example, which he proposeth to them for their imi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tation; and he declareth the great and frequent experi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ence which he had of its admirable sweetness and manifold benefits in all conditions, and especially in the times of his distresses. And because it was an hard thing rightly to understand this Word in all its parts, and harder to put it in practice, he therefore intermixeth many prayers to God for his help therein, thereby directing and encou<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />raging others to take the same course. And because this Psalm was very large, and the matter of it of greatest im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />portance, the Psalmist thought fit to divide it into two and twenty several parts, according to the number of the He<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />brew Letters, that so he might both prevent tediousness, and fix it in the memory. It is further observable, that the Word of God is here diversly called by the names of <ns0:hi>Law, Statutes, Precepts</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Commandments, Iudgments, Or<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dinances,</ns0:hi>
                        <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:504" />
                        <ns0:hi>Righteousness, Testimonies, Way</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Word.</ns0:hi> By which variety he designed to express the nature and the great perfection and manifold parts and uses of Gods Word. Which is called his <ns0:hi>Word,</ns0:hi> as proceeding from his mouth, and revealed by him to us; his <ns0:hi>way,</ns0:hi> as prescri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bed by him for us to walk in; his <ns0:hi>Law,</ns0:hi> as binding us to obedience; his <ns0:hi>Statutes,</ns0:hi> as declaring his Authority and Power of giving us Laws; his <ns0:hi>Precepts,</ns0:hi> as declaring and directing our duty; his <ns0:hi>Ordinances,</ns0:hi> as ordained and ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pointed by him; his <ns0:hi>Righteousness,</ns0:hi> as exactly agreeable to Gods righteous Nature and Will; his <ns0:hi>Iudgments,</ns0:hi> as pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ceeding from the great Judge of the World, and being his Judicial Sentence to which all men must submit; and his <ns0:hi>Testimonies,</ns0:hi> as it contains the witnesses of Gods mind and will, and of mans duty. And there are very few of these 176 verses contained in this Psalm, in which one or other of these Titles is not found.</ns0:p>
                  </ns0:argument>

                           </ns0:gap> 27. 11. & 16. 11.</ns0:note> teach me thy statutes.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="27">27 Make me to understand <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">More thorowly and more practically. Either, 1. the full mind and meaning of thy precepts, which are exceeding broad, as he saith afterwards: or, 2. the way wherein I may walk according to thy precepts.</ns0:note> the way of thy precepts <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">How to demean my self in all the varieties of my condition, and in all my affairs and actions, so as is most agreeable to thy precepts.</ns0:note>: so shall I talk of thy wondrous works <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Even the wonders of the Law mentioned before, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 18.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="28">28 My soul <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                           <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> droppeth.</ns0:note> melteth <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Like wax before the fire, it hath no strength nor con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sistency left in it, but consumeth or pineth away.</ns0:note> for heaviness <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Through grief, partly for my extreme danger and misery: and princi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pally for my sins, and thy wrath and terrors following upon them.</ns0:note>: strengthen thou me <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">That so I may bear my burdens patiently and cheerfully, and vanquish all my temptations.</ns0:note> according unto thy word.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="29">29 Remove from me the way of lying <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>of falshood:</ns0:hi> either, 1. the practice of lying and dis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sembling and cheating, which is so rise in <ns0:hi>Sauls</ns0:hi> Court, and in the Courts of most Princes; but, Lord, let it not be so in my Court: or rather, 2. every false way of doctrine or worship; for to this way he opposeth Gods <ns0:hi>Law</ns0:hi> in the next clause. And he justly prayeth to God to keep him from Apostasie, Heresie, Idolatry and Superstition, because his own corrupt nature of it self and without Gods grace, was prone to these errours, and not onely Heathens, but many Israelites did fre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quently fall into them.</ns0:note>; and grant me thy law graciously <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Vouchsafe unto me an accurate knowledge and firm belief of thy Word, and that I may con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stantly attend and adhere to it, and govern my self by it in all things.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="30">30 I have chosen the way of truth <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">To wit, thy Word or Law, for my portion and the rule of my worship and whole life.</ns0:note>: thy judgments have I laid <ns0:hi>before me</ns0:hi> 
                        <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>set</ns0:hi> before me, as the Phrase is fully expressed, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 16. 8. as a delightful ob<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ject; or as a mark to aim at; or as a rule to direct me.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="31">31 I have stuck unto thy testimonies <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">I have resolutely persisted in the practice of thy pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cepts in spight of all temptations, reproaches, persecutions and discouragements, to which I was exposed in and for so doing.</ns0:note>: O LORD, put me not to shame <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Either, 1. by giving me over to Apostasie or transgression, which will bring shame. Or rather, 2. by the disappointment of my hopes and confidence in those promi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ses of the blessings of this life, as well as of the next, which thou hast made to the obedient, of which I have made my boast.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="32">32 I will run the way of thy command<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ments <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">I will obey thy precepts with all readiness, fervency and diligence.</ns0:note>, when thou shalt enlarge my heart <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Either, 1. when thou shalt bring me out of my present straits or distresses. This indeed is called <ns0:hi>en<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />larging,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 4. 2. & 18. 36. but never, to my remem<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />brance, <ns0:hi>the enlarging of the heart.</ns0:hi> Or rather, 2. when thou shalt replenish my heart with more wisdom, and love to, and delight in thee and thy Law; for this <ns0:hi>enlargement of heart</ns0:hi> in Scripture is ascribed to wisdom, 1 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 4. 29. and love, 2 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 6. 11. and joy, <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 60. 5. When thou shalt knock off those fetters of remaining corruption, and give me a more noble and generous disposition towards thee, and stablish me <ns0:hi>with thy free Spirit,</ns0:hi> as it is expressed <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 51. 12. Thus <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> both ownes his duty, and asserts the absolute necessi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty of Gods grace to the performance of it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  </ns0:div>
                  <ns0:div type="part">
                     <ns0:head>HE.</ns0:head>
                     <ns0:p n="33">33 Teach me, O LORD, the way of thy sta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tutes, and I shall keep it <ns0:hi>unto</ns0:hi> the end <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>that I may keep it,</ns0:hi> &c. That I may persevere: for Apostasie proceeds from the want of a good understanding.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="34">34 Give me understanding, and I shall keep thy law, yea, I shall observe it with my whole heart.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="35">35 Make me to go <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">By directing my mind into the right way, by inclining my will, and strengthening my resolution.</ns0:note> in the path of thy com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mandments; for therein do I delight <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Forsake not him who delighteth in thee and in thy service: and as thou hast wrought in me to will, work in me also to do.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="36">
                        <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:505" />36 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 141. 4.</ns0:note> Incline my heart unto thy testimonies <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">To the love and practice of them.</ns0:note>, and not to covetousness <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Not to the inor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dinate love and desire of riches. Which particular lust he men<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tions, partly because this lust is most spreading and univer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sal, and there is scarce any man who doth not desire riches ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther for the love of riches, or upon pretence of necessity, or for the service of pride or luxury, or some other lust: partly be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause this lust is most opposite to Gods testimonies, and doth most commonly hinder men from receiving Gods word, and from profiting by it. See <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 13. 22. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 16. 14. and partly because this lust is most pernicious, as being the root of all evil, 1 <ns0:hi>Tim.</ns0:hi> 6. 20. and is most mischievous in Princes and Governors, such as <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> was, and therefore in a special manner forbidden to them, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 18. 21.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="37">37 <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                           <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> make to pass.</ns0:note> Turn away mine eyes from beholding vanity <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">The vain things and lusts of this present evil world, such as riches, honours, pleasures: <ns0:hi>from beholding</ns0:hi> them, to wit, with admiration and inordinate affection: for such a sight of the eyes doth usually affect the heart, and stir up mens lusts and passions. Of which see <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 15. 39. <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 31. 1. <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 4. 25. & 23. 5, 6. <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 5. 28.</ns0:note>: <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> quicken thou me in thy <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ver. 27.</ns0:note> way <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">As I desire that I may be dull and dead in affections to worldly vanities, so, Lord, make me lively and vigorous and servent in thy work and service.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="38">38 Stablish thy word <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Confirm and perform thy promises as concerning the Kingdom, so also for the giving of gracious assistances, di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rections, and comforts to those that fear thee, of which num<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ber I am one.</ns0:note> unto thy servant, who <ns0:hi>is devoted</ns0:hi> to thy fear.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="39">39 Turn away my reproach <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Either, 1. for the shameful disappointment of my hopes and confident boastings concerning the truth and certainty of thy promises: or, 2. for my manifold failings, and particu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />larly for that shameful matter about <ns0:hi>Uriah</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Bathsheba:</ns0:hi> or, 3. for my instability in or Apostasie from thy ways; which in respect of mine own weakness and folly, I have great cause to fear.</ns0:note> which I fear: for thy judgments <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> good <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">This may be a reason either, 1. why he prayed and hoped that God would turn away reproach from him, because Gods word and statutes were good, and therefore it was not fit for any to suffer reproach in and for his diligent observation of them: or, 2. why he feared reproach, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause he had, and feared he might hereafter, transgress those judgments or statutes of God which were and he very well knew to be <ns0:hi>good, i. e.</ns0:hi> just and holy and excellent, and there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore it was a shameful thing to violate them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="40">40 Behold, I have longed after thy pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cepts <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">After a more solid knowledge and constant performance of thy precepts.</ns0:note>: quicken me <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">Do thou preserve and maintain both my natural and spiritual life.</ns0:note> in thy righteousness <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">According to thy justice or faith<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fulness, which obligeth thee to make good thy promises.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  </ns0:div>
                  <ns0:div type="part">
                     <ns0:head>VAU.</ns0:head>
                     <ns0:p n="41">41 Let thy mercies come also unto me <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Let promised mercies be performed to me.</ns0:note>, O LORD; <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> thy salvation according to thy <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ver. 49.</ns0:note> word.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="42">42 <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                           <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> so shall I answer him that reproveth me in a thing.</ns0:note> So shall I have wherewithal to answer him that reproacheth me <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">That cha<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>geth me with folly for my piety and trust in thy promises.</ns0:note>: for I trust in thy word <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>because I trust,</ns0:hi> &c. This was the mat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter of their reproach.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="43">43 And take not the word of truth utterly out of my mouth <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Do not deal so with me, that I shall be altogether asha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />med to mention thy word, which I have so often affirmed to be a word of truth and infallible certainty, of which I have often made my boast.</ns0:note>; for I have hoped in thy judgments <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Either in thy word and promises, or in thy judicial administrations and government of the world, which as it is matter of terrour to the wicked, so it is matter of comfort and hope to me.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="44">44 So shall I keep thy law continually <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">So shall I be obliged and encouraged to the constant and perpetual study and observation of thy Laws.</ns0:note>, for ever and ever.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="45">45 And I will walk <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                           <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> at large.</ns0:note> at liberty <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>I shall walk at large,</ns0:hi> as it is in the margent; I shall be delivered from all my present straits both of the outward and inward man, and enjoy great freedom and comfort in thy ways.</ns0:note>: for I seek thy precepts.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="46">46 I will speak of thy testimonies also before kings <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Who commonly entertain all godly discourses with scorn and contempt.</ns0:note>, and will not be ashamed.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="47">47 And I will delight my self in thy com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mandments <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Whereas other Princes place their delight in the glories and vanities of this world, and the study and practice of Religion is generally irksom and loathsom to them, thy Law shall be my chief delight and recreation.</ns0:note> which I have loved.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="48">48 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Gen. 14. 2<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>, 23. Exod. 6. 8.</ns0:note> My hands also will I lift up <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">To lay hold upon them, to receive and embrace thy precepts and promises by faith and love, and chearfully and vigorously to put them in practice: for as the <ns0:hi>hanging down of the hands</ns0:hi> is a gesture of sloth and listlesness, as 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 15. 7. and elsewhere; so <ns0:hi>the lifting up of the hands</ns0:hi> is the posture of a man entring upon action, as <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 41. 44. 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 20. 21.</ns0:note> unto thy commandments which I have loved: and I will meditate in thy statutes <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">My deepest thoughts, as well as my hands, shall be exer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cised in them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  </ns0:div>
                  <ns0:div type="part">
                     <ns0:head>ZAIN.</ns0:head>
                     <ns0:p n="49">49 Remember the word <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Thy promises.</ns0:note> unto thy servant, upon which thou hast caused me to hope <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">By thy command requiring it of me, and by thy grace working it in me.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="50">50 This <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">To wit, thy word, as is evident both from the forego<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing and following words.</ns0:note> 
                        <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> my comfort in my affliction: for thy word hath quickned me <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Hath preserved my life in mani<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fold dangers, and hath revived and cheared my spirit.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="51">51 The proud have had me greatly in derisi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">For my godliness and trust in thy word, as the follow<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing words imply.</ns0:note>: <ns0:hi>yet</ns0:hi> have I not declined from thy law.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="52">52 I remembred thy judgments of old <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Thy former and ancient dispensations to the children of men in punishing the ungodly, and protecting and deliver<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing thy faithful servants, whose experience is my encourage<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment.</ns0:note>, O LORD, and have comforted my self.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="53">53 Horrour <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">A mixed passion made up of indignation at their per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sons as sinful, and abhorrency of their sins, and dread and sorrow at the consideration of the judgments of God coming upon them.</ns0:note> hath taken hold upon me, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause of the wicked that forsake thy law <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">For the dishonour which they bring to God, the scandal and mischief to others, and their own certain ruine.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="54">54 Thy statutes have been my songs <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">The matter of my songs, my delight and recreation.</ns0:note> in the house of my pilgrimage <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Either, 1. in this present world, which I do not owne for my home, wherein I am a stranger and pilgrim, as all my fathers were, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 39. 13. Comp. <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 47. 9. Or, 2. in mine exile and in the wildernesses and other places where I have been oft forced to wander, when I was banished from all my friends, and from the place of thy Worship, and had no other support or comfort but the remembrance of thy statutes.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="55">
                        <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:505" />55 I have remembred thy Name <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Thy holy Nature and Attributes, thy blessed Word, and thy wonderful Works: all which come under the title of Gods <ns0:hi>Name.</ns0:hi>
                        </ns0:note>, O LORD, in the night <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">When darkness causeth fear in others, I took pleasure in remembring thee: and when others abandon all business, and wholly give themselves up to rest and sleep, my thoughts and affection were working towards thee.</ns0:note>, and have kept thy law <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">This was the fruit of my serious remembrance of thee.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="56">56 This <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">This comfortable and profitable remembrance and con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />templation of thy name and statutes, of which he spoke <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 54, 55.</ns0:note> I had, because I kept thy precepts <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Which if I had wilfully and wickedly broken, the re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />membrance of these things would have been sad and frightful to me, as now it is comfortable, because I kept them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  </ns0:div>
                  <ns0:div type="part">
                     <ns0:head>CHETH.</ns0:head>
                     <ns0:p n="57">57 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                           <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap> 142. 5.</ns0:note> 
                        <ns0:hi>Thou art</ns0:hi> my portion <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Whereas other men place their portion and happiness in worldly things, I have chosen thee for my portion and chief treasure, as he said <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 16. 5. & 73. 26. and thou hast an all-sufficient and an excellent portion for me.</ns0:note>, O LORD, I have said <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">I have not onely purposed it in my own heart, but have professed and owne it before others, and I do not repent of it.</ns0:note>, that I would keep thy words.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="58">58 I intreated thy <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                           <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap> 
                           <ns0:hi>face.</ns0:hi>
                        </ns0:note> favour <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">Thy gracious presence and merciful assistance, as it fol<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lows.</ns0:note> with <ns0:hi>my</ns0:hi> whole heart: be merciful unto me according to thy word.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="59">59 I thought on my ways <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">I seriously considered both my former counsels and cour<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ses, that I might be humbled for my past errours, and might now amend them, and my duty in all my future actions.</ns0:note>, and turned my feet unto thy testimonies <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">And finding that my feet had too often swerved from thy rule, I turned them to it. And although the ways of sinful pleasure and advantage were presented to my mind, yet I rejected them, and turned my self wholly to thy ways.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="60">60 I made haste, and delayed not <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Being fully convinced of the necessity and excellency of obedience, I presently resolved upon it, and immediately put it in execution.</ns0:note> to keep thy commandments.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="61">61 The <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                           <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> bands of the wicked have robbed me <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>made a prey of me:</ns0:hi> done me many injuries, for my respect to thy Law.</ns0:note>: <ns0:hi>but</ns0:hi> I have not forgotten thy law.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="62">62 At midnight I will rise <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Out of my bed to praise thee in a solemn manner; not being contented with those short ejaculations which he might have used lying in his bed.</ns0:note> to give <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                           <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>. 164.</ns0:note> thanks unto thee: because of thy righteous judgments <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">
                           <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Laws, which are so use<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ful to direct and comfort me.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="63">63 I <ns0:hi>am</ns0:hi> 
                        <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                           <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>. 79.</ns0:note> a companion of all <ns0:hi>them</ns0:hi> that fear thee <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Not excepting the poorest and meanest, whose society other Princes disdain.</ns0:note>, and of them that keep thy precepts.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="64">64 The earth, O LORD, is full of thy mer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cy <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Thou dost satisfie the just desires and necessities of all men and all creatures with the fruits of thy goodness.</ns0:note>: teach me thy statutes <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">The generality of other men chiefly desire the blessings of this life; but, Lord, give me thy spiritual blessings, the saving knowledge, love and practice of thy Law.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  </ns0:div>
                  <ns0:div type="part">
                     <ns0:head>TETH.</ns0:head>
                     <ns0:p n="65">65 Thou hast dealt well with thy servant, O LORD, according unto thy word.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="66">66 Teach me <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                           <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>, <ns0:hi>goodness, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                                 <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                              </ns0:gap>, and <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                                 <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                              </ns0:gap>.</ns0:hi> So</ns0:note> good judgment <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Whereby I may rightly discern between truth and fals<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />hood, good or evil, between the mind of God, and my own or others inventions; that so I may be kept from those mi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stakes and errours in which many are involved, that I may truly judge what thy Law requires or permits, and what it forbids. Heb. <ns0:hi>the goodness of taste,</ns0:hi> an experimental sence and relish of Divine things. Comp. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 34. 9.</ns0:note> and know<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ledge <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">A spiri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tual and experimental knowledge. And <ns0:hi>judgment</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>taste</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>knowledge</ns0:hi> may, by an useful figure called Hendiadys, be put for <ns0:hi>judicious</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>solid</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>practical knowledge.</ns0:hi>
                        </ns0:note>: for I have believed thy command<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ments <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">I have believed the Divine authority of them, and the truth and certainty of those promises and threatnings which thou hast annexed to them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="67">67 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ver. 71. and 75.</ns0:note> Before I was afflicted I went astray <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">As men generally do in their prosperity. See <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 32. 15. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 73. 4, 5, 6, &c. <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 1. 32. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 22. 21.</ns0:note>: but now have I kept thy word.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="68">68 Thou <ns0:hi>art</ns0:hi> good <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Gracious and bountiful in thy nature.</ns0:note>, and dost good <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">To all men, both good and bad, <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 5. 45. and in all things, yea even when thou afflictest.</ns0:note>: teach me thy statutes <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Which is the good that I desire above all things.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="69">69 The proud have <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                           <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> sewed a lye upon me.</ns0:note> forged a lie <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">A slander, charging me with hypocrisie towards God, and rebellion against my Prince.</ns0:note> against me: but I will keep thy precepts <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">My practice shall con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fute their calumnies.</ns0:note> with <ns0:hi>my</ns0:hi> whole heart.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="70">70 Their heart is as fat as grease <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">The sence is, either 1. they are stupid and insensible and past feeling, not affected either with the terrours or comforts of Gods word. So the like phrase is used <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 6. 10. comp. with <ns0:hi>Iob.</ns0:hi> 12. 40. or, 2. they prosper exceedingly, and are even glutted with the wealth and comforts of this life.</ns0:note>: <ns0:hi>but</ns0:hi> I de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />light in thy law <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">But I do not envy them their jollity, and I have as much delight in Gods Law, as they have in worldly things.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="71">71 <ns0:hi>It is</ns0:hi> good <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Necessary and greatly beneficial.</ns0:note> for me that I have been afflict<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed, that I might learn thy statutes <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">He repeats what in effect he said before, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 67. partly to intimate the certainty and importance of this truth, and partly because it is a great Paradox to worldly men, who generally esteem afflictions to be evil, yea the worst of evils.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="72">72 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 19. 10. Prov. 8. 11.</ns0:note> The law of thy mouth <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> better unto me <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Not onely thy promises, but even thy precepts, which are so unpleasant and hard to ungodly men, to me they are more desirable and more needful and profitable, because they do not onely give me abundant satisfaction and comfort in this life, but also they conduct me with safety and delight unto that eternal and most blessed life, where gold and silver bear no price.</ns0:note>, than thousands of gold and silver.</ns0:p>
                  </ns0:div>
                  <ns0:div type="part">
                     <ns0:head>IOD.</ns0:head>
                     <ns0:p n="73">73 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Job 10. 8.</ns0:note> Thy hands have made me and fashioned me: give me understanding that I may learn thy commandments <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">I am thy creature, and therefore obliged to serve and obey thee with all my might; which that I may do aright I beg thy instruction or assistance. Or, thou hast made me once, make me a second time, and renew thy decayed image in me, that I may know and serve thee better, and that as I was made by thee, so I may be guided by thy grace to serve and glorifie my Creator.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="74">74 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ver. 79.</ns0:note> They that fear thee, will be glad <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Partly for my sake, of whose innocency and piety they are convinced, and therefore sympathize with me: and partly for their own sakes, both for the encouragement they have by my example to trust in God, and for the manifold benefits, both spiritual and temporal, which they expect from my government.</ns0:note> when they see me <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">To wit, alive and in safety, not<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />withstanding all the force and malice of mine enemies, and advanced to the Kingdom.</ns0:note>: because I have hoped in thy word <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">In thy promise, and have not been disappointed of my hope, which is a great confirmation of their faith and hope in God, that they shall obtain all the good things which God hath promised them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="75">
                        <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:506" />75 I know <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">By the convictions of my own conscience, and by expe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rience.</ns0:note>, O LORD, that thy judgments <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">
                           <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Thy corrections, as the next clause explains this.</ns0:note> 
                        <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> 
                        <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>righte<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ousness.</ns0:hi> Ps. 19. 8.</ns0:note> right, and <ns0:hi>that</ns0:hi> thou in faithfulness <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">In pursuance of thy promises, and in order to my good, that by my afflictions thou mightest purge me from those sins which might provoke thy wrath against me, and prepare me for a better administration, and more lasting and comfortable enjoyment of my Kingdom.</ns0:note> hast afflicted me.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="76">76 Let, I pray thee, thy merciful kindness be <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                           <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> to com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fort me.</ns0:note> for my comfort, according to thy word <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Yet in judgment remember mercy, and give me that comfort and assistance in and that deliverance out of my trou<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bles, which thou hast promised me.</ns0:note> unto thy servant.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="77">77 Let thy tender mercies come unto me, that I may live <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">That I may be preserved from that violent and untimely death which mine enemies design to bring upon me.</ns0:note>: for thy law <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> my delight <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">I humbly beg and expect thy protection, because I am thy faithful servant.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="78">78 Let the proud be ashamed, for they dealt perversly with me <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>they have perverted me,</ns0:hi> either by their calumnies, whereby they have put false and perverse constructions upon all my words and actions: or by endeavouring to overthrow and destroy me, or to turn me out of the way of thy pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cepts.</ns0:note> without a cause, <ns0:hi>but</ns0:hi> I will meditate in thy precepts <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">All their wicked attempts against me shall never drive me from the study and love and practice of thy pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cepts.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="79">79 Let those that fear thee, turn unto me <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Either, 1. turn their eyes to me as a spectacle of Gods wonderful mercy: or rather, 2. turn their hearts and affe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ctions to me, which have been alienated from me, either by the artifices and calumnies of my adversaries, or by my sore and long distresses, which made them prone to think that ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther I had deceived them with false pretences, or that God for my sins had utterly forsaken me. Which doubtless was a very grievous burden to <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> who had a far greater esteem and affection for such persons, than for all other men, and desired above all things to stand right in their opinions.</ns0:note>, and those that have known <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">
                           <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Loved and practised them, as words of knowledge are oft used.</ns0:note> thy testimonies.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="80">80 Let my heart be <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                           <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> persect.</ns0:note> sound <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>persect</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>entire,</ns0:hi> that I may love and obey them sincerely, constantly and universally.</ns0:note> in thy statutes; that I be not ashamed <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">To wit, for my sins, which are the onely just causes of shame, and for the disap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pointment of my hopes following upon them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  </ns0:div>
                  <ns0:div type="part">
                     <ns0:head>CAPH.</ns0:head>
                     <ns0:p n="81">81 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 84. 2.</ns0:note> My soul fainteth <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">With longing desire and earnest expectation and hope deferred, and hitherto disappointed.</ns0:note> for thy salvation: <ns0:hi>but</ns0:hi> I hope in thy word.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="82">82 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ver. 123.</ns0:note> Mine eyes fail <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">With looking hither and thither, and to thee for help.</ns0:note> for thy word, saying, When wilt thou comfort me!</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="83">83 For I am become like a bottle in the smoke <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Hung up in a smoaking chimney. My natural moisture is dried and burnt up, I am withered and deformed and de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />spised, and my case grows worse and worse every day.</ns0:note>: <ns0:hi>yet</ns0:hi> do I not forget thy statutes.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="84">84 How many <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> the days <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Either, 1. the days of my life, as the word <ns0:hi>days</ns0:hi> is com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />monly used <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 6. 3. <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 7. 1, 6. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 39. 5, 6. I have but a little while to live in the world; give me some respite before I die, and help me speedily, otherwise it will be too late: or rather, 2. the days of my misery, as the next clause implies, and as <ns0:hi>days</ns0:hi> are taken <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 37. 13. & 116. 2. and elsewhere. How long, Lord, shall my miseries last? for ever?</ns0:note> of thy servant? when wilt thou execute judgment on them that persecute me?</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="85">85 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 35. 7.</ns0:note> The proud have digged pits for me <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Have sought to destroy me by deceit and treachery, as well as by violence.</ns0:note>, which <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Either, 1. which men have no respect to thy Law, which forbids such things. Or rather, 2. which thing, to wit, to dig pits for me, an innocent and just man, is not agreeable to thy Law, but directly contrary to it.</ns0:note> 
                        <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> not after thy law.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="86">86 All thy commandments <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> 
                        <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                           <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> faithful<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness.</ns0:note> faithful <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">They are in themselves most just and true, and they re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quire justice and faithfulness from men, promising many bles<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sings to those that perform it, and severely forbid all fraud and falseness, threatning grievous punishments to those that use it; and such promises and threatnings are true, and shall certainly be executed.</ns0:note>: they persecute me wrongfully; help thou me.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="87">87 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ver. 109. and 143.</ns0:note> They had almost consumed me upon earth <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">As to my present life and all my happiness upon earth, whereby he implies that his immortal Soul and eternal happi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness in Heaven, of which he speaks, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 16. 11. & 17. 15. and elsewhere, was safe and out of their reach.</ns0:note>: but I forsook not thy precepts.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="88">88 Quicken me after thy loving kindness, so shall I keep <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>and I will keep.</ns0:hi> I will testifie my gratitude to thee by my obedience.</ns0:note> the testimony of thy mouth.</ns0:p>
                  </ns0:div>
                  <ns0:div type="part">
                     <ns0:head>LAMED.</ns0:head>
                     <ns0:p n="89">89 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 89. 2.</ns0:note> For ever, O LORD, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ver. 152. & 160.</ns0:note> thy word is set<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led in heaven <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Although many things happen upon earth which seem contrary to thy word, and at which men take occasion to question the truth of thy word, yet in Heaven it is sure and certainly true. <ns0:hi>In heaven,</ns0:hi> either 1. with thee in thy heaven<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly habitation, or in thy breast: as thy nature is unchangeable, so thy word is infallible. Or rather, 2. in the heavenly bo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dies, which are not subject to those changes and decays which are in this lower world, but constantly continue the same in their substance and order and courses, and this by virtue of that Word of God by which they were made and established in this manner; and therefore Gods word delivered to his people upon earth, which is of the same nature, must needs be of equal certainty and stability. This sence best suits with the following verses, and with other Scriptures wherein the certainty of Gods word is set forth by comparing it with the stability of the Heaven and the Earth, as <ns0:hi>Mat.</ns0:hi> 5. 18. and elsewhere.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="90">90 Thy faithfulness <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> 
                        <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                           <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> to gene<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ration and ge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />neration.</ns0:note> unto all generations <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Every age gives fresh proofs of the truth of thy Word.</ns0:note>: thou hast established the earth, and it <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>standeth<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                           </ns0:hi>
                        </ns0:note> abideth <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">In that place and state in which thou didst establish it. See <ns0:hi>Eccles.</ns0:hi> 1. 4.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="91">91 They <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">The Heaven and the Earth last mentioned.</ns0:note> 
                        <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                           <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> stand.</ns0:note> continue this day according to thine ordinances <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">As thou hast appointed and by virtue of thine appointment.</ns0:note>: for all <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> thy servants <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">All things are subject to thy power and pleasure, and none can resist thy will, or word.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="92">92 Unless thy law <ns0:hi>had been</ns0:hi> my delights, I should then <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">At the very instant; I could not have outlived one stroke of thine afflicting hand.</ns0:note> have perished in mine affliction.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="93">93 I will never forget thy precepts: for with them thou hast quickned me <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Revived and cheared me, when my heart was ready to sink and die within me.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="94">94 I <ns0:hi>am</ns0:hi> thine <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">By Creation and Redemption, and manifold obligations, as also by my own choice and designation. I have devoted my self to thy service, and committed my self to thy care.</ns0:note>, save me: for I have sought thy precepts.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="95">95 The wicked have waited for me to destroy me: <ns0:hi>but</ns0:hi> I will consider thy testimonies <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">As my best comforters and counsellers and defenders against all the assaults and designs of mine enemies.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="96">
                        <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:506" />96 I have seen an end of all perfection <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">I have observed by my experience, that the greatest and most perfect accomplishments and enjoyments in this world, the greatest glory, and riches and power and wisdom are too narrow and short-lived to make men happy.</ns0:note>; <ns0:hi>but</ns0:hi> thy commandment <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">Thy word, one part of it being Synecdochically put for the whole.</ns0:note> 
                        <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> exceeding broad <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>large,</ns0:hi> both for extent, and for continuance: it is useful to all persons in all times and conditions and for all purpose<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap> to inform, direct, quicken, comfort, sanctifie and save men: it is of everlasting truth and efficacy, it will never deceive nor forsake those who trust to it, as all wordly things will, but will make men happy both here and for ever.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="97">97 O how love I thy law <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">O Lord, thou knowest it, and to thee I appeal herein against all the censures and calumnies of mine enemies to the contrary.</ns0:note>! it <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> my medita<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion all the day.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="98">98 Thou, through thy commandments, hast made me wiser than mine enemies <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Because by that means I have thy wisdom to guide me and thy power engaged to protect and save me; which is a more certain and effectual way to obtain my desires and ends than all the policy and craft of mine enemies is to hinder them, as I have found by experience.</ns0:note>: for <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                           <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>eb. <ns0:hi>it is <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                                 <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                              </ns0:gap> for ever. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                                 <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                              </ns0:gap> Gr.</ns0:hi>
                        </ns0:note> they <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> ever with me <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">They are conti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nually before mine eyes, as a rule by which to govern all my actions, whereby I am kept from splitting upon those rocks whereby others are ruined.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="99">99 I have more understanding <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">He speaks not here of notional, but of spiritual and pra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ctical and experimental knowledge.</ns0:note> than all my teachers <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Than all or most (for that general word is oft so understood) of those who taught me formerly, or of the publick teachers in <ns0:hi>Sa<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                                 <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                              </ns0:gap>s</ns0:hi> time; which probably were for the generality of them neither so know<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing, nor so good, as they should have been.</ns0:note>: for thy testimonies <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> my medita<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">The matter of my constant and most diligent study.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="100">100 I understand more <ns0:hi>than</ns0:hi> the ancients: be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause I keep thy precepts <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">By which reason He intimates, that the practice of Reli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gion is the best way to understand it, and that mens vicious hearts and lives are the greatest hinderances of all true and solid knowledge of it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="101">101 I have refrained my feet from every evil way <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>way of evil,</ns0:hi> which either is evil or leads to it, sin and the temptations or occasions of sin.</ns0:note>: that I might keep thy word <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">I did this not for any carnal reasons, as some men abstain from divers sins for their credit or advantage, but out of pure respect to thy Word.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="102">102. I have not departed from thy judgments: for thou <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                           <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap> 26. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note> hast taught me <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">To wit, by thy blessed Spirit, illuminating my mind, and working upon my heart, which other teachers cannot do.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="103">103 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                           <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>. 19. 10. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>. 11.</ns0:note> How sweet are thy words unto my <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                           <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>. <ns0:hi>palate.</ns0:hi>
                        </ns0:note> taste! <ns0:hi>yea, sweeter</ns0:hi> than honey to my mouth <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">The study and obedience of thy words yields me more satisfaction and delight than any worldly men find in their sen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sual pleasures.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="104">104 Through thy precepts I get understand<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">True and useful and powerful knowledge.</ns0:note>: therefore <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Because that discovers to me, as the wickedness, so the folly and mis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />chief of such practices.</ns0:note> 
                        <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                           <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>. 128.</ns0:note> I hate every false way <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Every thing which is contrary to that rule of truth and right, all false doctrine and worship, and all <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap> or vicious courses.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  </ns0:div>
                  <ns0:div type="part">
                     <ns0:head>NUN.</ns0:head>
                     <ns0:p n="105">105 Thy word <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> a <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                           <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>
                           <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                           <ns0:hi>
                              <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                                 <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                              </ns0:gap>andle.</ns0:hi>
                        </ns0:note> lamp unto my feet <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">To direct me in all my doubts and difficulties, to pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />serve from sin and from sin and misery, both which oft come under the name of <ns0:hi>darkness,</ns0:hi> and to comfort me in all my fears and distresses.</ns0:note>, and a light unto my path.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="106">106 I have sworn <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Obliged my self by serious purpose and solemn vow, or by a formal oath, which was not unusual amongst Gods peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple, as 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 15. 15. <ns0:hi>Nehem.</ns0:hi> 10. 29.</ns0:note>, and I will perform <ns0:hi>i<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>
                        </ns0:hi> 
                        <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">I do not repent of it, but by Gods grace I will fulfil it.</ns0:note>, that I will keep <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ver. 144.</ns0:note> thy righteous judgments.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="107">107 I am afflicted very much: quicken me, O LORD, according unto thy word.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="108">108 Accept, I beseech thee, the free-will of<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ferings of my mouth <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Either, 1. those which I have promised with my mouth, though I am not now in a capacity of performing my promi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ses, as being banished from thy house. Or rather, 2. the sacrifices of prayer and praises, which I do freely and fre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />quently offer unto thee; which are called <ns0:hi>Sacrifices,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 50. 15. and <ns0:hi>calves of</ns0:hi> our <ns0:hi>lips, Hos.</ns0:hi> 14. 2.</ns0:note>, O LORD, and teach me thy judgments.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="109">109 My soul is continually in my hand <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Exposed to perpetual and extreme danger, as any pre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cious and frail thing is which a man carrieth openly in his hand, whence it may easily fall or be snatched away by a violent hand. See the same or like phrase <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 12. 3. 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 19. 5. <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 13. 14.</ns0:note>: yet do I not forget thy law.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="110">110 The wicked have laid a snare for me: yet I erred not from thy precepts.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="111">111 Thy testimonies have I taken as an <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Deut. 33. 4.</ns0:note> he<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ritage for ever <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">I have chosen them for my chief portion, from which I will never part.</ns0:note>: for they <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> the rejoicing of my heart.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="112">112 I have inclined my heart <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">As I prayed to thee to incline mine heart to them, a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bove <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 36. so I did not neglect my duty, but chearfully complied with the motions of thy Spirit, and yielded up my mind and heart to the study and practice of them.</ns0:note> 
                        <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                           <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> to do.</ns0:note> to perform thy statutes alway, <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> 
                        <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                           <ns0:hi>Gr.</ns0:hi> for the re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />compence of re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ward.</ns0:note> 
                        <ns0:hi>unto</ns0:hi> the end.</ns0:p>
                  </ns0:div>
                  <ns0:div type="part">
                     <ns0:head>SAMECH.</ns0:head>
                     <ns0:p n="113">113 I hate <ns0:hi>vain</ns0:hi> thoughts <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">This word signifies <ns0:hi>thoughts, Iob</ns0:hi> 4. 13. & 20. 2. or <ns0:hi>opinions,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>Kings</ns0:hi> 18. 21. Which being indifferent to good and evil, is here taken in an evil sence, for vain <ns0:hi>thoughts,</ns0:hi> as we render it, or for thoughts or opinions or devices of men differing from or opposite to Gods Law, as may be gathered from the next clause, where Gods <ns0:hi>Law</ns0:hi> is opposed to these, and as some both Jewish and Christian Expositors understand it. Nor is it unusual in the Hebrew Text for one and the same word to be taken both in a good and an ill sence in several places: whereof we have one instance in a word of the same signification with this, <ns0:hi>mezimmah,</ns0:hi> which signifies a <ns0:hi>thought,</ns0:hi> and is sometimes taken in a good sence, as <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 1. 4. & 3. 8. & 8. 12. & 13. 16. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 51. 11. but elsewhere in a bad sence, as <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 21. 27. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 10. 2, 4. <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 12. 2. & 14. 17. The like hath been observed concerning another Hebrew word of the same or near signification, <ns0:hi>hormah,</ns0:hi> which is taken in a good sence, <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 1. 4. & 13. 16, &c. and in an ill sence, as <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 21. 14. <ns0:hi>Ios.</ns0:hi> 9. 4. <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 5. 13. And the like may be said concer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ning this word also. But the ancient Interpreters understand this word not of things, but of persons, and so it may be un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derstood of men <ns0:hi>that think evil,</ns0:hi> that devise wicked devices, or that have false and evil opinions, opposite to Gods Law, or tending to seduce men from it.</ns0:note>: but thy law do I love.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="114">114 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 91. 1.</ns0:note> Thou <ns0:hi>art</ns0:hi> my hiding place, and my shield: I hope in thy word.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="115">115 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mat. 7. 23.</ns0:note> Depart from me, ye evil doers; for I will keep the commandments of my God <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">And therefore will avoid your society and conversation, lest I should be hindred from that which is good, and drawn to sin by your evil counsel or example.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="116">116 Uphold me according unto thy word, that I may live: and let me not be ashamed of my hope <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>because of my hope,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>confidence</ns0:hi> in thy promises, of the certainty whereof I have oft made my boast before o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thers.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                     <ns0:p n="117">
                        <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:507" />117 Hold thou me up, and I shall be safe: and I will have respect unto thy statutes conti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nually <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">And being freed from those distractions and diversions which my pressing dangers occasion, I will wholly devote my self to the study and practice of thy blessed word.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
